featuredPapers.title: Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation
featuredPapers.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies covering 19,188 prehospital first responders estimated pooled infection prevalence — hepatitis B 6.2%, hepatitis C 1.8%, MRSA colonisation about 4%, and COVID-19 13.6% in unvaccinated staff.
featuredPapers.relevance: 🟢 High — Occupational exposure risk is the same in uncontrolled prehospital environments everywhere — this is the evidence base behind PPE, vaccination and infection-control protocols Australian crews already work under.
featuredPapers.featuredReason: Occupational exposure risk is the same in uncontrolled prehospital environments everywhere — this is the evidence base behind PPE, vaccination and infection-control protocols Australian crews already work under.
featuredPapers.design: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (88 full texts screened, 22 studies included)
featuredPapers.finding: Pooled prevalence: hepatitis B 6.2% (95% CI 4.5–8.2), hepatitis C 1.8% (0.9–2.9), MRSA colonisation ~4% (2.6–5.9), COVID-19 among unvaccinated staff 13.6% (4.8–25.9), falling to 7.3% after excluding high-bias studies
featuredPapers.caveat: Very high heterogeneity across the 22 studies, and the pooled estimates mix paramedics with police and firefighters
featuredPapers.shortTitle: How common are blood-borne infections in first responders
featuredPapers.learningGoal: Understand how occupational exposure risks for blood-borne infections shape my infection prevention and vaccination practice.

featuredPapers.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study
featuredPapers.summary: An Australian pilot randomised simulation of 12 paramedic–ICP pairs found a one-hour airway assistant training course cut median intubation time in a continuously regurgitating airway from 102.5 to 53 seconds.
featuredPapers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Airway management at intubation is core business for crews across Australian services and the assistant role exists on every two-paramedic response — the open question is whether a 12-person manikin result holds on patients.
featuredPapers.featuredReason: Airway management at intubation is core business for crews across Australian services and the assistant role exists on every two-paramedic response — the open question is whether a 12-person manikin result holds on patients.
featuredPapers.n: 12 qualified paramedics in two groups of 6, paired with intensive care paramedics
featuredPapers.finding: Median intubation time 53 s (IQR 19) trained vs 102.5 s (IQR 36) untrained, p = 0.009, very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86); no oesophageal intubations in either group
featuredPapers.caveat: Pilot simulation with 12 participants — no patient outcomes, and the authors call for larger studies
featuredPapers.shortTitle: Airway assistant training halved sim intubation time
featuredPapers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to assist effectively during prehospital intubation in soiled or regurgitating airways.

featuredPapers.title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching
featuredPapers.summary: A Japanese nationwide registry cohort of 7,217 adults with traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found successful prehospital advanced airway management was not significantly associated with better 30-day survival or neurological outcome when resuscitation-time bias was corrected.
featuredPapers.relevance: 🟢 High — Supraglottic airways are standard Australian cardiac arrest care and intubation is an advanced-tier skill in most services, so the question is squarely ours; the physician-free Japanese EMS model resembles ours more than Europe's.
featuredPapers.featuredReason: Supraglottic airways are standard Australian cardiac arrest care and intubation is an advanced-tier skill in most services, so the question is squarely ours; the physician-free Japanese EMS model resembles ours more than Europe's.
featuredPapers.design: Nationwide retrospective registry cohort with time-dependent propensity score sequential matching
featuredPapers.n: 7,217 adults with traumatic OHCA (2,653 received advanced airway management)
featuredPapers.finding: Thirty-day survival 1.8% with advanced airway vs 1.4% matched controls (corrected RD 0.6%, 95% CI −0.1 to 1.2); favourable neurological outcome 0.2% vs 0.4% (corrected RD −0.2%, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.1) — no significant timing-dependent association
featuredPapers.caveat: Observational design with extremely low event rates, so even a real effect could hide in the confidence intervals
featuredPapers.shortTitle: Advanced airway not linked to traumatic arrest survival
featuredPapers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of advanced airway management during traumatic cardiac arrest against prioritising early ventilation and circulation.

featuredPapers.title: Positive pressure ventilation in newborns at birth: a systematic review of recipient characteristics and temporal trends
featuredPapers.summary: This multinational systematic review of 42 studies (1984–2024) on positive pressure ventilation (PPV) at birth found PPV incidence of 3.0%–8.0% in population-based studies excluding CPAP, with higher rates in preterm infants, rising overall and facemask PPV over time, and stable or declining tracheal-tube PPV.
featuredPapers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — PPV at birth is a core paramedic skill for births attended in the prehospital setting; understanding typical incidence, gestational-age patterns and reporting gaps can inform Australian practice expectations and documentation standards, though most included data come from hospital birthing settings rather than prehospital care.
featuredPapers.featuredReason: PPV at birth is a core paramedic skill for births attended in the prehospital setting; understanding typical incidence, gestational-age patterns and reporting gaps can inform Australian practice expectations and documentation standards, though most included data come from hospital birthing settings rather than prehospital care.
featuredPapers.n: 42 studies from 34 countries, 269 to 10,696,831 livebirths per study
featuredPapers.finding: PPV incidence 3.0%–8.0% in nine population-based/large multicentre studies excluding CPAP; rates much higher among very and extremely preterm infants; overall and facemask PPV increasing over time while tracheal-tube PPV was stable or declining; lower incidence in low-resource and lower-level birthing centres; few studies reported indications or timing of PPV initiation.
featuredPapers.caveat: Marked heterogeneity in CPAP distinction, interface definitions and eligibility criteria precluded meta-analysis, and reporting of indications and timing was limited and inconsistent.
featuredPapers.shortTitle: Systematic review of newborn PPV at birth
featuredPapers.learningGoal: Recognise which newborns at birth are most likely to need positive pressure ventilation and how practice patterns are changing.

featuredPapers.title: Association Between Capnographic Changes During Pulse Checks of Varying Durations and Clinical Outcomes During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Multicenter Study From Türkiye (CaPTuRe)
featuredPapers.summary: A 252-patient quasi-randomised multicentre study in Türkiye found pulse checks completed within 5 seconds were associated with roughly double the ROSC rate of checks lasting 6–10 seconds (36.3% vs 19.5%, OR 2.39), alongside better capnographic dynamics.
featuredPapers.relevance: 🟢 High — Pulse-check duration is something every rescuer on every arrest controls, wherever they work, and capnography-guided CPR quality is standard monitoring practice.
featuredPapers.featuredReason: Pulse-check duration is something every rescuer on every arrest controls, wherever they work, and capnography-guided CPR quality is standard monitoring practice.
featuredPapers.n: 252 cardiac arrest patients (124 with ≤5-second checks, 128 with 6–10-second checks)
featuredPapers.finding: Shorter pulse checks were linked to higher ROSC (36.3% vs 19.5%; OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.35–4.24) and more favourable ETCO2 loss and recovery patterns
featuredPapers.caveat: Quasi-randomised, not truly randomised, so healthier arrests may have had quicker checks; the abstract doesn't say whether arrests were in or out of hospital
featuredPapers.shortTitle: Shorter pulse checks linked to more ROSC
featuredPapers.learningGoal: Improve my technique for keeping pulse checks brief during cardiac arrest resuscitation while interpreting capnography trends.

funFacts.fact: Adrenaline's been thrown into cardiac arrests since 1906, but it didn't become standard CPR gear until the 1960s — meaning for over fifty years, we just sort of... hoped for the best.
VF is the most common initial rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — and survival drops roughly 10% for every single minute defibrillation is delayed. Every minute. Not exaggerating.

The first recorded mouth-to-mouth was around 800 BC — the biblical Elisha breathing life back into a child. Modern CPR didn't come together until 1960. So for about 2,800 years, we just... didn't have a plan.
Your body contains roughly 96,000 kilometres of blood vessels. That's enough to wrap around the Earth more than twice. You're basically a walking tube map.

Atropine got the boot from the cardiac arrest algorithm in 2010 after evidence showed it did precisely nothing for PEA or asystole. Still lifesaving for bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning though — just don't reach for it in a flatline.

The LUCAS device hammers away at exactly 102 compressions per minute and 5 cm depth, every single time. No fatigue, no drift, no arguments about whether you're pushing hard enough. The machine doesn't have an ego.

Tension pneumothorax doesn't just collapse a lung — the mediastinum shifts and kinks the vena cava, which is what actually kills the patient. The collapsed lung is almost a sideshow compared to obliterating venous return.

Glucagon treats severe beta-blocker overdose by sneaking in the back door — it activates adenylate cyclase through its own receptor, completely bypassing the blocked beta receptors. It's the pharmacological equivalent of going around the obstacle.

The cricothyroid membrane is roughly 10mm tall and 9mm wide in adults — just enough for a 6mm tube. It's the narrowest window into the airway, but when you're in a 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' nightmare, it's the only window that matters.

The earliest ambulance service on record was run by the Order of St John during the First Crusade in 1099 — carts dragging wounded knights to treatment tents. Nearly a thousand years later, we've upgraded from carts, but the job's the same.

Naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes — shorter than most opioids. So your freshly reversed patient can drift back into respiratory depression while you're busy feeling like a hero. Observation isn't optional.

Kussmaul breathing — those deep, desperate, rapid respirations in DKA — is your patient literally trying to breathe their way out of a metabolic acidosis by blowing off CO2. Respiratory compensation for a metabolic catastrophe.
At normal heart rates, the QT interval should be less than half the R-R interval. A corrected QT over 500ms? That's your ticket to torsades de pointes — a rhythm as dangerous as it sounds.

Modern paramedicine traces its roots to Freedom House in Pittsburgh, 1967 — where unemployed Black men and women were trained as America's first paramedics. They were so good that the city's white establishment tried to shut them down. They didn't succeed.

Intranasal fentanyl hits effective plasma levels in under 10 minutes without needing a cannula. For paediatric and burns patients — where getting access is its own special hell — it's a genuine game-changer.

Neurogenic shock from a spinal cord injury above T6 gives you hypotension with bradycardia — the mirror opposite of hypovolaemic shock. Your patient's blood pressure is in the basement but their heart's barely trying. Sympathetic tone: gone.

The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left — which is why ETTs and aspirated vomit both seem to prefer it. The right lung takes the hit more often than the left. No one said anatomy was fair.

Targeted Temperature Management (the artist formerly known as therapeutic hypothermia) was inspired by cases from the 1950s, but it took until the 2002 HACA trial to convince everyone that cooling dead-ish patients actually worked.

Amiodarone is about 37% iodine by weight — roughly 75mg of iodine per 200mg dose. A single loading dose can trigger both hyper- and hypothyroidism. It's an antiarrhythmic that moonlights as an endocrine wrecking ball.

The Star of Life on ambulances was designed by the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in 1973. The six points represent detection, reporting, response, on-scene care, care in transit, and transfer to definitive care — the full journey from disaster to survival.

In anaphylaxis, massive vasodilation can expand vascular capacity by up to 30%. The patient hasn't lost blood — their pipes just got dramatically bigger. That's why adrenaline (a vasoconstrictor) is the answer, not just drowning them in fluids.

Wellens' syndrome — biphasic or deeply inverted T waves in V2-V3 — means critical proximal LAD stenosis. These patients need the cath lab urgently. Putting them on a stress test can literally kill them. Don't.

IM adrenaline works in seconds because muscle is riddled with capillaries that suck it straight into circulation. Subcutaneous is slower and less effective — which is why the anterolateral thigh is the gold standard. More blood flow, faster rescue.

Epidural space: fat, veins, lymphatics — target for epidurals. Subarachnoid space: cerebrospinal fluid — target for spinals. The difference between them is one membrane: the dura mater. One membrane. Two completely different procedures.

PARAMEDIC2 showed adrenaline boosted survival to discharge from 2.3% to 3.2% in OHCA — a modest but statistically significant improvement. Survivors had higher rates of severe neurological impairment. We're saving more people, but not all of them are getting back the person they were.

Urban Australian ambulance response averages 8 to 10 minutes. In rural and remote areas, it can blow past 30 minutes — which is why community first-responder programs aren't a nice-to-have, they're essential.

Ketamine is a dissociative anaesthetic that preserves respiratory drive and gag reflex at typical doses — making it one of the safest RSI induction agents in the prehospital toolbox. It keeps breathing while everything else stops.

In hypovolaemic shock, the body throws skin, kidneys, and gut under the bus to keep the heart and brain perfused. By the time hypotension shows up, the patient's already lost 30 to 40% of their blood volume. The map is not the territory.

Sgarbossa criteria help you spot an MI hiding behind a LBBB — because standard STEMI criteria are basically useless when the conduction system's already doing its own thing. Concordant ST changes or wildly discordant STE >5mm are your clues.

HEMS cruises at 120 to 150 knots and can slash transport times dramatically — but the benefit is real only for time-critical cases where ground transport would exceed 30 minutes. Otherwise you've just got a very expensive, very noisy ambulance.

Adrenaline 1:1000 is 1mg per mL (for IM use). Adrenaline 1:10000 is 0.1mg per mL (for IV). Mix them up and you can cause a fatal intracerebral haemorrhage. This is not a drug that forgives carelessness.
Cushing's triad — hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing — is your brain's last-ditch alarm bell before herniation. If you spot it, you're already late to the party. Like, really late.
In cardiac arrest, the femoral pulse is your go-to — central pulses persist longer than peripheral ones. Palpate at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament. If you can't feel it, they don't have one.

Cardiac arrest has three phases: electrical (0 to 4 min, defib works best), circulatory (4 to 10 min, do CPR first then defib), and metabolic (>10 min, prognosis tanks). Timing isn't everything — it's the only thing.

GTN doesn't 'open blocked arteries' — it works mostly by venodilation, dropping preload and reducing the heart's workload. It's not fixing the problem, it's making the problem more survivable until someone with a catheter can.

UK paramedic practitioners trained in alternate care pathways can safely manage many patients without transport — cutting ED burden by up to 50% in some trials. Turns out not everyone needs a hospital. They just need someone who knows what they're doing.

At high altitude, hypoxia triggers cerebral vasodilation, which increases intracranial pressure. Diamox works by inducing a metabolic acidosis that forces you to breathe harder. It's hacky, but it works.

The LAD supplies roughly half the left ventricle's myocardium. Occlusion proximal to the first septal branch is why anterior STEMIs carry such brutal mortality — that's an enormous chunk of heart muscle starving.

Metaraminol is a pure alpha-agonist vasopressor that doesn't need a central line — you can run it through a peripheral cannula. But its slower onset means you'd better anticipate the blood pressure drop, not chase it.

C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive. A spinal cord injury above C3 paralyses the diaphragm entirely — these patients are immediately ventilator-dependent. It's one of the few injuries where the first seconds truly determine everything.

The log roll was gospel for spinal immobilisation for decades — but recent evidence says manual in-line stabilisation with a scoop stretcher actually causes less spinal movement. Sometimes the thing we've done forever is the wrong thing.

Crush injury releases myoglobin into circulation, which clogs renal tubules like mud in a pipe. The crush syndrome triad — hypovolaemia, hyperkalaemia, myoglobinuria — is why you hammer these patients with fluids early. The kidneys won't thank you if you wait.

Ondansetron revolutionised antiemetics because it blocks 5-HT3 receptors without the sedation or dystonic reactions of older drugs like metoclopramide. No one misses watching a patient's eyes roll back after an anti-nausea injection.

Since 2018, Australian paramedics have been nationally regulated under the Paramedicine Board of Australia — making paramedicine a formally recognised health profession. We're not just 'ambulance drivers' anymore. We were never just ambulance drivers.

The P-wave looks like one simple bump, but the left atrium depolarises slightly after the right. A notched or wide P-wave ('P mitrale') suggests left atrial enlargement — usually from mitral valve disease. The ECG sees things your eyes can't.

Sodium bicarb in TCA overdose alkalinises the serum, which reduces the fraction of free drug that binds to cardiac sodium channels. The wide QRS narrows within minutes. It's one of those rare antidotes that works so dramatically you can almost watch it happen.

The Fick principle says cardiac output equals oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference. Translation: the only levers for boosting oxygen delivery are heart rate and stroke volume. That's it. Two dials.

The radial nerve runs through the spiral groove of the humerus — so mid-shaft fractures commonly nail it, causing wrist drop. Always test wrist extension before and after you splint. Miss this and you'll hear about it from the orthopods.

Traumatic cardiac arrest is a different beast — you address reversible causes (hypovolaemia, tension pneumo, tamponade) before or alongside CPR. Standard ALS alone has near-zero survival here. The algorithm that saves lives in medical arrest won't save this one.

Midazolam is water-soluble at acidic pH but turns lipophilic at body pH — so it crosses the blood-brain barrier almost instantly after injection. That's why it's the fastest benzodiazepine for stopping seizures. Chemistry doing the heavy lifting.

The word 'ambulance' comes from the Latin 'ambulare' — to walk or move. The earliest documented ambulance was a horse-drawn wagon used by Spanish forces during the siege of Malaga in the 1480s. We've been moving the wounded for over 500 years.

Sepsis triggers a cytokine storm that causes vasodilation AND capillary leak simultaneously. Fluid pours into the interstitial space — 'third spacing.' The patient looks swollen but is dry on the inside. It's a cruel trick.

Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the left atrial appendage, where it clots. The CHA2DS2-VASc score decides who needs anticoagulation — score 2 or more for men, 3 or more for women. Miss this and you're one embolic stroke away from a very bad day.

Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator derived from atropine, but tweaked so it barely absorbs systemically. It relaxes airways without the tachycardia, dry mouth, and blurred vision. Pharmacology at its cleverest.

CPR only generates about 20 to 30% of normal cardiac output. Cardiocerebral resuscitation — continuous compressions without breaths for the first minutes of witnessed VF — may deliver better cerebral perfusion. Less Interruption, more pump.

The lethal triad of trauma — hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy — is a vicious cycle where each worsens the others. Warm fluids, early haemorrhage control, damage control surgery. Break the triangle or the patient breaks.

Magnesium sulphate — not a benzo — is first-line for eclamptic seizures. It antagonises calcium at NMDA receptors and causes cerebral vasodilation. It halves seizure risk compared to diazepam. In eclampsia, reach for the magnesium.

NSW flight and rescue paramedics train in aeromedical retrieval, winch operations, and wilderness medicine. NSW aeromedical services alone respond to over 7,000 missions a year. Most of those jobs don't have a road in sight.

Brugada syndrome is a sodium channelopathy that causes VF in young, otherwise perfectly healthy people. The ECG shows a pseudo-RBBB pattern with coved ST elevation in V1-V3. It's one of the reasons young people drop dead with no warning.
Adenosine's half-life is under 10 seconds — by the time you've finished pushing it, your body's already destroyed it. Hence the 'push, flush, pray' technique we all know and love.

Spinal shock wipes out all cord function below the lesion — flaccid paralysis, areflexia, nothing. Reflexes crawl back within 24 to 72 hours. The return of the bulbocavernosus reflex is the official 'spinal shock is over' signal.

Carotid sinus baroreceptors at the bifurcation respond to stretch — massage them and vagal tone spikes, slowing AV conduction. Handy for SVT termination, risky if they've got carotid stenosis. Feel before you rub.

ECMO during cardiac arrest (ECPR) has shown 30 to 50% survival in selected patients at specialised centres — massively better than conventional CPR for refractory VF/VT. The catch: you need the team, the gear, and the patient in the right place at the right time.

Calcium chloride packs three times more elemental calcium per gram than calcium gluconate. For hyperkalaemia-induced arrhythmias, it's the one you want — but it needs a central or big-bore peripheral line. Tissue extravasation is not pretty.

The 'golden hour' was coined by R Adams Cowley in the 1960s — the idea that trauma patients do best if they reach definitive care within 60 minutes. Modern evidence says it's more like 'golden minutes' for the actively bleeding. The clock starts before you arrive.

The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve shifts right — releasing more oxygen — with heat, acid, CO2, and 2,3-DPG. Active tissues produce all of these. It's a self-regulating system so elegant it almost looks designed.

De Winter T-waves — upsloping ST depression with tall peaked T waves across V1-V6 — are a STEMI equivalent for acute proximal LAD occlusion. They show up in about 2% of LAD occlusions and get missed all the time.

Tranexamic acid stops clots from breaking down by blocking plasminogen-to-plasmin conversion. The CRASH-2 trial showed it saves lives in trauma haemorrhage — but only if given within 3 hours. After that, the benefit vanishes. The clock is merciless.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch before heading up to the larynx — which means an aortic aneurysm or mediastinal mass can compress it and cause hoarseness. Sometimes the first sign of a thoracic catastrophe is a voice change.

End-tidal CO2 is the most reliable prognostic indicator during cardiac arrest. An ETCO2 below 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of CPR strongly predicts non-survival. It's the closest thing to a crystal ball we have.

In status epilepticus, the longer the seizure runs, the harder it is to stop — GABA receptors retreat inward while glutamate receptors multiply. The brain literally rewires itself to stay excited. Early benzos aren't just best practice, they're fighting a closing window.

Salbutamol drives potassium into cells by stimulating Na+/K+-ATPase. Throw enough nebs at an asthma exacerbation and serum potassium can tank to dangerous levels. The patient's breathing better — but their heart's in trouble.

The first defibrillator used on a human was in 1947 — Claude Beck, open-chest, on a 14-year-old boy during surgery. Closed-chest defibrillation didn't arrive until 1956. For nearly a decade, you had to crack the chest to shock the heart.

The Osborn wave — a little notch at the J-point — shows up in hypothermia, hypercalcaemia, and some genetic conditions. In hypothermia, the bigger the wave, the colder the patient. It's the ECG's built-in thermometer.

Flumazenil reverses benzo sedation by kicking benzodiazepines off the GABA-A receptor. In chronic users, this can trigger seizures — which is why it's handled with extreme caution prehospitally. The cure can be worse than the condition.

Type A aortic dissection (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with mortality climbing 1 to 2% per hour. Type B (descending only) is usually managed medically unless it ruptures or cuts off blood flow somewhere critical.

The chain of survival — early access, early CPR, early defibrillation, early advanced care — was introduced by the AHA in 1991. A fifth link, post-cardiac arrest care, was added in 2010. Surviving the arrest is just the first half.

Droperidol got an FDA black box in 2001 for QT prolongation — but the doses that caused problems were far higher than the 1.25 to 2.5mg used for nausea and agitation. Many toxicologists reckon the warning was a massive overreaction that scared everyone off a useful drug.

Australia's 000 emergency number launched in 1961. Before that, you just dialled your local police, fire, or ambulance station directly. 000 was chosen because '0' was the easiest digit to find on a rotary phone in the dark. Practicality over glamour.

Pulse pressure narrows in cardiac tamponade because pericardial fluid strangles diastolic filling — stroke volume tanks while vasoconstriction pushes diastolic pressure up. A pulse pressure under 25 mmHg? That's your red flag waving furiously.

Electrical alternans — the QRS amplitude bouncing up and down beat to beat — means the heart is literally swinging inside a fluid-filled pericardial sac. The ECG is showing you a heart doing loop-the-loops.

Paracetamol's mechanism is still debated — probably COX inhibition in the CNS where peroxide tone is low. That selectivity is why it kills pain and fever without gutting your stomach lining. A drug we've used for over a century and we're still not entirely sure how it works.

Double sequential defibrillation — two defibs firing at once — was a desperate move for refractory VF. The 2023 PARAMEDIC-DS trial found no survival benefit. Turns out sometimes the answer is 'more electricity' and sometimes it isn't.

The rule of nines for burns only works for adults. Kids have proportionally giant heads (up to 18% BSA in infants) and smaller legs. Use the Lund-Browder chart or you'll get the burn area badly wrong.

Hydroxocobalamin for cyanide poisoning turns the patient's skin and urine bright red. It works by binding cyanide to form cyanocobalamin — vitamin B12 — which the kidneys just excrete. You're literally turning poison into a vitamin.

NSW Ambulance's Special Operations Team covers urban search and rescue, hazmat, and tactical medicine. They were hammered during the 2019 to 2020 Black Summer bushfires — one of the biggest deployments in the service's history.

Takotsubo cardiomyopathy — broken heart syndrome — looks exactly like a STEMI with ST elevation and troponin rise. But the coronaries are clean. The apex balloons out from catecholamine stunning, usually triggered by severe emotional stress. The heart can literally break.

Hyperkalaemia progresses from peaked T-waves to widened QRS to a sine-wave pattern to asystole. The dialysis patient who missed their session and has a K+ over 6.5? That's a 'treat right now' emergency, not a 'monitor and see' situation.

Methanol and ethanol compete for the same enzyme — alcohol dehydrogenase — but methanol produces formic acid, which causes blindness. Fomepizole blocks the enzyme entirely, giving the kidneys time to excrete methanol unchanged. We block the poison by blocking its metabolism.

The Circle of Willis is supposed to provide collateral cerebral circulation — but it's anatomically complete in only about 20% of people. The other 80% have variations that leave some brain regions with less backup. When a stroke hits, luck matters.

Resuscitative thoracotomy for penetrating traumatic cardiac arrest can achieve survival up to 20% — but only if the patient had signs of life at some point during transport. No signs of life? The outcome is essentially zero.

The Bohr effect: more CO2 and lower pH in active tissues makes haemoglobin release more oxygen exactly where it's needed. It's one of the body's most elegant feedback loops — the harder a tissue works, the more oxygen it automatically gets.

Rocuronium is overtaking suxamethonium for RSI because it doesn't carry the hyperkalaemia risk in burns, crush injuries, and neurological conditions. Sugammadex can reverse it — if you can get your hands on it prehospitally in Australia.

The left main coronary artery — the 'widow-maker' — supplies such a massive territory that occlusion causes widespread ST elevation across most leads with reciprocal changes inferiorly. If this one goes, a huge chunk of heart muscle dies in minutes.

Australia's first paramedic program started at Charles Sturt University in 1995. Before that, ambulance officers were trained through in-service apprenticeships. We went from 'learn on the job' to university degrees in one leap.

The first blood transfusion on record was in 1667 — between a man and a sheep. It went about as well as you'd expect. Jean-Baptiste Denys, the doctor responsible, was eventually charged with murder. He was acquitted, but they stopped doing sheep transfusions.

In 2003, climber Aron Ralston amputated his own arm with a blunt pocketknife after being trapped by a boulder for five days. He then rappeled down a cliff one-armed and hiked out. He didn't pass out. He didn't bleed to death. The human body's stress response is absolutely terrifying when it works properly.

Your stomach lining replaces itself every 3 to 4 days. Any slower and your own gastric acid would digest your stomach from the inside. Your body is in a constant race against itself — and it wins, most of the time.

The longest survived cardiac arrest without CPR was around 2 hours — in deep hypothermia. The cold slowed metabolism enough that the brain survived. It's the principle behind ECPR and targeted temperature management, taken to its extreme.

In WWI, medics used sphagnum moss as wound dressings because it's naturally antiseptic — it can hold up to 20 times its weight in fluid and has a pH that inhibits bacterial growth. It actually worked better than cotton. Nature had the answer the whole time.

In 1921, a surgeon named Evan O'Neill Kane operated on himself — removing his own appendix under local anaesthetic — to prove it could be done. He reportedly leaned up during the procedure to watch. He recovered fine and went back to work.

The first successful tracheostomy on a human was probably performed by Antonio Musa Brasavola in 1546 on a patient with an airway obstruction from tonsillar abscess. The operation had been described for centuries but most doctors considered it essentially a death sentence.

Your body produces about 25 million new cells per second. By the time you finish reading this fact, you've made roughly 75 million. Most of those are red blood cells — your bone marrow is a 24/7 factory that never shuts down.

There's a documented case of a patient sneezing their way into an MI — the vasovagal response to a particularly violent sneeze triggered enough bradycardia and hypotension to cause coronary hypoperfusion. One sneeze. One heart attack.

Rigor mortis sets in because ATP depletion locks myosin heads onto actin filaments — the muscles literally can't let go. It starts in the small muscles (jaw, face) and spreads. The body isn't stiffening; the muscles are frozen mid-contraction.

In the 1800s, doctors treated 'hysteria' in women with pelvic massage — basically bringing them to orgasm. When their hands got tired, they invented the vibrator. The world's first electromechanical vibrator was a medical device.

Bee venom (melittin) is being studied as a potential treatment for arthritis and even some cancers. It punches holes in cell membranes — which sounds bad, but if you point it at cancer cells, it's actually useful. The ancients who used bee stings therapeutically weren't entirely wrong.

In 1999, a Swedish radiologist named Anna Bågenholm fell into a frozen stream and was trapped under ice for 80 minutes. Her core temperature dropped to 13.7 degrees Celsius. She survived with no lasting brain damage. The coldest surviving human on record.

The average person produces enough saliva in a lifetime to fill two swimming pools. Saliva contains histatins — antimicrobial peptides that can kill fungi and bacteria. Your spit is genuinely medicinal.

Ancient Egyptians used honey on wounds — and it actually works. Honey is hyperosmolar, produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide, and has a low pH that inhibits bacterial growth. Medical-grade honey dressings are still used in wound care today.

In the 19th century, arsenic was sold as a health tonic. 'Fowler's solution' — potassium arsenite — was prescribed for everything from asthma to malaria. Patients developed a tolerance and arsenic-eaters were a real thing. The dose makes the poison, apparently.

Your nose can remember 50,000 different scents. The olfactory bulb has a direct line to the amygdala and hippocampus — which is why smells trigger memories and emotions more powerfully than any other sense. It's a straight wire to the feeling brain.

In 1822, a fur trapper named Alexis St Martin sustained a gunshot wound to the stomach that healed with a permanent fistula — a hole straight into his stomach. His doctor, William Beaumont, used it to study digestion in a living human for years, literally watching food digest through the hole.

Your skeleton replaces itself completely about every 10 years through continuous remodelling. The bone you have now is not the same bone you had a decade ago. You're wearing a whole new skeleton and didn't even notice.

In the 1940s, lobotomies were performed with an ice pick through the eye socket — hammered through the thin bone and waggled to sever frontal lobe connections. The inventor, Walter Freeman, drove around the US in a van he called the 'lobotomobile' performing them. Over 40,000 Americans were lobotomised.

A human head remains conscious for about 10 to 15 seconds after decapitation — long enough for the eyes to track movement and possibly even register what's happened. This was observed during the French Revolution and confirmed by more recent animal studies. Gruesome, but physiologically fascinating.

The antibiotic streptomycin was discovered in soil bacteria from heavily manured compost. The high-yield strain of penicillin used for mass production came from mould on a cantaloupe in a Peoria market — far more productive than Fleming's original lab contaminant. Some of medicine's greatest breakthroughs came from literal garbage.

In medieval Europe, wound treatment sometimes involved applying mouldy bread. This wasn't entirely crazy — some bread moulds produce antibiotics. They had no idea why it sometimes worked, but they were onto something.

There's a condition called auto-brewery syndrome where gut fungi ferment carbohydrates into ethanol. People with it can get genuinely drunk just from eating carbs. They blow positive on breathalysers without touching a drop.

The plasticiser DEHP, once common in IV bags and giving sets, was found to leach into fluids — especially lipophilic drugs. It's also an endocrine disruptor. PVC IV equipment has quietly been phased out in many countries for exactly this reason.

In 1961, a surgeon named Leonid Rogozov was stationed at a remote Antarctic base when his appendix burst. With no other doctor for thousands of kilometres, he operated on himself — removing his own appendix under local anaesthetic while his non-medical colleagues handed him instruments. He recovered fully.

Your liver can regenerate from just 25% of its tissue. It's the only internal organ that can do this. Hepatocytes divide until the original mass is restored, then they just... stop. Nobody's entirely sure how they know when to stop.

Maggot therapy is still used in modern wound care. Sterile maggots of the green bottle fly are placed in wounds where they eat dead tissue, secrete antimicrobial compounds, and stimulate healing. Medicare covers it in the US. It's gross. It works.

During the American Civil War, wounded soldiers reported that glowing wounds healed faster and with less infection. The 'Angel's Glow' was likely caused by Photorhabdus luminescens — bioluminescent bacteria that produce antibiotics and kill other bacteria. The soldiers weren't hallucinating.

You can survive without your spleen, gallbladder, appendix, colon, one kidney, most of your liver, one lung, your stomach, your bladder, and most of your intestines. The human body is absurdly modular. You just need your brain, heart, and at least one functioning kidney.

In 2007, a woman named Jennifer Strange died from water intoxication after drinking nearly 7.5 litres of water in a radio station contest called 'Hold Your Wee for a Wii.' Hyponatraemia can kill just as dead as hypernatraemia — water isn't always benign.

There are documented cases of people being struck by lightning and developing sudden new skills or personality changes — called 'acquired savant syndrome.' One man was hit by lightning and suddenly became a piano prodigy. Nobody knows how.

In 1844, a dentist named Horace Wells pioneered the use of nitrous oxide as an anaesthetic — after witnessing a laughing gas demonstration where someone injured themselves without feeling pain. He later became addicted to chloroform and committed suicide in prison in 1848. Anaesthesia's founding story is genuinely tragic.

Your gut produces about 95% of your body's serotonin — not your brain. The enteric nervous system is so complex it's sometimes called the 'second brain.' When you have a gut feeling, it's not entirely a metaphor.

In the 16th century, Paracelsus dosed patients with mercury to treat syphilis. It sort of worked — mercury does kill the bacteria — but it also caused terrible toxicity. Patients died from the cure almost as often as the disease.

CPR was developed in part from observations of asphyxiated dogs. In the 1950s, researchers at Johns Hopkins found that external chest compressions could maintain circulation. Before that, the standard response to cardiac arrest was essentially to open the chest and squeeze the heart by hand.

In the 18th century, resuscitation attempts for drowning victims included rectal tobacco smoke enemas. The Royal Humane Society kept resuscitation kits along the Thames that included bellows for blowing smoke up the rectum. The phrase 'blowing smoke up your arse' comes from literal medical practice.

There's a documented phenomenon called 'cognitive skew' where experienced clinicians become less accurate at reading ECGs as they gain experience — not because they forget, but because they start pattern-matching instead of reading systematically. Experience can be its own trap.

In 2013, surgeons in Pakistan removed a bullet from a man's heart that had been sitting there for 12 years. He'd been shot in the chest at age 16 and didn't know the bullet was lodged in his myocardium. He found out when he went to hospital with chest pain over a decade later.

A woman named December Levy (yes, really) went to hospital with a headache and was found to have a nail in her brain — from an incident where a nail gun had been fired near her a year earlier. She didn't remember it. The brain has no pain receptors. She literally never felt it go in.

In 2015, a man in China went to hospital with a headache and doctors found he'd been living with a knife blade embedded in his head for four years after a robbery. The knife had been stuck in his skull so long that the tissue had grown around it.

Digoxin comes from the foxglove plant — digitalis. William Withering published his findings on it in 1785 after learning about it from a folk herbalist. One of modern cardiology's most important drugs came from a witch's remedy.

Aspirin was derived from willow bark, which Hippocrates recommended for pain in 400 BC. The synthetic version (acetylsalicylic acid) was developed by Bayer in 1897. A drug that old and still on the cardiac guidelines. Not many medications have that kind of staying power.

Warfarin was originally developed as rat poison in the 1940s. It started being used in humans after a US army recruit attempted suicide by eating rat poison and survived — which made researchers think, 'hang on, maybe we can control the dose.' One of pharmacology's weirder origin stories.

Viagra was discovered by accident — researchers at Pfizer were testing sildenafil for angina when trial participants reported an unexpected side effect. A very specific, very marketable side effect. Sometimes the best discoveries are the ones you weren't looking for.

Insulin was first extracted from dogs' pancreases by Banting and Best in 1921. Before that, type 1 diabetes was a death sentence — patients survived on starvation diets for months at most. The first human treated was a 14-year-old boy who'd been given weeks to live.

The first ever antibiotic — Salvarsan — was developed in 1909 to treat syphilis. It was an arsenic compound. It worked, mostly. But the side effects were brutal. The name literally means 'that which saves by arsenic.' Medicine was a contact sport back then.

Lidocaine was synthesised in 1943 and originally called 'xylocaine' — from the Greek 'xylon' meaning wood, because one of the starting materials came from wood pulp. The local anaesthetic that's in every ED and ambulance on Earth has a name that means 'wood thing.'

Prednisone and other corticosteroids were developed after a rheumatoid arthritis patient at the Mayo Clinic dramatically improved after being given cortisone in 1948. The 'miracle' drug turned out to have a dark side — long-term use causes osteoporosis, diabetes, immunosuppression, and adrenal suppression.

Clozapine — one of the most effective antipsychotics — can cause agranulocytosis in about 1% of patients, which is potentially fatal. It requires regular blood monitoring. But for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, nothing else comes close. The best drug is sometimes the most dangerous one.

Metformin comes from the French lilac plant (Galega officinalis), which was used to treat 'sweet urine' in medieval Europe. The active compound, galegine, was identified in the early 1900s. A diabetes drug with roots in medieval herbalism.

Suxamethonium can trigger malignant hyperthermia — a rare but catastrophic reaction where the body's temperature rockets upward and muscles break down. It kills fast if untreated. Dantrolene is the antidote. If you're giving sux, you'd better know where the dantrolene is.

Naloxone was patented in 1961. Before that, opioid overdose was essentially untreatable in the field. The drug has saved hundreds of thousands of lives and is now carried by police, teachers, and community workers — not just paramedics.

Thiopental — the barbiturate once used for induction — was part of the lethal injection protocol in the US. The same drug that anaesthetised surgical patients was used to execute prisoners. Pharmacology is morally neutral. Its applications aren't.

During the American Civil War, amputation was the most common surgery — performed over 60,000 times. Surgeons would hold the bloody saw between their knees while working. Infection rates were astronomical, but it beat the alternative.

The first blood bank was established in 1937 in Chicago. Before that, doctors did direct person-to-person transfusions — literally connecting a donor's artery to a recipient's vein with tubing. It was as chaotic as it sounds.

Before the stethoscope was invented in 1816, doctors listened to hearts by pressing their ear directly against the patient's chest. Rene Laennec rolled up a piece of paper to avoid putting his ear on a woman's chest — and invented the stethoscope out of awkwardness.

In ancient Rome, Galen performed surgeries on gladiators and developed theories about anatomy that were wrong but lasted 1,400 years — because dissecting humans was banned. He based everything on animal dissections. Monkeys don't have the same anatomy as humans. Nobody checked for over a millennium.

The Iron Lung was invented in 1928 and saved thousands of polio patients who couldn't breathe on their own. Some patients lived in them for decades. The machine breathed for them by creating negative pressure around the chest — a mechanical ghost of normal breathing.

Penicillin wasn't mass-produced until 1943 — and the first batches were so precious that patients' urine was collected to extract and reuse the drug. It was literally recycled from piss. The drug that changed medicine was too valuable to waste.

The first successful kidney transplant was in 1954 — between identical twins, so no rejection. The surgeon, Joseph Murray, later won a Nobel Prize. Before immunosuppressants, the only transplant option was finding your genetic clone.

In 1846, William Morton demonstrated ether anaesthesia in a public operation at Massachusetts General Hospital. The audience was stunned — the patient didn't scream. The room became known as the 'Ether Dome' and still exists. Surgery before anaesthesia was... spirited.

Florence Nightingale's statistical analysis of Crimean War deaths showed that far more soldiers died from preventable diseases than from combat. She essentially invented the use of statistics in healthcare — a nurse did more for data-driven medicine than most doctors of her era.

The first ECG machine, built by Willem Einthoven in 1903, used a wire immersed in a bucket of saline. It weighed 270 kilograms. He won a Nobel Prize for it. Your 12-lead traces its ancestry to a bucket of salt water.

In the 19th century, 'railway spine' was a recognised diagnosis — back pain and neurological symptoms after train accidents. Doctors thought it was a physical injury; others thought it was hysteria. It was probably what we now call whiplash and PTSD. Some debates never change.

Ambulances in World War I were often driven by volunteers — including many women. The American ambulance corps in France was initially staffed almost entirely by volunteers from US universities before America even entered the war.

The first ambulance service in Australia was the St John Ambulance, established in the late 1800s. Initially it was volunteers with first aid certificates and a stretcher. We've come a long way from 'enthusiastic bloke with a blanket.'

Your heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day — about 2.5 billion times in an average lifetime. It never gets a proper rest. The 'resting' between beats is its version of a holiday. A fraction of a second, then back to work.

The SA node generates electrical impulses at about 60 to 100 per minute. The AV node can only conduct about 170 impulses per minute before it starts blocking — which is actually protective. In atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular rate, the AV node is the only thing standing between your ventricles and chaos.

The left ventricle has myocardium three times thicker than the right — because it's pushing blood through the entire systemic circulation, not just the lungs. On an ECG, the left ventricle's dominance is why we see the QRS complex so prominently.

Sudden cardiac death in young athletes is rare but devastating — about 1 in 50,000. The most common cause is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where the heart muscle is abnormally thick. A thick heart sounds strong but it's actually a time bomb — obstructing outflow and predisposing to lethal arrhythmias.

Atrial flutter produces a classic sawtooth pattern on ECG — regular, repetitive flutter waves at about 300 per minute. The AV node usually blocks most of them, giving a ventricular rate of about 150. If you see a rate of exactly 150, think flutter until proven otherwise.

The coronary arteries fill during diastole — not systole. The myocardium squeezes its own blood vessels shut during contraction. This is why tachycardia is dangerous for ischaemic patients: shorter diastole means less coronary perfusion time. The heart can literally outrun its own blood supply.

Prinzmetal's angina — vasospastic angina — causes transient ST elevation that resolves on its own. The coronary artery spasms, the ECG looks like a STEMI, then it relaxes and everything goes back to normal. It's a heart attack that changes its mind.

Commotio cordis — sudden cardiac death from a blunt impact to the chest — happens when the blow lands during the vulnerable repolarisation window (the T-wave upstroke). It doesn't need to be hard. It needs to be perfectly timed. It's most common in young male athletes. And it's terrifying.

The ECG lead aVR is the most neglected lead on the 12-lead — but widespread ST depression with ST elevation in aVR suggests severe triple-vessel or left main disease. The ugly duckling lead might be the most important one on the page.

Right ventricular infarction complicates about 30 to 50% of inferior STEMIs. These patients are preload-dependent — giving nitrates or diuretics can crash their blood pressure because the right ventricle can't pump forward. Fluids first. Always.

Your spleen is basically a giant lymph node that also recycles old red blood cells. It stores about a third of your platelets, ready to dump them into circulation when needed. Rupture it, and you can bleed out into your own abdomen in minutes.

The aorta is about the diameter of a garden hose. At peak systolic pressure, blood moves through it at about 1 metre per second. It's not a passive pipe — it's an elastic structure that stores energy during systole and releases it during diastole.

The epiglottis is made of elastic cartilage — one of the few places in the body that uses it. It needs to snap shut fast during swallowing to protect the airway. That springiness is literally what stops you from inhaling your dinner.

Your kidneys filter about 180 litres of blood per day and produce 1 to 2 litres of urine. The rest is reabsorbed. They process your entire blood volume roughly 60 times a day. The tubules are where the real work happens — filtration is just the start.

The median nerve runs through the carpal tunnel at the wrist — compress it and you get carpal tunnel syndrome. But if you lacerate it at the wrist, you lose sensation to the lateral three and a half fingers and can't oppose your thumb. It's why wrist lacerations always get a proper neurological exam.

The brain weighs about 1.4 kg but consumes 20% of the body's oxygen and 25% of its glucose. It has essentially no energy reserves — cut off supply for 4 to 6 minutes and neurons start dying. The brain is a high-performance engine with no fuel tank.

The thoracic duct drains lymph from everything below the diaphragm and the left side above it — it's the largest lymphatic vessel in the body and empties into the venous system at the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. One puncture in the wrong place and you've got a chyle leak.

There are 206 bones in the adult human body — but babies are born with about 270. Many fuse together as you grow. By the time you're an adult, you've lost about 60 bones. You didn't break them. Your body just decided it didn't need them anymore.

The pericardial sac contains about 15 to 50 mL of serous fluid — just enough to lubricate the heart's constant movement. Add more than about 200 mL quickly (blood, effusion) and tamponade develops. Slow accumulation? The sac can stretch to hold over 2 litres. Speed kills.

The sciatic nerve is the thickest nerve in the body — about as wide as your thumb at its thickest point. A misplaced IM injection into the glute can hit it. That's why you aim for the upper outer quadrant. Miss, and your patient might never walk properly again.

In DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), the body simultaneously clots AND bleeds. Clotting factors get consumed by widespread microthrombi, leaving nothing to stop bleeding elsewhere. The patient is clotting and haemorrhaging at the same time. It's a pathological paradox.

Decorticate posturing (arms flexed, legs extended) means damage above the red nucleus in the midbrain. Decerebrate posturing (arms and legs extended) means damage at or below the red nucleus. Decerebrate is worse. Both mean the brainstem is in trouble.

In acute pancreatitis, the pancreas digests itself. Enzymes activate prematurely inside the gland instead of in the duodenum. The pain radiates straight through to the back and the patient looks genuinely unwell — because their organs are being dissolved from the inside.

Fat embolism syndrome typically appears 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone fracture. Fat globules enter the circulation, lodge in capillaries, and cause a triad of respiratory distress, neurological changes, and petechial rash. The rash is pathognomonic — see it and you know.

In hypothermia, the cold-induced diuresis can dump massive volumes of urine. Vasoconstriction shunts blood centrally, the kidneys perceive volume overload, and they start excreting. The patient is cold, wet, and getting hypovolaemic from their own kidneys.

The blood-brain barrier is formed by tight junctions between endothelial cells in cerebral capillaries. It keeps most drugs and toxins out — which is great for brain protection but terrible for drug delivery. Getting a drug into the brain is pharmacology's hardest problem.

In aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, the classic presentation is a 'thunderclap headache' — the worst headache of the patient's life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds. About 1 in 8 people who present with thunderclap headache have had an SAH. Don't brush it off as a migraine.

The normal anion gap is about 8 to 12. A high anion gap metabolic acidosis means there's an unmeasured acid — lactate, ketones, salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol. The mnemonic MUDPILES exists for a reason. It's one of the most useful calculations in emergency medicine.

Auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP) happens when a patient on positive pressure ventilation doesn't fully exhale before the next breath arrives. Air stacks up, intrathoracic pressure rises, venous return drops, and blood pressure tanks. The fix? Slow down. Let them breathe out.

In hepatic failure, the liver stops clearing ammonia, which crosses the blood-brain barrier and causes cerebral oedema and encephalopathy. The patient gets confused, then drowsy, then comatose. The liver and brain are more connected than most people think.

Reperfusion injury is real — when blood flow returns to ischaemic tissue, the sudden influx of oxygen generates free radicals that cause additional damage. Saving the tissue also hurts it. Sometimes the cure and the injury arrive on the same ambulance.

In Addisonian crisis (acute adrenal insufficiency), the patient is hypotensive, hyponatraemic, hyperkalaemic, and hypoglycaemic — a biochemical disaster. The treatment is IV hydrocortisone and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Without cortisol, the body can't maintain vascular tone or glucose.

Decompression sickness — the bends — happens when dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution and forms bubbles in blood and tissues during rapid ascent. The bubbles can obstruct vessels, compress nerves, and trigger a systemic inflammatory response. It's not just 'surfacing too fast' — it's physics in your bloodstream.
The original AED was developed in the 1970s and weighed over 10 kg. Modern AEDs weigh under 2 kg and talk you through the whole process. The machine that can restart a heart now fits in a backpack.

During CPR, chest compressions generate a 'thoracic pump' effect — pressure changes in the thorax squeeze blood through the circulatory system. It's not the heart being manually squeezed. It's the entire chest acting as a pump.

The survival rate for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest globally sits at about 7 to 10%. In places with excellent bystander CPR and AED access (like certain parts of Scandinavia), it can reach 20 to 25%. The difference isn't the paramedics — it's the public.

Bystander CPR doubles or triples survival from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Yet in many countries, less than half of cardiac arrest patients receive bystander CPR before ambulance arrival. The single biggest survival lever is a bystander willing to push on a chest.

In neonatal resuscitation, the first step is always warmth, drying, and stimulation — not ventilation. Most newborns respond to this alone. Only about 1% of term births need intubation. The smallest intervention that works is the right one.

The 'sniffing the morning air' position — slight neck extension — is the optimal airway position for bag-valve-mask ventilation. Head too far back or too far forward and you've obstructed the airway. The sweet spot is surprisingly narrow.

In paediatric cardiac arrest, the overwhelming majority are respiratory in origin — not cardiac. The heart stops because the child stopped breathing. This is why paediatric BLS emphasises ventilation alongside compressions. Fix the oxygen and you might fix the arrest.

Defibrillation doesn't 'restart' the heart. It stops it — briefly — in the hope that the natural pacemaker (SA node) reasserts control when the electrical chaos settles. You're not jump-starting a battery. You're hitting reset on a system gone haywire.

The RECOVERY trial showed that dexamethasone reduced mortality in COVID-19 patients on ventilators by about a third. A cheap, old drug outperformed many newer, flashier treatments. Sometimes the best medicine is the one that's been on the shelf for decades.

The first 911 system in the US was established in Haleyville, Alabama, in 1968. The first 911 call was made by a state legislator to test the system. It connected him to the local police station. Anti-climactic, but historic.

In Australia, the Triple Zero (000) service receives about 8 million calls a year across police, fire, and ambulance. Not all are genuine emergencies. A non-trivial number are people calling to ask what time it is, or to report that their cat won't come inside.

The first air ambulance in Australia was the Royal Flying Doctor Service, founded in 1928 by Reverend John Flynn. It started with a single de Havilland aircraft covering vast stretches of the outback. It's now one of the largest aeromedical services in the world.

In the 1970s, the TV show 'Emergency!' — about two fictional Los Angeles paramedics — was so popular that it drove public demand for real paramedic services across the US. A TV show literally created political pressure for better EMS. Hollywood's most useful contribution to medicine.

The highest cardiac arrest survival rate in the world is in Seattle, Washington — around 20 to 22% overall, and much higher for witnessed VF. They achieved this through massive public CPR training, widespread AED placement, and a coordinated EMS system. It can be done. Most places just don't.

In some Scandinavian countries, ambulance crews include a physician on scene for critical calls. In Australia and the UK, paramedics handle most of this themselves. Different systems, same goal. The debate about whether doctors belong on ambulances is older than most paramedics.

The longest ambulance in the world is a custom-built vehicle in Dubai that's essentially a mobile hospital — complete with ICU beds, ventilators, and monitoring equipment. Useful for a city that occasionally needs to transport patients between palaces.

Paramedic burnout rates are high — studies suggest 20 to 30% of paramedics meet criteria for PTSD, and burnout affects up to 40%. Shift work, repeated trauma exposure, and organisational pressure all contribute. The people who show up for everyone else often need someone to show up for them.

Before GPS, paramedics navigated using map books — often the Melway in Melbourne or the UBD in Sydney. Knowing your grid reference was a core skill. Some veteran paramedics still remember their patch's grid numbers better than their own postcode.

In remote Australia, cattle stations can be larger than some European countries. The RFDS might fly for hours to reach a single patient. In the time it takes some Australian paramedics to reach a job, a European paramedic could have transported three patients and had lunch.

The first documented use of an AED on a human was in 1979 — an experimental device tested in Brighton, England. It was designed to be used by ambulance crews with minimal training. Before that, defibrillation required a physician and an ECG machine the size of a small car.

In the 1800s, 'resurrection men' dug up freshly buried corpses and sold them to medical schools for dissection. It was a lucrative trade. Some even resorted to murder — the Burke and Hare case being the most infamous. Medical education has a surprisingly dark supply chain history.

Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 because he was messy. He left a petri dish uncovered and mould grew on it, killing the surrounding bacteria. He almost threw it away. The most important discovery in modern medicine came from forgetting to wash up.

The first person to survive a tracheostomy was probably performed in the 1500s, but the procedure was described in ancient Egyptian texts and by Hippocrates. For most of history, surgeons avoided it because it almost always killed the patient. Then someone finally got it right.

Ignaz Semmelweis figured out that hand-washing saved lives in 1847 — and his colleagues mocked him for it. He was right. He was committed to an asylum and died of sepsis from a beating. The man who discovered infection control died of an infection. History doesn't always have a happy ending.

In WWII, medics on the front lines faced extraordinary danger — they were unarmed, marked with red crosses, and still took fire. The survival rate for wounded soldiers who reached a medic was about 70%. Those medics earned every statistic. Those medics earned every statistic.

There are roughly the same number of bacterial cells as human cells in your body — about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells, mostly in your gut. For decades we thought the ratio was 10:1, but a 2016 study revised it to roughly 1:1. Either way, you're never alone.

In 2004, a man in the UK was admitted to hospital with severe abdominal pain. X-rays revealed he'd swallowed 78 pieces of cutlery — mostly spoons. He told doctors he 'liked the taste of metal.' He survived. The surgeons had to remove them one by one.

Priapism — a persistent, painful erection — is a genuine emergency. It can be caused by spinal cord injury, sickle cell disease, or cocaine use. The treatment involves aspirating blood from the corpora cavernosa with a large-bore needle. Patients remember this procedure forever.

The longest surgery on record lasted 96 hours — a marathon operation to remove an ovarian cyst that had essentially become a second body (a teratoma with hair, teeth, and bone). The patient survived. The surgeons needed therapy.

In 2010, a man in Serbia survived being impaled through the chest by a 1.5-metre fence post. The post entered through his back and exited through his neck. Surgeons removed it in a 5-hour operation. He was back at work within months. Sometimes the human body just refuses to die.

Your eyes have a separate immune system. If your body's main immune system discovers your eyes exist, it can attack them as foreign tissue. This is why eye injuries that breach the globe can trigger sympathetic ophthalmia — the immune system suddenly realises there's something in the socket and attacks both eyes.

In the 1700s, patients were sometimes submerged in horse manure as a treatment for various ailments — the thinking being that the warmth and 'vapours' were therapeutic. It was neither warm enough nor vapoury enough to actually help. But they tried.

funFact.fact: Rocuronium is overtaking suxamethonium for RSI because it doesn't carry the hyperkalaemia risk in burns, crush injuries, and neurological conditions. Sugammadex can reverse it — if you can get your hands on it prehospitally in Australia.

tldr.summary: An Australian pilot simulation found a one-hour airway-assistant course nearly halved intubation time in a continuously regurgitating airway, while Japanese Utstein data quantified how quickly the odds of on-scene ROSC collapse after 10 minutes of resuscitation.

highlights.title: Airway assistant training halved sim intubation time
highlights.note: Median intubation time 53 s (IQR 19) trained vs 102.5 s (IQR 36) untrained, p = 0.009, very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86); no oesophageal intubations in either group

highlights.title: Numbers for when on-scene ROSC stops happening
highlights.note: Probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC 6.97% at 10 min and 0.50% at 20 min after EMS contact; favourable neurological outcome (CPC 1–2 at 1 month) in 50.0% of patients <75 and 20.5% of those ≥75 with on-scene ROSC at or after 10 min

highlights.title: Co-dispatch modelled to cut OHCA response times
highlights.note: Median first-unit response 9.81 min with EMS alone vs 5.45 min with police added, 7.36 min with fire added, 5.41 min with triple dispatch (paired median gain 4.34 min); locations reached within 10 min rose from 51.1% to 94.6%

highlights.title: Social support buffers the violence-to-burnout pathway
highlights.note: Workplace violence exposure associated with burnout indirectly through post-traumatic stress symptoms; social support moderated the violence–PTSS (p = 0.002) and violence–burnout (p = 0.015) associations; resilience findings did not survive correction

highlights.title: Dispatch stress, depression and suicidal ideation linked
highlights.note: Conditional indirect association of secondary traumatic stress with suicidal ideation through depression fell from 0.191 at low social support to 0.013 at high; emotional labour pathways held only at low and mean support

highlights.title: Hot days, more injury calls to ambulance services
highlights.note: Cumulative OR 1.21 (95% CI 1.12–1.31) comparing the 99th percentile apparent temperature (42.5 °C) with the exposure minimum; traffic injuries OR 1.80 (95% CI 1.56–2.07); adults 18–64 OR 1.38; heat waves OR 1.07

highlights.title: Mapping 50 years of EMS cardiac arrest research
highlights.note: Annual output peaked at 244 publications in 2021 and stayed above 200 from 2022–2025; Resuscitation published 23.1% of records; the US led with 34.0%, then Japan 12.5% and Canada 9.4%

papers.title: Effect of airway assistant training on intubation time during simulated prehospital airway management: A pilot study
papers.summary: An Australian pilot randomised simulation of 12 paramedic–ICP pairs found a one-hour airway assistant training course cut median intubation time in a continuously regurgitating airway from 102.5 to 53 seconds.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Airway management at intubation is core business for crews across Australian services and the assistant role exists on every two-paramedic response — the open question is whether a 12-person manikin result holds on patients.
papers.design: Pilot randomised simulation study (SALAD manikin)
papers.n: 12 qualified paramedics in two groups of 6, paired with intensive care paramedics
papers.finding: Median intubation time 53 s (IQR 19) trained vs 102.5 s (IQR 36) untrained, p = 0.009, very large effect size (Cohen's d = 1.86); no oesophageal intubations in either group
papers.caveat: Pilot simulation with 12 participants — no patient outcomes, and the authors call for larger studies
papers.shortTitle: Airway assistant training halved sim intubation time
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to assist effectively during prehospital intubation in soiled or regurgitating airways.

papers.title: On-Scene Time-Dependent Probabilities of Return of Spontaneous Circulation and Favorable Neurological Outcome in Cases of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with an Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Retrospective Study Using the National Utstein Data in Japan
papers.summary: A Japanese national Utstein cohort of 22,383 adults with shockable cardiogenic OHCA found the probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC fell from 6.97% at 10 minutes to 0.50% at 20 minutes of resuscitation, with favourable neurological outcome in 50.0% of under-75s achieving on-scene ROSC at or after 10 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Shockable-rhythm resuscitation duration and transport decisions are made by paramedics across Australia, and this is a 22,383-patient national registry over six years.
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide Utstein descriptive cohort, 2017–2022
papers.n: 22,383 adults with cardiogenic OHCA and an initial shockable rhythm
papers.finding: Probability of subsequent on-scene ROSC 6.97% at 10 min and 0.50% at 20 min after EMS contact; favourable neurological outcome (CPC 1–2 at 1 month) in 50.0% of patients <75 and 20.5% of those ≥75 with on-scene ROSC at or after 10 min
papers.caveat: Descriptive Japanese EMS data — no causal claims, and the authors state it does not establish age-based criteria for prolonged resuscitation or transport
papers.shortTitle: Numbers for when on-scene ROSC stops happening
papers.learningGoal: Weigh when ongoing on-scene resuscitation in shockable cardiac arrest remains worthwhile against early transport decisions.

papers.title: Modelled Response Times for Police and Fire Brigade Co-Dispatch to Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Geospatial Simulation Study in Vorarlberg, Austria
papers.summary: An Austrian geospatial simulation of 500 modelled OHCA locations found police and volunteer fire brigade co-dispatch cut modelled median first-unit response time from 9.81 to 5.41 minutes and lifted 10-minute coverage from 51.1% to 94.6%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A modelled European system with volunteer fire stations, but first-responder co-response to cardiac arrest is a live resourcing question for Australian services too.
papers.design: Geospatial routing simulation
papers.n: 500 modelled OHCA locations served by 18 EMS, 28 police and 121 volunteer fire stations
papers.finding: Median first-unit response 9.81 min with EMS alone vs 5.45 min with police added, 7.36 min with fire added, 5.41 min with triple dispatch (paired median gain 4.34 min); locations reached within 10 min rose from 51.1% to 94.6%
papers.caveat: Purely modelled — fixed stations, assumed turnout times, continuous availability assumed, and the authors say operational validation is required
papers.shortTitle: Co-dispatch modelled to cut OHCA response times
papers.learningGoal: Understand how co-dispatching first responders could reduce time to first unit in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Workplace Violence Exposure and Burnout Among Fire-Service-Based Paramedics in South Korea: The Indirect Association Through Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms and the Moderating Roles of Social Support and Resilience
papers.summary: A South Korean cross-sectional study of 210 fire-service paramedics found workplace violence exposure was associated with burnout indirectly through post-traumatic stress symptoms, with social support weakening that pathway.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — South Korean fire-service paramedics, but violence exposure, PTSD symptoms and burnout are occupational realities for paramedics everywhere, and social support is something services can build.
papers.design: Cross-sectional moderated mediation survey
papers.n: 210 fire-service-based paramedics in Busan
papers.finding: Workplace violence exposure associated with burnout indirectly through post-traumatic stress symptoms; social support moderated the violence–PTSS (p = 0.002) and violence–burnout (p = 0.015) associations; resilience findings did not survive correction
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional self-report, and some social-support findings depended on excluding one influential observation
papers.shortTitle: Social support buffers the violence-to-burnout pathway
papers.learningGoal: Understand how social support buffers the impact of workplace violence on my wellbeing and burnout risk.

papers.title: Associations of Secondary Traumatic Stress and Emotional Labor with Suicidal Ideation Among Emergency Dispatch Personnel in South Korea: A Cross-Sectional Moderated Mediation Analysis
papers.summary: A South Korean survey of 211 emergency dispatch personnel found secondary traumatic stress and depression were associated with suicidal ideation, with the indirect pathway through depression weakening as social support rose.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Dispatchers sit upstream of every ambulance response, and the secondary-trauma and social-support findings speak to Australian ambulance communications centres too.
papers.design: Cross-sectional moderated mediation survey
papers.n: 211 fire-service emergency dispatch personnel in Busan and Gyeongnam
papers.finding: Conditional indirect association of secondary traumatic stress with suicidal ideation through depression fell from 0.191 at low social support to 0.013 at high; emotional labour pathways held only at low and mean support
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional, and key suicidal-ideation interaction terms were not significant in a Tobit sensitivity analysis
papers.shortTitle: Dispatch stress, depression and suicidal ideation linked
papers.learningGoal: Understand how social support buffers secondary traumatic stress and depression in my emergency communication workforce.

papers.title: Apparent temperature, heat waves, and unintentional injury-related emergency medical service calls: A case-crossover study
papers.summary: A Shanghai case-crossover study of 170,538 unintentional injury-related EMS calls found extreme apparent temperature (42.5 °C vs −2.9 °C) was associated with 21% higher odds of injury calls, peaking at 80% higher for traffic injuries.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Shanghai demand data, but heat-driven injury call surges map straight onto Australian summers and the dispatch resourcing that comes with them.
papers.design: Time-stratified case-crossover with distributed lag models
papers.n: 170,538 unintentional injury-related EMS calls, July 2021 – June 2025
papers.finding: Cumulative OR 1.21 (95% CI 1.12–1.31) comparing the 99th percentile apparent temperature (42.5 °C) with the exposure minimum; traffic injuries OR 1.80 (95% CI 1.56–2.07); adults 18–64 OR 1.38; heat waves OR 1.07
papers.caveat: Single Shanghai district, and comparisons across heat-wave definitions and exposure windows were exploratory
papers.shortTitle: Hot days, more injury calls to ambulance services
papers.learningGoal: Understand how extreme heat drives demand surges and injury risk in Australian ambulance operations.

papers.title: The global research landscape of emergency medical services in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: A US-led bibliometric analysis of 3,005 Web of Science records from 1972–2026 mapped EMS-focused OHCA research, showing output above 200 papers a year since 2022 and registry-centred international collaboration.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A map of the research field rather than a clinical result — background on where EMS-OHCA evidence comes from and how much of it flows through the big registries.
papers.design: Retrospective bibliometric analysis (Web of Science, VOSviewer)
papers.n: 3,005 records, 1972 – June 2026
papers.finding: Annual output peaked at 244 publications in 2021 and stayed above 200 from 2022–2025; Resuscitation published 23.1% of records; the US led with 34.0%, then Japan 12.5% and Canada 9.4%
papers.caveat: Bibliometrics only — publication counts and co-citations, no clinical findings
papers.shortTitle: Mapping 50 years of EMS cardiac arrest research
papers.learningGoal: Understand how international registry-based collaboration shapes the prehospital cardiac arrest evidence I apply in practice.

papers.title: Prehospital Advanced Airway Management in Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Cohort Study Using Time-Dependent Propensity Score Sequential Matching
papers.summary: A Japanese nationwide registry cohort of 7,217 adults with traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found successful prehospital advanced airway management was not significantly associated with better 30-day survival or neurological outcome when resuscitation-time bias was corrected.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Supraglottic airways are standard Australian cardiac arrest care and intubation is an advanced-tier skill in most services, so the question is squarely ours; the physician-free Japanese EMS model resembles ours more than Europe's.
papers.design: Nationwide retrospective registry cohort with time-dependent propensity score sequential matching
papers.n: 7,217 adults with traumatic OHCA (2,653 received advanced airway management)
papers.finding: Thirty-day survival 1.8% with advanced airway vs 1.4% matched controls (corrected RD 0.6%, 95% CI −0.1 to 1.2); favourable neurological outcome 0.2% vs 0.4% (corrected RD −0.2%, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.1) — no significant timing-dependent association
papers.caveat: Observational design with extremely low event rates, so even a real effect could hide in the confidence intervals
papers.shortTitle: Advanced airway not linked to traumatic arrest survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of advanced airway management during traumatic cardiac arrest against prioritising early ventilation and circulation.

papers.title: Prehospital recognition and differentiation of seizure presentations by paramedics and ambulance nurses: A scoping review
papers.summary: An Australian scoping review of 18 studies found paramedic recognition of seizure presentations remains suboptimal, with sensitivity of 54.0–58.5% and non-recognition of non-convulsive seizures reaching 53.0–81.4%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Diagnostic accuracy of seizure recognition is a crew-level problem everywhere, and the review covers paramedic practice directly comparable to Australian scope.
