papers.design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 18 studies across five databases
papers.n: 18 studies (16 paramedic, 2 ambulance nurse) from 1,264 citations
papers.finding: Sensitivity 54.0–58.5% and specificity 95.9–96.6% against variable reference standards; recognition rates 56.8–89.7%; non-convulsive seizures missed in 53.0–81.4% of cases
papers.caveat: Included studies used variable reference standards and EMS workforce configurations, limiting pooled interpretation
papers.shortTitle: Paramedics miss many non-convulsive seizures
papers.learningGoal: Recognise non-convulsive seizure presentations in the field to reduce missed diagnoses.

papers.title: Dispatch suspicion of sepsis and time from emergency department arrival to antibiotic administration: a Norwegian registry study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Norwegian registry study of 527 sepsis admissions found dispatch suspicion of sepsis was associated with a 31-minute shorter adjusted time from ED arrival to antibiotic administration.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Dispatch triage criteria and sepsis recognition are core ambulance functions in Australia, and the Nordic dispatch model is close to ours.
papers.design: Retrospective registry-based cohort linking prehospital and hospital records
papers.n: 527 sepsis admissions (371 with emergency dispatch contact; 31 classified as suspected sepsis at dispatch)
papers.finding: Dispatch suspicion of sepsis was associated with a 31-minute shorter adjusted time to antibiotics (95% CI −59.9 to −1.8 min)
papers.caveat: Only 31 patients carried the sepsis dispatch flag, so the estimate rests on a small subgroup
papers.shortTitle: Sepsis suspicion at dispatch, earlier antibiotics
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how early prehospital suspicion of sepsis can accelerate antibiotic administration for deteriorating patients.

papers.title: Frequent Callers to Emergency Medical Services: an observational cohort study from Region Zealand, Denmark (2018-2025)
papers.summary: A Danish observational cohort of 443,977 emergency calls found 3.0% of callers (6,415 people) generated 19.9% of all calls, with post-threshold frequent callers seeing more telephone resolution (23.8%) and non-conveyance (27.4%).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Frequent-caller patterns and dispatch load are universal ambulance problems, and the Danish single-tier system maps well onto Australian operations.
papers.design: Observational cohort of emergency medical dispatch centre calls, 2018–2025
papers.n: 214,091 individuals making 443,977 calls in Region Zealand, Denmark
papers.finding: Frequent callers (5+ calls in 12 months) were 3.0% of callers but 19.9% of calls; alcohol/intoxication/overdose and suicidal presentations were top contact causes only in the highest-volume post-threshold groups
papers.caveat: Single-region data and a dispatch-centre definition of frequent calling that may not match other systems' operational definitions
papers.shortTitle: 3% of callers drive a fifth of all calls
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system factors that drive frequent calling to ambulance services and how coordinated responses reduce demand.

papers.title: Cycle-to-Cycle Prediction of Return of Spontaneous Circulation Using End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide Dynamics in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: A Taiwanese retrospective multicentre study of 1,480 patients with OHCA built a two-layer LSTM model on sequential EtCO2 that predicted ROSC well at event level (AUROC 0.876) but only 0.685 per two-minute cycle.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — EtCO2 monitoring is routine on Australian cardiac arrests, but this is a retrospective modelling study needing prospective, real-time validation before it guides cycle decisions on the road.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective study with LSTM prediction model, internally validated by 10-fold cross-validation
papers.n: 1,651 EtCO2 sequences from 1,480 adults with OHCA (583 ROSC events)
papers.finding: Event-level AUROC 0.876 (Brier 0.140); cycle-level AUROC 0.685 across 17,029 two-minute prediction points, with systematic overestimation of ROSC probability (Brier 0.285)
papers.caveat: Retrospective, single-country dataset with internal validation only and poor cycle-level calibration
papers.shortTitle: EtCO2 trends predict ROSC cycle by cycle
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of EtCO2 trend monitoring for anticipating return of spontaneous circulation during resuscitation.

papers.title: A national cross-sectional analysis of regional and rural-urban variation in emergency medical services naloxone administration for suspected opioid overdose
papers.journal: Journal of Substance Use and Addiction Treatment
papers.summary: A US cross-sectional analysis of 110,261 EMS activations for suspected opioid overdose found documented naloxone administration in 33.9%, with regional variation (South aOR 2.10 vs Northeast) that persisted while the rural-urban difference attenuated to null after clinical adjustment.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Naloxone is carried by every Australian ambulance service, and the finding is about how documented practice varies with case mix rather than a foreign service model.
papers.design: National cross-sectional analysis of the 2025 NEMSIS public-release dataset with multivariable logistic regression
papers.n: 110,261 EMS activations with suspected opioid involvement (37,412 naloxone administrations)
papers.finding: Adjusted odds of EMS naloxone administration were higher in the South (aOR 2.10, 95% CI 2.01–2.18), Midwest (aOR 1.92) and West (aOR 1.31) versus the Northeast; rural-versus-urban odds were null after clinical adjustment (aOR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94–1.09)
papers.caveat: Administrative documentation of naloxone as a surveillance marker, not a clinical endpoint — variation may reflect documentation and case-mix differences
papers.shortTitle: US naloxone use varies by region, not rurality
papers.learningGoal: Understand how regional and rural factors shape naloxone use and documentation in suspected opioid overdose care.

papers.title: Toward a Definition and Differentiation of Secondary Traumatic Stress, Vicarious Trauma, Post-Traumatic Stress, and Compassion Fatigue in Relation to First Responders: An Integrative Literature Review
papers.summary: A French integrative review of 76 studies on first responders (including paramedics) found the concepts of secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and PTSD overlap symptomatically, with organisational constraints playing a central role in traumatic responses.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Workforce psychological injury is a universal ambulance problem, and the review's emphasis on organisational drivers rather than individual resilience speaks directly to Australian services.
papers.design: Integrative literature review of 76 studies across six databases to January 2026
papers.n: 76 studies of adult first responders (firefighters, police, paramedics, ambulance workers)
papers.finding: Conceptual overlap between secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma, compassion fatigue and PTSD is maintained by symptomatic overlap and measurement tools designed for other professions; organisational constraints emerged as central to trauma emergence
papers.caveat: Conceptual synthesis with no intervention data, and heterogeneous included professions
papers.shortTitle: Untangling trauma terms for first responders
papers.learningGoal: Understand how secondary traumatic stress, vicarious trauma and compassion fatigue differ and how organisational constraints shape my wellbeing.

papers.title: Prehospital Videolaryngoscope Availability and Use in Belgium: A Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.summary: A Belgian nationwide survey of mobile intensive care units found 91.4% of responding units had videolaryngoscope access, yet only 6.2% of physician users reached for it first-choice and 81.5% reserved it for failed direct laryngoscopy.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Belgian crews are physician-staffed, but the airway-device question is one Australian advanced-tier crews face too — the availability-versus-use gap transfers even if the crew model doesn't.
papers.design: Nationwide cross-sectional survey of all Belgian MICUs (two questionnaires)
papers.n: 35 of 96 MICU department heads and 115 MICU physicians responded
papers.finding: 91.4% of responding MICUs reported videolaryngoscope availability; 70.4% of physician respondents used one, but only 6.2% as first-choice device and 81.5% used it after failed direct laryngoscopy
papers.caveat: 36.5% unit response rate and self-reported use patterns
papers.shortTitle: Video laryngoscopes available but rarely first choice
papers.learningGoal: Refine my judgement on when to choose videolaryngoscopy first-line rather than after failed direct laryngoscopy.

papers.title: The impact of simulation with debriefing on developing clinical competence and performance in paramedicine students
papers.summary: An Australian retrospective analysis of 305 paramedicine students across 1,243 simulated scenarios found weekly practice frequency was positively correlated with summative exam performance (r = 0.257, p < 0.001), with competence scores rising across the trimester.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It's an Australian paramedicine programme, so the finding is directly about local education — but a modest correlation from one university's assessment data doesn't settle how programmes should schedule simulation.
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of performance-based assessment data (2019–2024) from a single university programme
papers.n: 305 second-year paramedicine students and 1,243 practice scenarios
papers.finding: Practice frequency correlated with exam performance (r = 0.257, p < 0.001), strongest in the final trimester tertile (r = 0.229), and a 2020 performance dip during reduced COVID-19 simulation exposure highlighted the role of consistent practice
papers.caveat: Single-institution retrospective correlation, not a causal test of simulation dosage
papers.shortTitle: Weekly simulation linked to better student exams
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my commitment to regular simulation practice and structured debriefing to sustain clinical competence across the year.

papers.title: Technology-enhanced training for prehospital mass-casualty incident preparedness: A scoping review
papers.summary: A scoping review of 28 studies on technology-enhanced prehospital mass-casualty training found virtual reality was the most common modality (43%) and 56% of completed studies demonstrated applied learning, but 75% lacked an explicit training design framework.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — MCI preparedness training is a live issue for Australian services expanding simulation, though the mapped literature comes mostly from higher-resourced systems abroad.
papers.design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 28 studies, 2015–2025, with modified Kirkpatrick outcome mapping
papers.n: 28 studies of technology-enhanced prehospital MCI training
papers.finding: Virtual reality was the most common modality (43%, n = 12), 50% of studies used dual-purpose training-and-assessment platforms, and 75% lacked an explicit training design framework; 56% of completed studies showed applied learning
papers.caveat: Scoping design with no outcome pooling, and no studies from low- or lower-middle-income countries
papers.shortTitle: VR leads mass-casualty training but frameworks lag
papers.learningGoal: Understand how simulation-based training can strengthen my preparedness for mass-casualty incident response.

papers.title: Concordance between prehospital Glasgow Coma Scale–based classification and diagnosis-based injury severity in destination decisions for suspected severe trauma: a linked EMS–hospital cohort study
papers.summary: A South Korean linked EMS–hospital cohort of 5,841 suspected severe trauma patients found weak agreement between prehospital GCS classification and diagnosis-based injury severity (κ 0.192), with one in ten patients (10.0%) severely injured despite GCS 9–15 and destination undertriage of 33.6% (GCS-based) and 47.3% (diagnosis-based), roughly doubled in rural areas.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — GCS-based trauma triage and destination decisions are core practice on every Australian ambulance crew, and the rural undertriage gap mirrors our own geography.
papers.design: Linked EMS–hospital population-based cohort
papers.n: 5,841 suspected severe trauma patients aged ≥15 (6,179 analysed)
papers.finding: GCS 3–8 detected diagnosis-based severe injury with 54.2% sensitivity (κ 0.192); one in ten patients (10.0%) met the anatomical severity criterion despite GCS 9–15; destination undertriage was 33.6% (GCS-based) and 47.3% (ICISS-based), with rural disparity (aOR 2.65 and 2.04).
papers.caveat: ICISS severity is a post-hoc, diagnosis-based measure, and undertriage definitions differ between systems.
papers.shortTitle: GCS-based triage misses seriously injured trauma patients
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when normal GCS still warrants transport to a major trauma centre in Australia.

papers.title: Neurological Outcomes of Rhythm Transitions in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Initial Nonshockable Rhythms: A Nationwide Population-Based Study
papers.summary: A South Korean nationwide registry study of adults with initial nonshockable OHCA found rhythm transitions during CPR graded neurological outcome: asystole converting to PEA was linked to better outcomes than persistent asystole (OR 2.28), and persistent PEA carried the best odds (OR 8.70 versus persistent asystole).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — rhythm checks every two minutes are universal practice on Australian ambulances, and a national registry makes the pattern robust.
papers.design: Nationwide registry cohort with inverse-probability weighting
papers.n: Adults with nonshockable OHCA, South Korea 2016–2021 (size not reported in abstract)
papers.finding: Weighted good-neurological-outcome risks were 0.101% (asystole–asystole), 0.231% (asystole→PEA), 0.384% (PEA→asystole) and 0.874% (PEA–PEA); versus persistent asystole, asystole→PEA OR 2.28 (95% CI 1.78–2.93) and PEA–PEA OR 8.70 (95% CI 6.98–10.83).
papers.caveat: Observational registry with very small absolute differences (0.1–0.9 percentage points); rhythm transitions may track the underlying arrest trajectory rather than drive outcome.
papers.shortTitle: Rhythm changes during CPR track neurological outcomes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how rhythm transitions during resuscitation shape my prognostication and continuation decisions in nonshockable cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Circadian rhythmicity in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: a scoping review
papers.summary: A Czech-led scoping review of 18 studies found OHCA and STEMI incidence peaks in the morning with a secondary afternoon/evening peak, and night-time events were linked to lower ROSC and worse one-month and one-year survival, explained by limited bystander availability, less bystander CPR and defibrillation and longer times to hospital intervention rather than time of day itself.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The circadian pattern is universal, but this is a descriptive review of observational studies — the actionable part is the bystander-availability explanation, which supports community CPR and defibrillator awareness rather than any change to clinical practice.
papers.design: Scoping review (18 studies, 2010–2024)
papers.n: 18 studies
papers.finding: Highest OHCA and STEMI incidence in the morning with a secondary afternoon/evening peak and lowest at night; night-time events had lower ROSC and worse one-month and one-year survival and neurological outcomes, attributed to less bystander CPR and defibrillation and longer times to intervention; events were more frequent in winter.
papers.caveat: Scoping review of heterogeneous observational studies with no pooled effect estimates.
papers.shortTitle: Night-time OHCA outcomes linked to bystander availability
papers.learningGoal: Understand how time of day and seasonal patterns in cardiac arrest incidence shape my resuscitation practice and system readiness.

papers.title: Admission arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a single-centre retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: A Chinese single-centre retrospective cohort of 617 adults resuscitated from OHCA found admission PaCO2 above 50 mmHg associated with higher one-month mortality in a stepwise gradient (each 10-mmHg increase aOR 1.45, 95% CI 1.24–1.70).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Admission blood gases are an in-hospital measurement, but the reading partly reflects prehospital ventilation, which is the part a crew controls.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort
papers.n: 617 adults resuscitated from OHCA, 2014–2023
papers.finding: One-month mortality was 73.6% overall and rose across PaCO2 groups (49.7%, 81.1% and 90.7% for ≤50, >50–70 and >70 mmHg); each 10-mmHg increase carried aOR 1.45 (95% CI 1.24–1.70) for mortality, with a matching gradient for neurological outcome (common aOR 1.53).
papers.caveat: Single-centre retrospective design; the authors state all analyses are strictly associational, so high PaCO2 may mark severity rather than cause harm.
papers.shortTitle: Higher admission PaCO2 linked to worse post-arrest survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the evidence linking ventilation targets after cardiac arrest to survival and neurological outcomes.

papers.title: SUDDEN CARDIAC ARREST IN NEW SOUTH WALES (NSW), AUSTRALIA: A DATA LINKAGE STUDY
papers.summary: An Australian data-linkage study identified 13,345 presumed sudden cardiac arrests aged 1–50 in NSW from 1.7 million linked records — 54% cardiac in aetiology and 83% fatal — and extrapolated roughly 370 cardiac SCA deaths a year among Australians aged 1–35.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian data built on the NSW Ambulance OHCA register, but it maps the size and shape of the problem rather than changing what crews do.
papers.design: Retrospective multi-source administrative data linkage
papers.n: 13,345 presumed SCA cases aged 1–50 in NSW
papers.finding: 54% of cases had cardiac aetiology and 83% were fatal; rhythm-related and structural diagnoses dominated ages 1–11 while ischaemic disease dominated ages 35–50; older cardiac cases were more likely to die prehospital (aOR 3.56 for 35–50 vs 1–11 years); extrapolated ~370 cardiac SCA deaths per year in Australians aged 1–35.
papers.caveat: Retrospective coded administrative data with cardiac aetiology assigned from hospital and death records, and national figures extrapolated from one state.
papers.shortTitle: NSW data linkage tracks sudden cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Understand the national burden and age-related causes of sudden cardiac arrest in young Australians.

papers.title: Child representatives’ conceptions of children's participation in prehospital emergency care: A phenomenographic study
papers.summary: A Swedish qualitative interview study of ambulance child representatives found children's participation in prehospital emergency care conceived as shaped chiefly by clinicians' attitudes and experience, then by the child's age and situational urgency, and constrained by the adult-oriented ambulance environment.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Interviews from a Swedish ambulance service, but communicating with children on scene is the same challenge for crews anywhere.
papers.design: Qualitative phenomenographic interview study
papers.n: Child representatives in the Swedish ambulance service (number not reported)
papers.finding: Three hierarchical conceptions: participation shaped by ambulance clinicians' attitudes and experience, conditioned by age, developmental level and urgency, and influenced by the adult-oriented ambulance environment; participation was more constrained in very young children and time-critical situations.
papers.caveat: Interviews with child representatives only — not children, parents or frontline ambulance clinicians.
papers.shortTitle: Children's participation in ambulance care depends on clinicians
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how my communication style and the ambulance environment affect children's participation in their own emergency care.

papers.title: Positive pressure ventilation in newborns at birth: a systematic review of recipient characteristics and temporal trends
papers.summary: This multinational systematic review of 42 studies (1984–2024) on positive pressure ventilation (PPV) at birth found PPV incidence of 3.0%–8.0% in population-based studies excluding CPAP, with higher rates in preterm infants, rising overall and facemask PPV over time, and stable or declining tracheal-tube PPV.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — PPV at birth is a core paramedic skill for births attended in the prehospital setting; understanding typical incidence, gestational-age patterns and reporting gaps can inform Australian practice expectations and documentation standards, though most included data come from hospital birthing settings rather than prehospital care.
papers.design: Systematic review (PROSPERO-registered, PRISMA 2020)
papers.n: 42 studies from 34 countries, 269 to 10,696,831 livebirths per study
papers.finding: PPV incidence 3.0%–8.0% in nine population-based/large multicentre studies excluding CPAP; rates much higher among very and extremely preterm infants; overall and facemask PPV increasing over time while tracheal-tube PPV was stable or declining; lower incidence in low-resource and lower-level birthing centres; few studies reported indications or timing of PPV initiation.
papers.caveat: Marked heterogeneity in CPAP distinction, interface definitions and eligibility criteria precluded meta-analysis, and reporting of indications and timing was limited and inconsistent.
papers.shortTitle: Systematic review of newborn PPV at birth
papers.learningGoal: Recognise which newborns at birth are most likely to need positive pressure ventilation and how practice patterns are changing.

papers.title: Prehospital Whole Blood Resuscitation in Pediatric Patients: A San Antonio Cohort Descriptive
papers.summary: A US retrospective cohort from San Antonio Fire Department's mature prehospital whole-blood program described 73 paediatric recipients (4.3% of 1,703 transfusions, 2018–2025): mostly adolescent males with penetrating trauma, 45% with an elevated age-adjusted shock index and 50% surviving to discharge.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is limited to a few Australian services, so this informs the debate more than current practice — but TXA and intraosseous access are standard, and paediatric trauma physiology is universal.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort
papers.n: 73 paediatric whole-blood recipients (of 1,703 total transfusions)
papers.finding: Trauma caused 96% of paediatric transfusions (74% gunshot, 84% all penetrating); 45% had elevated age-adjusted SIPA, 20% were pulseless; survival 50%, died 39%, unknown 11%; younger children showed the largest drop in shock index after resuscitation
papers.caveat: Descriptive single-program cohort with no comparator, and 11% of outcomes unknown
papers.shortTitle: Whole blood in paediatric trauma: early program data
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on recognising paediatric haemorrhagic shock and when prehospital blood transfusion is indicated.

papers.title: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores
papers.journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A US national registry study (CARES, 2013–2023) developed and internally validated paediatric OHCA risk scores from prehospital variables, classifying 26,895 children into low/moderate/high survival groups with AUROC 0.76–0.82 and average discharge-survival probabilities from 3% to 48%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Built from a 26,895-patient national arrest registry using variables crews already record — bystander CPR, AED use, first rhythm — so the score travels well beyond the US.
papers.design: Registry-based risk-score development and internal validation
papers.n: 26,895 paediatric OHCA patients
papers.finding: 27.8% survived to admission and 11.9% to discharge; scores using gender, arrest location, witness status, aetiology, bystander CPR, prehospital AED use and first rhythm reached AUROC 0.76–0.82, with average survival 3–48% across low/moderate/high groups
papers.caveat: Internal validation only — not yet externally validated or prospectively tested at the bedside
papers.shortTitle: Risk scores sort survival odds in paediatric OHCA
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how prehospital arrest features shape prognostic conversations in paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Out-of-hospital rapid sequence intubation practices by emergency care practitioners in selected provinces of South Africa: a retrospective cross-sectional review
papers.summary: A South African multicentre record review of 354 out-of-hospital RSIs performed by emergency care practitioners across three provinces found trauma accounted for 67% of cases, ketamine was documented in 75% and rocuronium in 52%, with pre-oxygenation in 99% and capnography in 84% of cases.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Drug-assisted intubation is an intensive care paramedic skill in most Australian services, and rocuronium is not carried by all of them — but the drug choices, monitoring standards and adverse-event questions are the same debates.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective cross-sectional record review
papers.n: 354 RSI cases (from 535,479 patient care records screened)
papers.finding: Trauma caused 238/354 (67.2%) of RSIs; ketamine documented in 74.9%, rocuronium in 52.3%, pre-oxygenation in 99.4%, end-tidal CO2 monitoring in 83.6% and post-intubation sedation/analgesia in 72%
papers.caveat: Retrospective documentation review — missing records may undercount care and adverse events
papers.shortTitle: Out-of-hospital RSI practice across South African services
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my documentation of post-intubation sedation, analgesia and capnography to support safer out-of-hospital RSI.

papers.title: Pooled prevalence of infectious diseases among first responders in the prehospital setting: A systematic review with meta-analysis by occupation
papers.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies covering 19,188 prehospital first responders estimated pooled infection prevalence — hepatitis B 6.2%, hepatitis C 1.8%, MRSA colonisation about 4%, and COVID-19 13.6% in unvaccinated staff.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Occupational exposure risk is the same in uncontrolled prehospital environments everywhere — this is the evidence base behind PPE, vaccination and infection-control protocols Australian crews already work under.
papers.design: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (88 full texts screened, 22 studies included)
papers.n: 19,188 first responders across 22 studies
papers.finding: Pooled prevalence: hepatitis B 6.2% (95% CI 4.5–8.2), hepatitis C 1.8% (0.9–2.9), MRSA colonisation ~4% (2.6–5.9), COVID-19 among unvaccinated staff 13.6% (4.8–25.9), falling to 7.3% after excluding high-bias studies
papers.caveat: Very high heterogeneity across the 22 studies, and the pooled estimates mix paramedics with police and firefighters
papers.shortTitle: How common are blood-borne infections in first responders
papers.learningGoal: Understand how occupational exposure risks for blood-borne infections shape my infection prevention and vaccination practice.

papers.title: Longer collapse-to-first-medical-contact interval is independently associated with ROSC in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a paradoxical finding that may reflect case-mix differences
papers.summary: A Chinese single-centre retrospective cohort of 152 OHCA cases found longer collapse-to-first-medical-contact intervals were independently associated with prehospital ROSC — a paradox the authors attribute to case-mix differences rather than a real benefit of slower response.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Response-interval questions are core to any ambulance service, but this is a small single-centre Chinese system with case-mix confounding the authors themselves flag.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort with dispatch-log and onboard timestamps
papers.n: 152 consecutive OHCA patients, single emergency centre
papers.finding: Longer collapse-to-first-medical-contact interval was independently associated with prehospital ROSC; the authors attribute the paradoxical direction to case-mix differences (arrest aetiology, shockable rhythm)
papers.caveat: Small single-centre cohort where sicker patients reaching crews faster likely explains the association
papers.shortTitle: Longer collapse-to-contact times linked with ROSC
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how case-mix differences shape my interpretation of response interval data when judging cardiac arrest outcomes.

papers.title: Emergency Response and Patient Transport in Remote Indigenous Communities: A Scoping Review
papers.summary: A global scoping review of 76 publications on prehospital emergency response and transport for rural and remote Indigenous communities found air retrieval dominated the literature (71% of publications) while community first response was rarely evaluated — only 16% of publications used an evaluative design.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Directly relevant to remote Australian communities, where long retrieval distances and infrastructure gaps are everyday reality; the review's gaps mirror how little of this pathway has been formally evaluated here.
papers.design: Scoping review (PubMed, Embase, Scopus; March 2026 search)
papers.n: 76 publications reviewed
papers.finding: Air transport/medical evacuation described in 71% of publications and ground transport in 51%; explicit paramedic/EMS detail in 24% and dispatch in 12%; top barriers were infrastructure and communications (92%), cost and jurisdiction (87%), distance to definitive care (83%); only 16% of publications evaluated a pathway
papers.caveat: Descriptive scoping review of mostly unevaluated literature — no outcome data to guide practice
papers.shortTitle: Mapping emergency transport in remote Indigenous communities
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system barriers shaping emergency transport and retrieval for patients in remote Indigenous communities.

papers.title: From sirens to systems: Characterizing EMS and trauma care across America
papers.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
papers.summary: A survey of EMS and trauma system leaders in all 50 US states plus DC found broad protocol and registry coverage — 84% statewide trauma triage protocols, 88% mandatory registry participation — but weak operational coordination, with only 6% a single point of contact for helicopter dispatch and 55% rating their system as needing at least moderate improvement.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US state-patchwork survey — Australian state systems are more centralised, but the coordination, funding and rural-gap themes read familiar from this side of the Pacific.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey of state EMS and trauma system leaders (56-item instrument)
papers.n: 51 US jurisdictions (all 50 states plus DC)
papers.finding: 84% had a state EMS medical director and statewide trauma triage protocols; 88% mandatory trauma registry participation; only 29% a centralised trauma communications centre and 6% a single HEMS dispatch contact; over half rated EMS funding in the two lowest adequacy categories and 55% wanted at least moderate system improvement
papers.caveat: Self-reported leader perceptions describing a US state-based structure that differs from Australian arrangements
papers.shortTitle: How US states organise EMS and trauma systems
papers.learningGoal: Understand how system-level structures like trauma triage protocols and registry participation shape Australian prehospital trauma care.

papers.title: Acute Suffering, Act of Togetherness and On-Scene Space: A Concept Synthesis for Caring in Prehospital Emergency Care
papers.summary: A Swedish-Finnish concept synthesis developed the STOP framework — acute Suffering, act of Togetherness, On-scene space — positioning holistic, patient-centred caring, not just biomedical intervention, as the core of prehospital emergency care.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A theoretical caring-science framework from Nordic nurse-paramedic practice — nothing here changes a protocol, but on-scene patient-centredness is a live conversation in Australian education too.
papers.design: Concept synthesis (deductive-inductive, caring science framework)
papers.n: Concept synthesis integrating theory, clinical experience and literature
papers.finding: Proposes three interlinked concepts — acute Suffering, act of Togetherness and On-scene space — as a structured way to understand caring beyond a biomedical model in the prehospital setting
papers.caveat: Purely theoretical — the framework has not been tested or evaluated in practice
papers.shortTitle: A framework for caring at the scene: STOP
papers.learningGoal: Understand how suffering, togetherness and on-scene space shape holistic caring in paramedic practice.

papers.title: Prospective Observational Study Assessing Patient Characteristics, Management and Early Outcomes of Major Trauma Patients With Prehospital Shock. A preliminary report of the Sydney COAST study
papers.summary: An Australian prospective multicentre registry enrolled 257 adults with prehospital trauma shock over 12 months in Sydney, finding hypotension drove 90% of shock definitions, 53% received prehospital blood, and mortality was 4.7% at 4 hours and 21% at 30 days.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian data, but the prehospital blood that half these patients got is limited to a few Australian services — the shock epidemiology travels nationally, the blood component doesn't yet
papers.design: Prospective multicentre registry, first 12 months (prehospital medical teams)
papers.n: 257 adults with prehospital trauma shock
papers.finding: Hypotension was the shock criterion in 90%; 53% received prehospital blood, 31% needed interventional haemorrhage control, 74% in-hospital transfusion; median ISS 27; mortality 4.7% at 4 hours, 9% at 24 hours, 21% at 30 days
papers.caveat: Preliminary descriptive report — no outcome comparisons, and not all shocked patients had haemorrhage
papers.shortTitle: Sydney COAST registry: trauma shock first year
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my recognition of occult shock in major trauma patients who are not yet hypotensive.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of prehospital capillary high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I in patients with acute chest pain: the prospective multicenter VALIDATE study
papers.summary: A French prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study (VALIDATE) tested prehospital capillary high-sensitivity troponin I on a point-of-care device against NSTEMI at hospital discharge in adults with acute chest pain, with treating clinicians blinded to results.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Point-of-care troponin isn't something Australian ambulances carry — adoption would need a guideline change — and the French systems that ran it are physician-staffed
papers.design: Prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study, blinded index test (physician-staffed)
papers.n: Adults with acute chest pain across 4 French EMS systems and 10 mobile intensive care units
papers.finding: Diagnostic performance expressed as AUC with 95% CIs against predefined thresholds; the indexed abstract's main-results section carries no numbers
papers.caveat: Physician-staffed French setting and no numeric results in the indexed abstract
papers.shortTitle: Roadside capillary troponin for chest pain
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of prehospital point-of-care troponin testing in my assessment of acute chest pain.

papers.title: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: comparing interventions across the UK
papers.summary: A UK literature review of eight articles found bystander CPR rates increasing in England and Scotland while AED use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest has shown little improvement, with demographics and socioeconomic factors shaping prehospital intervention rates.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — UK bystander-intervention data, but the CPR-up/AED-flat pattern is the same battle Australian OHCA registries describe
papers.design: PRISMA-guided literature review
papers.n: 8 peer-reviewed UK articles (544 screened)
papers.finding: Bystander CPR rates increased in England and Scotland; AED use in OHCA showed little improvement; intervention rates varied with demographics and socioeconomic factors
papers.caveat: Small review — eight articles spanning four UK health systems
papers.shortTitle: UK bystander CPR up, AED use flat
papers.learningGoal: Understand the system and socioeconomic factors that shape bystander CPR and AED use in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: FAST Performance Changes After a Training Sequence Including Augmented Reality Guidance Among Paramedic Students
papers.summary: A Japanese single-arm training study gave 18 undergraduate paramedic students a two-hour FAST course including augmented-reality-guided scans, and total examination time fell by a median 263.5 seconds with quality scores improving significantly.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Point-of-care ultrasound is carried by several Australian services but not most, and this was a small student cohort with no control group
papers.design: Single-arm interventional training study, pre/post design
papers.n: 18 undergraduate paramedic students
papers.finding: Median total FAST time fell 263.5 s (95% CI 177–352.5, P<0.001); Task-Specific Checklist and Global Rating Scale scores both improved (P<0.001); no time gain in the Douglas pouch view
papers.caveat: No parallel control group and a fixed scan sequence — the authors call the findings cautious
papers.shortTitle: AR-guided FAST training sped up students
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my FAST scanning technique, including the Douglas pouch view, when using point-of-care ultrasound in the field.

papers.title: Supply of Fibrinogen Concentrate Across Queensland Health
papers.summary: A ten-year Queensland Health supply analysis of 24,717 g of fibrinogen concentrate found 97% went to 54 hospitals and only 1% to ambulance services, while population-adjusted supply rose from 8.19 to 59.2 g per 100,000 between 2016 and 2025.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Fibrinogen concentrate isn't carried by Australian ambulances, so this is supply-chain context for the bleeding debate rather than current practice
papers.design: Retrospective statewide supply analysis
papers.n: 24,717 g of fibrinogen concentrate supplied across Queensland, 2016–2026
papers.finding: 97.0% of supply went to 54 hospitals, 2.0% to retrieval services and 1.0% to ambulance services; 66.2% went to major trauma services and 92.9% to viscoelastic-assay-capable hospitals; population-adjusted supply rose from 8.19 to 59.2 g per 100,000 (2016–2025)
papers.caveat: Supply data only — no patient outcomes, no link to bleeding control or mortality
papers.shortTitle: Fibrinogen concentrate supply grows in Queensland
papers.learningGoal: Understand the supply pathways and access barriers that shape prehospital availability of fibrinogen concentrate in Australia.

papers.title: Interprofessional simulation in prehospital maternity care: learning from joint training
papers.summary: A UK peer-led interprofessional simulation put paramedic and midwifery students through prehospital maternity emergencies together, with students reporting better role clarity, confidence and shared decision-making.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A UK student programme, but joint obstetric training with midwives speaks directly to how Australian paramedic courses could run the same low-frequency, high-risk scenarios
papers.design: Peer-led interprofessional simulation, reflective report
papers.n: Paramedic and midwifery students at one UK university (count not reported)
papers.finding: Students reported improved understanding of professional roles, increased confidence and better appreciation of collaborative decision-making; the student-led format fostered psychological safety
papers.caveat: Reflective practice report with no outcome measures
papers.shortTitle: Paramedic and midwifery students train together
papers.learningGoal: Understand how interprofessional training with midwifery colleagues strengthens role clarity and shared decision-making in prehospital maternity emergencies.

papers.title: Emergency medical services personnel's work capability sets: associations with job demands, job resources, and flourishing at work
papers.summary: A South African cross-sectional survey of 197 EMS personnel found emotional demands were associated with lower work capability and flourishing, while autonomy and co-worker support — not job demands — distinguished the strongest capability group.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — South African EMS, but the demands-resources pattern echoes what Australian paramedic wellbeing studies keep finding
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey with latent class analysis
papers.n: 197 EMS personnel
papers.finding: Three capability sets emerged (weak 48%, constrained 30%, robust 22%); emotional demands correlated negatively with capability and flourishing, while autonomy and co-worker support differentiated the groups and job demands did not
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional self-report in one country — no causal claims possible
papers.shortTitle: Autonomy and support, not workload, drive flourishing
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how autonomy and co-worker support shape my work capability and flourishing under emotionally demanding conditions.

papers.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
papers.summary: A nationwide Dutch study compared HEMS with prehospital ECPR against conventional HEMS in adults 50 or younger with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and found 40% survival to discharge with ECPR versus 20% without, with better neurological outcomes at 6 months.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital ECPR runs from physician-staffed helicopter services — an intensive care tier well beyond Australian road practice — so this informs where the evidence is heading rather than what crews do today.
papers.design: Nationwide nonrandomised comparative cohort (OnScene, Netherlands)
papers.n: 231 adults ≤ 50 with refractory OHCA (144 ECPR-capable HEMS vs 87 conventional)
papers.finding: Survival to discharge 40% with ECPR vs 20% without (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.59–4.66); favourable neurological outcome at 6 months 36% vs 13% (OR 4.22, 95% CI 2.82–6.32); 32 adverse events with ECPR vs 11
papers.caveat: Not randomised — patients attended by ECPR-capable HEMS may differ systematically, and the ECPR group had nearly three times the adverse events
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital ECPR linked to doubled arrest survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and harms of prehospital ECPR for young adults in refractory cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest
papers.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
papers.summary: A cluster-randomised trial across 55 North Carolina county clusters (22,459 patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest) found a multifaceted community and EMS programme did not improve survival with good neurological outcome (9.0% vs 9.4%).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Dispatch recognition, telephone CPR instructions, community CPR training and first-responder AED use are core parts of Australian systems, and this is a large cluster-randomised trial with a clear null result.
papers.design: Registry-based cluster-randomised trial (CARES registry, North Carolina)
papers.n: 22,459 adults with OHCA across 55 county clusters
papers.finding: Survival to discharge with good neurological outcome 9.0% (intervention) vs 9.4% (usual care), adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.75–1.26, P = 0.80
papers.caveat: The intervention bundled four components, so it can't show whether one element — such as telecommunicator CPR instructions — underperformed
papers.shortTitle: Big community arrest programme didn't change survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how bundled community and EMS resuscitation interventions influence survival outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Prehospital endotracheal intubation and return of spontaneous circulation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients: a retrospective cohort study based on prehospital emergency registry data
papers.summary: A Chinese regional EMS registry cohort of 6,162 adult non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients found prehospital endotracheal intubation associated with more prehospital ROSC than basic airways (21.1% vs 3.8%, propensity-matched OR 6.33).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A physician-staffed Chinese system where on-scene doctors chose the airway; intubation is an intensive care paramedic skill in most Australian services, and the association almost certainly reflects who was selected for a tube.
papers.design: Retrospective registry cohort with propensity-score matching
papers.n: 6,162 adults with non-traumatic OHCA (1,448 intubated vs 4,714 basic airway)
papers.finding: ROSC 21.1% with intubation vs 3.8% with basic airway (multivariable OR 7.61, propensity-matched OR 6.33); the unadjusted association was not significant in the shockable-rhythm stratum
papers.caveat: Airway strategy was chosen by on-scene physicians, so sicker or different patients were selected for intubation, and the registry had no long-term survival or neurological data
papers.shortTitle: Intubation linked to more ROSC in OHCA registry
papers.learningGoal: Weigh advanced airway management against basic airway techniques when managing cardiac arrest in the Australian prehospital setting.

papers.title: Whole blood transfusion vs. component therapy for trauma resuscitation in the prehospital and emergency department settings: a systematic review
papers.journal: International Journal of Medicine in Developing Countries
papers.summary: A PRISMA systematic review of 22 comparative studies (about 95,000 patients) on whole blood versus component therapy for trauma resuscitation found mixed mortality results — survival signals in hypotensive, penetrating and geriatric subgroups but not everywhere — with consistently lower transfusion requirements and comparable or better safety with whole blood.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Blood products are carried by several Australian services but not most, and the review spans prehospital and ED settings, so it informs the whole-blood-versus-components debate rather than everyday practice.
papers.design: Systematic review (PRISMA 2020, ROBINS-I) of comparative studies
papers.n: 22 comparative studies, about 95,000 trauma patients
papers.finding: Survival benefit with whole blood in some studies — hypotensive patients (aOR 0.72 for SBP<90), penetrating injury (RR 0.36), geriatric (OR 0.60) — but no difference in others including one randomised trial; transfusion requirements consistently lower with whole blood; VTE risk lower (OR 0.70)
papers.caveat: Narrative synthesis only due to heterogeneity, and the publishing journal is low-profile — treat the pooled direction with caution
papers.shortTitle: Whole blood vs components: mixed mortality, lower transfusion needs
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and limitations of prehospital whole blood versus component therapy when resuscitating hypotensive trauma patients.

papers.title: Temporal Changes in the Association between Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature and Heat-Related Emergency Ambulance Dispatches across Japan: A Multi-Prefecture Time-Series Analysis Spanning the COVID-19 Pandemic and National Heatstroke Alert Implementation (2015–2023)
papers.summary: A Japanese multi-prefecture time-series analysis of 577,027 heat-related ambulance dispatches (2015–2023) found the association between wet-bulb globe temperature and dispatches attenuated by 44% after the pandemic and national heatstroke alerts, yet absolute heat-attributable demand still grew 18%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Heat-driven ambulance demand peaks are an Australian summer reality, and the finding that public alerts softened relative risk without containing absolute workload speaks directly to summer deployment planning.
papers.design: Two-stage distributed lag nonlinear model time-series analysis across 47 prefectures
papers.n: 577,027 heat-related ambulance dispatches, Japan 2015–2023
papers.finding: At the 95th WBGT percentile the pooled cumulative relative risk fell from 10.45 (2015–19) to 5.90 (2022–23), a 43.6% reduction; severe-case relative risks also declined while age 65+ became the strongest effect modifier; heat-attributable counts still rose 18.1%
papers.caveat: Ecological time-series design — the attenuation can't be attributed to the heatstroke alert system specifically versus pandemic-era behaviour change
papers.shortTitle: Heat alerts eased heat-dispatch risk but demand still grew
papers.learningGoal: Understand how heat alert systems and changing community behaviour shape surging heat-related ambulance demand in Australia.

papers.title: Educational challenges in teaching obstetric and gynecologic emergencies: perspectives of EMS students
papers.summary: An Iranian qualitative study of 14 EMS students and recent graduates identified six categories of educational challenge in obstetric and gynaecologic emergencies, centred on a disconnect between educational preparation and real-world demands, with calls for more simulation, clinical exposure and gender-sensitive communication training.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Obstetric emergencies are low-frequency, high-stakes ambulance work, and the gaps described — limited clinical exposure, reliance on simulation — mirror those reported by Australian paramedic students.
papers.design: Qualitative conventional content analysis, semi-structured interviews
papers.n: 14 EMS students and recent graduates, Iran
papers.finding: 1,532 codes distilled to six challenge categories: educational content and approaches, clinical education barriers, communication and cultural barriers, resource limitations, motivation and educational justice, and process management; higher-order category: disconnects between preparation and real-world demands
papers.caveat: Single-country student perspectives with no measure of actual clinical performance
papers.shortTitle: EMS students report obs/gyn training gaps
papers.learningGoal: Understand how gaps in obstetric emergency education affect paramedic preparedness and gender-sensitive patient communication.

papers.title: Smart Alerting in Smartphone‐Based First Responder Systems and Arrival Before Emergency Medical Services:The ALARM Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
papers.summary: A three-arm German RCT across 823 activations found smartphone smart-alerting got community first responders to OHCA before EMS in 58% of missions — better than a 600 m fixed radius (31%) but no better than a 2500 m radius (57%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Community first-responder alerting already runs in several Australian systems; the radius-versus-estimated-travel-time question transfers directly, though German dispatch geography and responder density differ.
papers.design: Prospective randomised three-arm trial
papers.n: 823 activations, 1482 dispatched community first responders
papers.finding: CFR arrived before EMS in 58% (smart alerting), 57% (2500 m) and 31% (600 m); smart alerting vs 600 m risk difference +26.8% (95% CI 18.6–34.4), vs 2500 m +1.2% (95% CI −7.0 to +9.3, p=0.80)
papers.caveat: No advantage over simply widening the alert radius, response rates were lower with the larger radius, and patient outcomes were not measured
papers.shortTitle: Smart first-responder alerting vs fixed-radius alerts in OHCA
papers.learningGoal: Understand how community first responder alerting systems influence arrival before EMS in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Association between mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure and outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A single-centre Belgian cohort of intubated OHCA patients managed by a physician-staffed team found mechanical ventilation with PEEP during CPR was associated with higher odds of ROSC (adjusted OR 1.58) than manual ventilation without PEEP.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Mechanical ventilation with PEEP is an intensive care paramedic capability in most services, and the study comes from a physician-staffed team — the ventilation question is relevant, the crewing model isn't ours.
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective cohort with continuous intratracheal pressure monitoring, physician-staffed EMS
papers.n: 362 intubated adults with OHCA
papers.finding: Adjusted OR for ROSC with mechanical ventilation using PEEP 1.58 (95% CI 1.01–2.50, p=0.048); unadjusted OR for survival to hospital discharge 2.22 (95% CI 1.03–4.78)
papers.caveat: Observational single-centre design, and the survival-to-discharge association was not adjusted for confounders
papers.shortTitle: PEEP during CPR linked with more ROSC
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and risks of applying positive end-expiratory pressure during ventilation in cardiac arrest resuscitation.

papers.title: Added value of brain perfusion ultrasound to prehospital stroke scales-a secondary analysis of the SONAS trial
papers.summary: A German exploratory reanalysis of the 20-patient SONAS trial found portable non-imaging brain perfusion ultrasound combined with prehospital stroke scales sorted suspected stroke into likely-LVO, likely-non-LVO and unassessable groups better than either method alone.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Portable ultrasound is carried by a handful of Australian services, most don't, and prehospital LVO triage is an active question here — the approach informs that debate rather than current practice.
papers.design: Exploratory secondary analysis of a 20-patient portable ultrasound device trial
papers.n: 20 patients with acute ischaemic stroke
papers.finding: Combining brain perfusion ultrasound with prehospital stroke scales shifted sensitivity and negative predictive value higher and reclassified all patients misdiagnosed by either method alone; three prehospital-ICH false positives showed severe perfusion deficits suggesting LVO
papers.caveat: Only 20 patients, retrospective design, and the authors themselves call validation critical
papers.shortTitle: Ultrasound added to stroke scales for LVO triage
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of portable brain perfusion ultrasound in improving prehospital triage of suspected large vessel occlusion stroke.

papers.title: Differences between Mainstream and Sidestream Capnography during Resuscitation
papers.summary: A Spanish retrospective analysis of 23 OHCA recordings with concurrent mainstream and sidestream capnography found mainstream systematically recorded higher ETCO2 (bias 3.94 mmHg, limits of agreement -3.21 to 11.09 mmHg), though trends and abrupt rises/drops were consistently co-detected.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — ETCO2-guided CPR quality monitoring is standard practice on Australian ambulances, and the numbers crews chart or hand over at hospital depend on which technology the monitor uses.
papers.design: Retrospective device-comparison analysis of synchronized capnography waveforms
papers.n: 23 OHCA recordings (3,460 paired ventilations)
papers.finding: Mainstream ETCO2 bias +3.94 mmHg vs sidestream (limits of agreement -3.21 to 11.09 mmHg, proportional bias 0.0746); trends matched (-1.44 vs -1.41 mmHg/min, p=0.93); abrupt rises >=10 mmHg co-detected in 7/8 and drops in 10/15
papers.caveat: Small sample — 23 recordings from one region, so the wide limits of agreement are imprecisely estimated
papers.shortTitle: Mainstream and sidestream capnography give different ETCO2
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how differences between mainstream and sidestream capnography affect my interpretation of EtCO2 trends during cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Characteristics and experiences of community first responders in suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A survey of early adopters prior to local system implementation
papers.summary: A cross-sectional survey of 2,704 registered community first responders in two Swedish regions before local system launch found most were CPR-trained and felt prepared (97.3%) but real dispatch experience was low (15.1% ever dispatched, 1.9% performed CPR).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Community first responder schemes run in parts of Australia and the same readiness-versus-experience question applies wherever a new scheme launches.
papers.design: Multicentre cross-sectional survey (two regions, pre-implementation)
papers.n: 2,704 respondents of 14,141 registered first responders (19.1%)
papers.finding: 84.3% had CPR training within two years and 97.3% felt prepared (both associated with healthcare/emergency background and recent training, p<0.001), yet only 15.1% had ever been dispatched, 2.8% arrived before EMS and 1.9% performed CPR
papers.caveat: Self-reported readiness in volunteers with almost no real-world dispatch experience; 19.1% response rate
papers.shortTitle: Community first responders trained but rarely dispatched
papers.learningGoal: Understand how volunteer readiness and dispatch integration shape community responder impact in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Chest pain risk-stratification tools used or trialled in Ambulance Health Service settings: A Scoping Review
papers.summary: A scoping review of 27 articles mapped eight chest-pain risk-stratification tools used or trialled in ambulance settings, finding the HEART score and derivatives most studied but with varying and incomplete validation for ambulance use.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Safely triaging chest pain without transport is an active question for Australian ambulance services, but the tools reviewed are mostly hospital-derived and inconsistently validated for prehospital use.
papers.design: Scoping review (JBI methodology, PRISMA-ScR)
papers.n: 27 articles, 8 risk-stratification tools
papers.finding: Eight chest-pain risk-stratification tools were used or trialled in ambulance settings; HEART and its derivatives were the most frequently studied, with performance varying across settings and validation for ambulance use incomplete
papers.caveat: Scoping review — descriptive mapping only, no pooled performance estimates
papers.shortTitle: Mapping chest pain risk tools in ambulance care
papers.learningGoal: Compare chest pain risk-stratification tools and their validity for prehospital use to strengthen my cardiac triage decisions.

papers.title: Human-in-the-Loop in AI-assisted Resuscitation Protocols: Conceptual Pitfalls and Practical Considerations
papers.summary: A conceptual analysis of AI-assisted OHCA resuscitation protocols argues that time pressure, protocol-driven practice and ambiguous authority can turn human-in-the-loop oversight of AI recommendations into symbolic governance rather than real crew control.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — AI decision support is arriving in dispatch and clinical systems worldwide, and whether crews can meaningfully override it is a governance question every ambulance service will face.
papers.design: Conceptual/policy analysis (no empirical data)
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: No empirical data — proposes five policy measures including ecological trialling, designed-in explainability, defined escalation triggers and authority, and protection for justified deviation from AI recommendations
papers.caveat: Purely conceptual; no data on how crews actually behave with AI recommendations
papers.shortTitle: AI in cardiac arrest: oversight may be symbolic
papers.learningGoal: Understand how authority, escalation triggers and justified deviation shape real oversight of AI-assisted resuscitation recommendations.

papers.title: Is prehospital opioid administration safe in children? A register-based study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Danish register study of 1,531 children given prehospital opioids (99.7% fentanyl) found 15.1% had at least one clinical sign compatible with opioid adverse effects, serious signs were uncommon (bradycardia and respiratory depression 0.7% each), and 63.6% were still in pain at hospital arrival.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Fentanyl is standard prehospital analgesia across Australian services, and a national registry like this speaks directly to how crews dose paediatric pain relief.
papers.design: Retrospective register-based cohort with medical record review
papers.n: 1,531 children aged 0–14 given prehospital opioids, Denmark 2017–2022
papers.finding: 15.1% had at least one clinical sign compatible with opioid-related adverse effects; bradycardia 0.7%, respiratory depression 0.7%; no opioid antidote given; 63.6% in pain at arrival and 51% received further in-hospital analgesia.
papers.caveat: Retrospective register review — nonspecific signs such as nausea and drowsiness can't be firmly attributed to opioids (no other explanation identified in 9.2%).
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric prehospital fentanyl: serious adverse effects rare
papers.learningGoal: Refine my assessment and monitoring of prehospital opioid analgesia in paediatric patients to reduce under-treatment of pain.

papers.title: The CARE framework for traumatic cardiac arrest: integrating parallel priorities in resuscitation
papers.summary: A framework for integrating parallel priorities in traumatic cardiac arrest resuscitation — abstract not yet available, so no results to report.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Traumatic cardiac arrest management is core paramedic work in Australia, but this comes from a physician-staffed European system and the framework details can't be assessed without the abstract.
papers.design: Framework / consensus-style paper
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Not reported — abstract not yet available.
papers.caveat: Abstract not yet available; title-only look after 14 days in the pending queue.
papers.shortTitle: CARE framework for traumatic cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Refine my prioritisation of reversible causes and parallel interventions when managing traumatic cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Forecasting the rate of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in the United States based on recent trends in prehospital transfusion
papers.summary: US researchers forecast that growing prehospital transfusion of RhD-positive blood to females of childbearing potential will lead to haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, with one predicted case every 0.5–20 years depending on region and model.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is limited to a few Australian services, so this informs the debate more than current practice.
papers.design: Forecasting model (regression on US transfusion trends, 500 instantiations per model)
papers.n: 779 females of childbearing potential projected to receive prehospital transfusion in the US in 2029
papers.finding: One HDFN case forecast every 0.5–20 years depending on region and model (base case: 0.5 years in the South, 20.0 in the Northeast).
papers.caveat: A forecasting exercise built on US trends and assumptions — no observed HDFN cases.
papers.shortTitle: Forecast: prehospital transfusion growth and HDFN risk
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the risk of haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn when giving RhD-positive blood to females of childbearing potential.

papers.title: Implementing Handle With Care: A Cross-Sector Model Linking Schools and First Responders to Support Children Exposed to Potentially Traumatic Events
papers.summary: A US evaluation of the Handle With Care programme linking first responders with schools after potentially traumatic child events found it feasible in an under-resourced Mississippi district, with significant gains in staff trauma-informed attitudes but low notification volume in year one.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US police–fire–ambulance-to-school notification model that doesn't map directly onto Australian practice, though the trauma-informed training findings travel.
papers.design: Mixed-methods first-year implementation evaluation (training, notification process, surveys, qualitative interviews)
papers.n: 75 school staff and 64 first responders, one Mississippi school district
papers.finding: Significant gains in school staff trauma-informed attitudes; greater first-responder training exposure linked with lower burnout; disciplinary referrals decreased overall while in-school suspensions increased; attendance stable.
papers.caveat: Single under-resourced district, first year of implementation, student outcomes exploratory.
papers.shortTitle: First responders notifying schools after child trauma
papers.learningGoal: Understand how early notification between emergency services and schools can support children exposed to traumatic events.

papers.title: Pocket Mask versus Face Shield Ventilation by Laypersons during Simulated Pediatric CPR: A Randomized Crossover Study
papers.summary: In a randomised crossover simulation study, laypersons using a pocket mask achieved the ≥200 mL mean tidal volume threshold more often than with a face shield during simulated paediatric CPR (89.2% vs 77.5%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian first-aid and CPR education, including bystander-facing resources promoted nationally, relies on laypersons delivering rescue breaths; this suggests pocket masks may be more effective barrier devices than face shields for lay rescuers performing paediatric CPR, informing community CPR training and public-access equipment decisions across Australia.
papers.design: Randomised crossover simulation study
papers.n: 102 adult laypersons
papers.finding: 89.2% achieved mean tidal volume ≥200 mL with the pocket mask vs 77.5% with the face shield (adjusted OR 4.36, 95% CI 1.33–14.32; paired absolute difference 11.8 percentage points, 3.3–20.2); mean tidal volume was 38.8 mL higher (13.6–64.0) with the pocket mask; insufficient breaths were less frequent (6.5% vs 15.2%, adjusted OR 0.23, 0.14–0.37), adequate breaths more frequent (65.2% vs 57.6%, 1.46, 1.15–1.86), and excessive breaths did not differ significantly (28.4% vs 27.2%, 1.21, 0.91–1.61); high willingness to ventilate a stranger was 73.5% (pocket mask) vs 51.0% (face shield).
papers.caveat: Manikin simulation with laypersons does not establish real-world effectiveness, and willingness was rated only once after both devices were used, so device-order and behavioural effects are unknown.
papers.shortTitle: Layperson CPR: pocket mask versus face shield
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and limitations of barrier devices for paediatric rescue ventilation when supporting layperson CPR in the community.

papers.title: 2026 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations: Summary from the Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid Task Forces
papers.summary: This annual ILCOR Consensus on Science with Treatment Recommendations (multinational) systematically reviewed the latest resuscitation evidence across six task forces (BLS, ALS, paediatric, neonatal, education/implementation/teams, and first aid) using GRADE criteria; no single headline finding or figure is reported.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — ILCOR consensus statements underpin the Australian Resuscitation Council guidelines that govern paramedic resuscitation practice nationally, so the updated evidence syntheses and identified knowledge gaps shape future ambulance clinical practice guidelines across Australia.
papers.design: Systematic evidence review and consensus statement (GRADE methodology)
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Summary of the most recent published resuscitation evidence reviewed by the six ILCOR task forces, with consensus treatment recommendations, justification and evidence-to-decision highlights, and priority knowledge gaps; no specific effect estimates given in the abstract.
papers.caveat: It is a consensus summary without a single quantified result, and the abstract does not detail the scope, numbers of studies, or certainty of the specific recommendations.
papers.shortTitle: 2026 ILCOR resuscitation consensus published
papers.learningGoal: Update my knowledge of current international resuscitation evidence and how it shapes my arrest management across adult and paediatric patients.

papers.title: Layperson naloxone administration and subsequent emergency medical services care for opioid overdose
papers.summary: In a US cross-sectional study of 26,087 EMS activations for opioid overdose, layperson-administered naloxone (30.7% of cases) was associated with less subsequent EMS naloxone (24.4% vs 34.8%) and lower odds of transport (aOR 0.78).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Community and take-home naloxone programs run across Australia, and bystander response before EMS arrival is the same question everywhere.
papers.design: Cross-sectional analysis of a national EMS registry
papers.n: 26,087 EMS activations for opioid overdose (adults 16 and over)
papers.finding: Layperson naloxone preceded 30.7% of activations; any subsequent EMS naloxone 24.4% vs 34.8% (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.68–0.78) and transport 79.4% vs 84.4% (aOR 0.78, 95% CI 0.73–0.84); advanced airway attempts (1.6% vs 1.4%) and cardiac arrest (6.6% vs 6.0%) uncommon in both groups.
papers.caveat: Registry cross-section — why transports were lower (refusal versus genuine recovery) isn't known.
papers.shortTitle: Layperson naloxone linked to fewer EMS interventions
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how prehospital naloxone given by bystanders affects my assessment and transport decisions in opioid overdose.

papers.title: Focus Where It Matters: Design and Implementation of a Physiology‐Based Care Pathway for Traumatic Shock
papers.summary: An Australian Level 1 trauma centre implemented a physiology-based traumatic shock pathway (SBP ≤ 90 mmHg, shock index > 1, prehospital blood or senior clinician concern) and post-implementation staff surveys rated the equipment, interventions and roles highly, though clinical effectiveness wasn't assessed.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — An ED trauma-bay implementation study, and prehospital blood — one of its activation triggers — is limited to a few Australian services, so this informs the debate more than current practice.
papers.design: Single-centre quality-improvement implementation study with pre/post staff surveys
papers.n: 3,667 major trauma patients, of whom 324 (8.8%) met shocked trauma criteria
papers.finding: Shocked patients had markedly higher ED mortality (6.8% vs 0.4%); favourable ratings of trauma bay equipment rose from about one-quarter to 87.0%, with 85.2–88.9% favourability for timely life-saving interventions, pathway embedding and role confidence.
papers.caveat: Evaluation was staff experience only — no clinical outcome assessment.
papers.shortTitle: Physiology-based traumatic shock pathway rolled out
papers.learningGoal: Recognise early physiological indicators of traumatic shock to guide timely activation of blood-based resuscitation pathways.

papers.title: Long-term outcomes and quality of life of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and their caregivers
papers.summary: An Italian tertiary centre followed refractory OHCA survivors treated with ECPR (63 of 406 discharged alive) and their caregivers, finding long-term survival largely confined to good neurological recovery but preserved quality of life, with cognitive impairment and sleep problems common and anxiety more frequent in caregivers.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ECPR is a hospital-initiated therapy Australian ambulances don't deliver, but the survivor and caregiver outcomes inform the recovery conversations crews have with families.
papers.design: Single-centre cohort with long-term multidimensional follow-up
papers.n: 406 ECPR-treated patients; 17 survivors and 19 caregivers formally assessed
papers.finding: 63/406 (16%) discharged alive; at median 3.1 years 61% were alive, 82% with favourable neurology, and only 1.7% of all treated were alive with poor neurology; mild cognitive impairment in 6/16 survivors, poor sleep in 10/17, anxiety symptoms more common in caregivers (6/18 vs 1/17).
papers.caveat: Single centre with only 17 assessed survivors — survivor and selection bias likely.
papers.shortTitle: Long-term life after ECPR for cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Understand the long-term survivor and caregiver outcomes that follow ECPR for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Consensus Statement on Traumatic Brain Injury in First Responders: The 1st International Conference on TBI in First Responders
papers.journal: The Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation
papers.summary: A 52-member international group used a modified Delphi process to produce the first consensus recommendations on traumatic brain injury in first responders — 28 statements covering injury reporting, assessment, return to duty, mental health and workplace policy, all reaching consensus.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A US-led consensus, but the occupational questions — nonpunitive reporting, return to duty, mental health — apply to Australian first-responder agencies equally.
papers.design: Consensus statement (modified Delphi, two voting rounds)
papers.n: 52 panel members; 28 final recommendations
papers.finding: 27 of 29 preliminary statements reached consensus in round 1 and all 28 final recommendations reached the 80% threshold in round 2, across six domains from injury risk and reporting to workplace policy.
papers.caveat: Consensus opinion rather than evidence of effectiveness, and focused on TBI suffered on the job rather than patient care.
papers.shortTitle: First consensus on TBI in first responders
papers.learningGoal: Understand how workplace TBI risks, reporting culture and return-to-duty practices affect my own wellbeing and professional practice.

papers.title: Implementation and Evaluation of the Stroke Triage App Among Paramedics in Prehospital Emergency Care: Sequential Mixed Methods Study
papers.summary: A Dutch mixed-methods evaluation of the Stroke Triage App across two EMS regions found good initial adoption (median 120 app triages/month) but inconsistent routine integration, with workflow fit and limited perceived added value the main barriers.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — A Dutch paramedic service, but the adoption-versus-integration gap for clinical decision-support apps is the same one Australian services face.
papers.design: Sequential mixed-methods implementation evaluation (usage data, survey, interviews)
papers.n: 246 paramedics with app accounts; 76 surveyed, 9 interviewed
papers.finding: Median 120 triages/month (IQR 107–131) and median 7 uses per paramedic (IQR 3–13); the app was well accepted and supported structured neurological assessment, but clinical urgency, poor workflow integration and limited perceived added value hampered routine use.
papers.caveat: Only 31% of account holders responded, and usage data can't show whether triage advice changed decisions.
papers.shortTitle: Stroke triage app adopted but not embedded
papers.learningGoal: Understand how digital decision support tools fit into prehospital stroke workflows and where barriers to routine use arise.

papers.title: Emergency Life-Saving Technician-Performed Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma in Moving Ambulances: A Pilot Innovation Report
papers.summary: Twenty Japanese Emergency Life-Saving Technicians performed FAST on a manikin in a moving ambulance with near-identical checklist scores stationary, at 15 km/h and 30 km/h, with transmitted image quality adequate for remote physician review.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital ultrasound is carried by a handful of Australian services and most don't, and Japan's physician-supervised technician model adds a layer we don't have.
papers.design: Prospective observational simulation pilot with non-inferiority analysis
papers.n: 20 Emergency Life-Saving Technicians, three speed conditions
papers.finding: Mean Task-Specific Checklist scores 23.4 stationary, 23.4 at 15 km/h and 23.7 at 30 km/h (of 24); non-inferiority met at both speeds, and specialist physicians could review transmitted images.
papers.caveat: Manikin pilot in a controlled setting — no patients, and Japanese ELSTs can't yet perform ultrasound clinically.
papers.shortTitle: FAST feasible in a moving ambulance (manikin)
papers.learningGoal: Understand how prehospital ultrasound skill requirements and image quality vary when scanning during transport.

papers.title: Efficiency of Rescue Paramedic Hoist versus Underslung Antenna in Helicopter-Based Avalanche Searches: A Randomized Trial
papers.summary: In a Norwegian randomised field trial with a live search-and-rescue helicopter crew, hoisting a rescue paramedic with a handheld transceiver found buried avalanche transceivers 143 seconds faster on average than an underslung antenna search across 25 runs.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A niche alpine rescue question, but the crew-on-ground-versus-equipment trade-off applies to any Australian rescue helicopter tasking.
papers.design: Dual randomised experimental field trial with an operational SAR helicopter crew
papers.n: 25 trial runs (13 antenna, 12 hoist) over three days, six buried transceivers
papers.finding: Hoist search cut time to transceiver found by 143 seconds (95% CI 113–172, p<0.001), time to optimal signal by 29 seconds and time to paramedic on ground by 124 seconds.
papers.caveat: Simulated 80 × 150 m field with one active transceiver per run — real avalanches mean multiple burials and harder terrain.
papers.shortTitle: Hoisted paramedic beat antenna in avalanche search
papers.learningGoal: Understand how hoist-based avalanche search tactics shape prehospital retrieval times in alpine rescue operations.

papers.title: Development and Initial Assessment of a Low-Cost Skin Tear Management Task Trainer for Paramedic Education
papers.summary: A Canadian team 3D-printed a skin tear management task trainer for paramedic education costing about CAD 35 in materials, and learners rated 14 trainers highly for realism and educational value.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Canadian paramedic education project, but low-cost trainers and community wound management are the same challenge here.
papers.design: Technical report with iterative prototyping and acceptability assessment
papers.n: 14 type 1 task trainers assessed with paramedic learners
papers.finding: Perceived self-efficacy 4.68/5, realism 4.64/5 and educational value 4.85/5; each unit took 20–30 minutes of active fabrication plus 80–90 minutes curing.
papers.caveat: Perception ratings only — no objective measure of skill acquisition.
papers.shortTitle: Low-cost 3D-printed skin tear trainer for paramedics
