papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my wound care technique for skin tears using realistic simulation before managing them in the field.

papers.title: Transcutaneous Pacing in the Prehospital Setting – A Retrospective Cohort Study of Electrical Capture
papers.summary: A US EMS agency reviewed continuous monitor ECGs from 56 patients given prehospital transcutaneous pacing between 2017 and 2024 and found electrical capture in only 32%, often intermittent, with clinician-verbalised pulses coinciding with capture in just 15% of instances.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Transcutaneous pacing is carried by only a handful of Australian services, so this speaks most directly to the services that pace rather than day-to-day practice everywhere.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort with continuous ECG review
papers.n: 56 patients who received prehospital transcutaneous pacing
papers.finding: Electrical capture in 18/56 (32%); among capturers, complete capture occurred only 27.2% of pacing time; median SBP change +22 mmHg with capture vs 0 mmHg without (p=0.031); clinician-verbalised pulse coincided with electrical capture in only 4/26 (15%) instances
papers.caveat: Single US agency, small sample, and capture judged from monitor recordings rather than patient-centred outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Electrical capture uncommon in prehospital transcutaneous pacing
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when prehospital transcutaneous pacing is likely to achieve electrical capture and meaningful perfusion.

papers.title: The Accuracy and Precision of Gravity-Driven Infusions
papers.summary: In a controlled US laboratory simulation, 55 paramedics setting nine drip rates on a standardised gravity set produced overall flow errors from -45.3% to +5.8%, with imprecision driven mainly by human counting and whole-number target rates more accurate than fractional ones.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Gravity sets and counted drip rates are standard kit on Australian ambulances, so these accuracy numbers apply directly to crews.
papers.design: Controlled laboratory simulation
papers.n: 55 paramedics, nine drip rates each
papers.finding: Overall inaccuracy ranged from -45.3% to +5.8%; imprecision was primarily human; 1 gtt/s targets more accurate than all others (absolute error 31.1% vs 48.5%); whole-number rates more accurate than fractional (40.7% vs 54.1%)
papers.caveat: Laboratory setup with a standardised giving set; field conditions, movement and different tubing not tested
papers.shortTitle: Counted drip rates vary widely between paramedics
papers.learningGoal: Refine my technique for setting and counting gravity-driven infusion rates to reduce dosing error in the field.

papers.title: Compliance with French Military Health Service guidelines for prehospital transfusion of blood products during forward aeromedical evacuations in Sahel (2015 to 2023)
papers.summary: A French military review of 206 forward aeromedical evacuations for trauma in Sahel (2015–2023) found 64 casualties transfused prehospital, with 65% of transfused patients not meeting guideline criteria, while heart rate above 110, shock index above 1, penetrating or pelvic trauma and FAST effusion were more frequent among them.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is limited to a few Australian services, and this comes from a military aeromedical evacuation chain, so it informs the transfusion-trigger debate more than current civilian practice.
papers.design: Multicentre retrospective observational study
papers.n: 206 trauma casualties evacuated, 64 transfused with 89 blood products
papers.finding: Meeting transfusion criteria was associated with requiring transfusion (RR 3.20, 95% CI 2.29–4.47); 65% of transfused patients did not meet criteria; median transfusion rate 25 mL/min
papers.caveat: Retrospective military cohort with no civilian comparison; authors call for prospective evaluation before any guideline revision
papers.shortTitle: Military prehospital transfusion often outside guideline criteria
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the risks and benefits of prehospital blood transfusion when my trauma patients fall outside guideline criteria.

papers.title: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty in Paramedic Students: A START Triage Perspective
papers.journal: Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness
papers.summary: A Turkish cross-sectional survey of 121 paramedic students found theoretical START triage knowledge (mean 69.99 ± 14.76) was not significantly associated with intolerance of uncertainty or decision-making style subscale scores.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — A paper-based knowledge test with self-reported psychosocial measures only — no simulation or field performance — so there is little here that transfers to triage practice on the road.
papers.design: Cross-sectional questionnaire study
papers.n: 121 paramedic students
papers.finding: Mean START knowledge score 69.99 ± 14.76; no significant association with intolerance of uncertainty or any decision-making style subscale
papers.caveat: Declarative knowledge only, single training program, self-reported psychosocial measures
papers.shortTitle: START triage knowledge unrelated to student decision styles
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement when applying mass casualty triage under uncertainty in the Australian prehospital context.

papers.title: What works well for children and young people suffering acute pain attended by ambulance? A realist evaluation
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A UK realist evaluation across three English ambulance services and two children's EDs — 44 interview transcripts plus 34,068 clinical records — refined the programme theory for paediatric pain care, with clinician preparedness and compassionate person-centred care emerging as the key mechanisms.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Paediatric pain is core ambulance work across Australia and the mechanisms described — preparedness, privacy, reassurance, allaying negative assumptions — are actionable in any service, whatever the drug chart looks like.
papers.design: Realist evaluation (qualitative interviews, diaries, artwork + routine clinical records)
papers.n: 44 participants (21 ambulance clinicians, 14 parents/carers, 9 children/young people); 34,068 clinical records
papers.finding: Around 60% of children and young people needing an ambulance for a painful condition experience poor pain management; preparedness (education, training, exposure, experience) and compassionate person-centred care were the refined programme theory's central mechanisms
papers.caveat: Realist evaluation generating theory, not effectiveness evidence, and participants were self-selected
papers.shortTitle: What helps kids in pain in ambulances
papers.learningGoal: Improve my paediatric pain assessment and management by strengthening clinician preparedness and delivering compassionate, person-centred care.

papers.title: Revalidation of the M-DIRECT scale in prehospital identification of acute stroke patients for endovascular treatment
papers.summary: A Spanish prospective study of 1,950 prehospital code-stroke patients revalidated the M-DIRECT scale five years after implementation, showing 77% sensitivity and 76% specificity for identifying endovascular-treatment candidates, with a positive score more than tripling the odds of EVT.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Stroke destination decisions are everyday paramedic work here, but M-DIRECT isn't used on Australian roads and Spain runs a physician-dispatch model the scale was built into.
papers.design: Prospective observational cohort
papers.n: 1,950 prehospital code-stroke patients, urban network of 6.75 million
papers.finding: Sensitivity 77%, specificity 76%, AUC 0.768 for EVT; 58% of M-DIRECT-positive patients had LVO/MeVO and 50% underwent EVT; positive score independently associated with EVT (aOR 3.05, 95% CI 1.65–5.68); only 10% of EVT patients needed a secondary transfer
papers.caveat: Scale is embedded in a Spanish regional system with physician involvement, and only about a third of screened patients were M-DIRECT-positive
papers.shortTitle: M-DIRECT stroke triage scale revalidated
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and risks of using a prehospital stroke triage scale to route patients directly for endovascular treatment.

papers.title: Post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation and coronary angiographic phenotypes in angiography-evaluable survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest
papers.summary: A Japanese single-centre review of 149 angiography-evaluable OHCA survivors with presumed culprit lesions found post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation marked an acute occlusive coronary phenotype but was not independently linked to neurological outcome once prehospital factors were accounted for.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The cath-lab call after ROSC sits mostly with receiving hospitals here, but the practical message for crews — absence of ST elevation doesn't rule out a coronary culprit — belongs in the handover.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort
papers.n: 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients undergoing post-resuscitation angiography
papers.finding: ST elevation was associated with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury; patients without ST elevation more often had multivessel disease or chronic total occlusion; ST elevation was not independently associated with neurological outcome after adjustment for prehospital factors
papers.caveat: Heavy selection: single centre, angiography-evaluable survivors with presumed culprit lesions only
papers.shortTitle: Post-ROSC ST elevation tracks acute coronary occlusion
papers.learningGoal: Refine my interpretation of post-ROSC ECG patterns when deciding coronary cause and destination in cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Long-Term Survival Following Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Two-Center Five-Year Analysis
papers.summary: A US–Czech retrospective cohort of 728 patients given ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA found 29% survived to hospital discharge and, among those survivors, about two-thirds were still alive at five years with favourable cerebral performance in most.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ECPR-capable centres are scarce in Australia, so this informs destination decisions and which refractory arrests are worth a fast transport rather than anything crews do on scene.
papers.design: Retrospective two-centre cohort (Minnesota, USA and Prague, Czechia)
papers.n: 728 ECPR patients, 211 discharged alive
papers.finding: 211/728 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 76.9% and 67.2% of hospital survivors were alive at 1 and 5 years; CPC 1–2 in 78.7% at discharge and above 93% among survivors beyond 1 year; five-year survival ranged from 91.6% (18–39 years) to 52.9% (>70 years)
papers.caveat: Highly selected patients within established ECPR systems, no control group, and most deaths clustered in the first 90 days after discharge
papers.shortTitle: Two-thirds of ECPR survivors alive at five years
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of ECPR eligibility criteria in improving long-term outcomes for patients in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Optimizing US Prehospital Care of ST-Segment–Elevation Myocardial Infarction Because Time Is Life, Not Just Muscle
papers.summary: A US Circulation viewpoint argues that because most STEMI deaths now occur out of hospital, the biggest gains lie in shortening symptom-onset-to-reperfusion, and sets out five recommendations spanning patient education, prehospital pharmaceuticals and reimbursement reform.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The funding machinery is American, but the central argument — most STEMI deaths are prehospital — applies here, and thrombolytics are carried by a handful of Australian services while most don't.
papers.design: Perspective/viewpoint article
papers.n: Not applicable
papers.finding: Five recommendations to shorten symptom onset to reperfusion: patient education, prehospital glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors or thrombolytics, rapid PCI access, and changes to prehospital care reimbursement
papers.caveat: Opinion piece with no new data, and the prehospital-drug recommendations assume a system that doesn't exist in every Australian service
papers.shortTitle: STEMI deaths now mostly prehospital
papers.learningGoal: Recognise the patient and system factors that delay reperfusion in Australian STEMI care.

papers.title: Occupational Conditions and Sleep Duration, Continuity, and Quality among First Responders: Evidence from the 2025 Los Angeles Wildfires
papers.journal: Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine
papers.summary: A US survey of 90 first responders during the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires found 24-hour shifts were associated with 1.65 fewer total sleep hours and four or more consecutive shifts with shorter sleep, with 83% reporting poor or very poor sleep quality.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Wildfire deployment isn't routine rostering, but long shifts and fragmented sleep are a familiar problem in Australian emergency services and this adds exposure-specific numbers.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey
papers.n: 90 first responders
papers.finding: 24-hour shifts associated with 1.65 fewer total sleep hours (95% CI −2.45 to −0.84) and 1.93 fewer consecutive hours; four or more consecutive shifts and poorer working conditions also associated with shorter sleep; 83% reported poor or very poor sleep quality
papers.caveat: Small self-selected sample, self-reported sleep, and a disaster-deployment setting that may not generalise to routine work
papers.shortTitle: Long wildfire shifts linked to broken sleep
papers.learningGoal: Understand how extended shift patterns during disaster deployments affect my sleep quality and performance.

papers.title: Coffee and cases (C&C) – perceptions of helicopter emergency medical service teams towards a quality improvement project aimed at enhancing organisational learning from team debriefs: A qualitative focus group study
papers.summary: Focus groups with 30 HEMS clinicians found a quality improvement project capturing routine debriefs ('Coffee and Cases') strengthened organisational learning through three themes: education, accessibility and calibration of learning points.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It comes from a helicopter crew model, but the underlying problem — debrief learning evaporating unless it's captured and shared — applies to any Australian ambulance service.
papers.design: Qualitative descriptive study, four semi-structured focus groups
papers.n: 30 HEMS clinicians in 4 focus groups
papers.finding: Organisational learning was the global theme, organised into education (knowledge generation, engagement, incidental learning), accessibility (learning reaching staff who missed debriefs) and calibration (moderation and vetting of learning points)
papers.caveat: Single-service perceptions with no measure of whether learning outcomes actually changed
papers.shortTitle: Turning HEMS debriefs into shared learning
papers.learningGoal: Understand how routine team debriefs can be captured and calibrated to strengthen organisational learning in my practice.

papers.title: For Emergency Medical Services, An Old Threat Resurfaces: Medicaid Cuts
papers.summary: A US Health Affairs commentary warns that H.R. 1 and subsequent Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services rules will deepen financial strain on local EMS systems already struggling with inadequate reimbursement.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — EMS financing in the US has no Australian counterpart — ambulance services here don't bill patients — so this is a window into another system, not a practice signal.
papers.design: Policy commentary
papers.n: Not applicable
papers.finding: H.R. 1 and subsequent CMS rules are expected to place financial strain on local EMS systems already struggling with inadequate reimbursement
papers.caveat: US financing policy commentary with no data of its own
papers.shortTitle: US Medicaid cuts threaten EMS funding
papers.learningGoal: Understand how constrained funding and reimbursement pressures affect the sustainability and safety of ambulance systems.

papers.title: Performance of the Lausanne Ischemic Stroke Pathway prehospital triage system in identifying acute reperfusion candidates: a quality-control study
papers.summary: A Swiss single-centre quality-control study of a prehospital stroke triage pathway found EMS undertriaged 21% and overtriaged 63% of acute reperfusion candidates, with both rates falling when a coordinated medical team (including a neurologist) was phone-consulted.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The second-assessment step rests on a physician-staffed call team Australian services don't run, but the under- and overtriage rates are a useful benchmark for our own stroke screens.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre quality-control study
papers.n: 1,071 patients with suspected acute ischaemic stroke
papers.finding: 41% were eligible for reperfusion; EMS undertriage 21%, overtriage 63%; the physician-led call-team step reduced undertriage to 11% and overtriage to 57%
papers.caveat: Physician-staffed call-team model is not how Australian dispatch works, and single-centre retrospective design
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital stroke triage: high under- and overtriage rates
papers.learningGoal: Refine my prehospital stroke assessment to better identify patients suitable for acute reperfusion and reduce undertriage.

papers.title: Post‐Traumatic Amnesia Testing for Suspected Concussion in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective Study
papers.summary: An Australian retrospective cohort of 6,259 adults tested with the Abbreviated Westmead PTA Scale after head injury found 91.8% passed, with post-traumatic amnesia associated with initial GCS 13–14 but not with reported loss of consciousness.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The A-WPTAS is an ED tool rather than something ambulance crews administer, but crew handover observations — GCS and reported LOC — feed straight into this assessment, and LOC alone looks like a weak signaller.
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective cohort
papers.n: 6,259 adults presenting to ED with head injury
papers.finding: 91.8% passed the A-WPTAS; PTA was more frequent with GCS 13–14, in male patients, after low falls and after hours, but pass rates were similar with documented LOC (90.6%) and without (92%, p=0.13)
papers.caveat: ED population only, retrospective electronic records, and no link back to prehospital documentation
papers.shortTitle: Reported LOC didn't flag post-traumatic amnesia in ED
papers.learningGoal: Recognise post-traumatic amnesia in head injury patients even when loss of consciousness is not reported.

papers.title: Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: A systematic review
papers.summary: This systematic review of wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection found 13 studies (predominantly wristbands using photoplethysmography) with sensitivities of 43.8–100%, ten reporting ≥90%, but false alert rates ranging from multiple per day to one per 21 user-years; the multinational evidence base remains largely unvalidated in real life.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Wearables that alert EMS to unwitnessed cardiac arrest could shorten time to bystander CPR and dispatch across Australia, but until devices are externally validated and false-alarm burdens are resolved, Australian paramedics should treat this as an emerging technology rather than current practice.
papers.design: Systematic review (PRISMA) of diagnostic accuracy studies of wearable cardiac arrest detection systems
papers.n: 13 studies, with 18 to 1,423 participants each
papers.finding: Sensitivity ranged from 43.8% to 100%, with ten studies reporting ≥90%; false-positive alert rates ranged from multiple per day to one per 21 user-years; wristbands (n=9) and photoplethysmography (n=9) were the most common device and sensor types.
papers.caveat: External validation and real-life performance data are scarce, and study populations were small and heterogeneous, so reported sensitivity and false-alarm rates may not reflect actual EMS-linked use.
papers.shortTitle: Wearables detecting cardiac arrest: systematic review
papers.learningGoal: Understand how wearable cardiac arrest detection technology may shape early warning and community response pathways.

papers.title: Development and validation of methods to predict ground- and helicopter-based emergency medical service travel times
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A modelling study validated open-source routing and historical-data methods for predicting ground and helicopter EMS travel times, achieving R² of 0.79 for ground drive time to scene but only 0.38 for helicopter time to hospital.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — HEMS dispatch decisions are made by every Australian service and time-benefit estimation is the crux of helicopter versus ground selection; the open-source tools are there for any service to adapt.
papers.design: Model development and validation using open-source routing and historical travel times
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Best ground EMS models explained R² 0.79 (drive time to location) and 0.70 (to hospital) versus R² 0.46 and 0.38 for helicopter flight times; mean absolute percentage error 18–20% across all methods
papers.caveat: Helicopter times were much harder to predict, and accuracy varies with local geography and data quality
papers.shortTitle: Predicting ground vs helicopter EMS travel times
papers.learningGoal: Understand how travel time prediction accuracy shapes my decisions when requesting helicopter transport over ground crews.

papers.title: Violence-related measures against ambulance personnel: a study protocol for a scoping review with multi-framework conceptual mapping
papers.summary: An Irish scoping-review protocol will map measures against verbal and physical violence toward ambulance personnel — reported by 57–93% of prehospital responders in a career — across five safety-science and human-factors frameworks.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It's a protocol for research not yet done, but occupational violence is a live issue for Australian crews and the framework mapping should show which measures sit where in the prevention hierarchy.
papers.design: Scoping review protocol (JBI methodology, PRISMA-ScR reporting)
papers.n: Literature from 2014 to May 2026 across five databases
papers.finding: Protocol only — no results yet; between 57% and 93% of prehospital responders report at least one episode of verbal or physical violence in their career
papers.caveat: A protocol with no findings, and title/abstract screening by a single principal investigator
papers.shortTitle: Mapping anti-violence measures for ambulance personnel
papers.learningGoal: Understand how safety-science frameworks can inform my strategies for preventing and responding to occupational violence.

papers.title: Prehospital Detection of Acute Pulmonary Embolism and Its Association with Clinical Outcomes: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: A German retrospective cohort of 171 EMS-transported patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism found prehospital crews correctly suspected PE in only 5.3% of cases, but correct detection was associated with time to CT pulmonary angiography halving (median 2.1 vs 4.0 hours).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Done in a physician-staffed German system, so the detection rate isn't directly comparable — but the core message, that PE is rarely suspected before hospital and detection speeds imaging, applies in any paramedic-led system.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort, EMS protocols 2019-2024
papers.n: 171 EMS-transported patients with in-hospital confirmed PE, Bochum, Germany
papers.finding: PE correctly suspected prehospital in 9/171 (5.3%, 95% CI 2.8-9.7%); time to CTPA 2.1 vs 4.0 hours with detection (p<0.001); detection only in physician-staffed encounters (10.8% vs 0%, p=0.003); 22.5% diagnosed only after 24 hours
papers.caveat: Single centre, retrospective, detection defined by EMS documentation, physician-staffed system, exploratory analyses
papers.shortTitle: EMS rarely suspects PE, but detection speeds CT
papers.learningGoal: Recognise prehospital presentations of pulmonary embolism to speed diagnosis and improve patient outcomes.

papers.title: Violence Against Out-Of-Hospital Emergency Healthcare Professionals: A Qualitative Exploration of Lived Experiences, Microaggressions, and Coping Mechanisms
papers.summary: An Italian qualitative study of 15 prehospital nurses and ambulance drivers who had experienced workplace violence described violence being taken home, under-recognised microaggressions shaped by gender and culture, and coping built on de-escalation, situational awareness and peer support amid thin organisational backing.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Workplace violence is a live issue for crews everywhere, and the lived-experience themes — microaggressions, carrying it home, patchy organisational support — translate directly to Australian ambulance work.
papers.design: Qualitative interpretative study, semi-structured interviews, inductive content analysis
papers.n: 15 prehospital nurses and ambulance drivers, northeastern Italy
papers.finding: Three themes: 'Violence is taken home', 'Microaggressions: the invisible violence', and coping via communication, de-escalation, situational awareness and peer support; organisational support perceived as insufficient
papers.caveat: Purposive sample of staff who had all experienced violence, single region, qualitative design not generalisable
papers.shortTitle: Workplace violence follows prehospital staff home
papers.learningGoal: Understand how workplace violence and microaggressions affect my wellbeing and the coping strategies I rely on.

papers.title: Prehospital paediatric and neonatal ventilatory support by a South African public emergency medical service: A retrospective descriptive study
papers.summary: A South African retrospective review of 1,548 ventilated under-fives in Western Cape EMS found 99.4% were interfacility transfers, mostly for respiratory distress, with non-invasive support dominating (nCPAP 66.5%, high-flow 14.5%) over invasive ventilation (18.9%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A practice-pattern description from a resource-constrained public service rather than an outcome study, but the nCPAP-first, transfer-heavy caseload is a useful benchmark for paediatric transport practice anywhere.
papers.design: Retrospective descriptive study of electronic records, 2023
papers.n: 1,548 ventilated under-5s among 61,775 paediatric/neonatal activations, Western Cape public EMS
papers.finding: Interfacility transfers 99.4%; respiratory distress 73.5%; nCPAP 66.5%, high-flow nasal cannula 14.5%, invasive ventilation 18.9%; high FiO2 (>0.6) documented in 11.6% of nCPAP cases
papers.caveat: Descriptive single-service data from a resource-constrained setting, documentation-based, no clinical outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric transport ventilation: nCPAP first, transfers dominate
papers.learningGoal: Refine my selection of non-invasive ventilatory support for paediatric and neonatal patients during transport.

papers.title: Beyond the Hype: Artificial Intelligence as Decision Support in Emergency and Prehospital Medicine—A Critical Narrative Review
papers.summary: A critical narrative review of AI in emergency and prehospital care found the most credible near-term uses are bounded decision support — triage, risk stratification, stroke pathways, forecasting, documentation — while retrospective designs, thin external validation and workflow gaps keep real-world benefit unproven.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — No new data and no single setting, but a sober map of where AI actually stands in prehospital care — useful context for the stream of AI papers crossing the desk.
papers.design: Critical narrative review
papers.n: Not reported (narrative review)
papers.finding: Most credible near-term uses are bounded decision support in triage, early risk stratification, stroke pathways, operational forecasting and supervised documentation; field constrained by retrospective designs, limited external validation and workflow integration gaps
papers.caveat: Narrative review without systematic search or formal appraisal
papers.shortTitle: AI in prehospital care: cautious optimism, thin validation
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and limitations of AI decision support tools before integrating them into my prehospital practice.

papers.title: Utilization of Large Language Models in Prehospital Triage: A Focus on ChatGPT’s Performance According to Pre-KTAS
papers.summary: A Korean simulation study of 100 prehospital triage scenarios found a Pre-KTAS-trained ChatGPT matched 10 active-duty paramedics on accuracy (0.81 vs 0.80) with the lowest under-triage rate (6.1%), while an untrained LLM lagged well behind at 0.69.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Text scenarios, a Korean triage scale and no field testing — but LLM triage support is coming, and this is a tidy early look at how much the training material matters.
papers.design: Simulation-based comparative study, 100 Pre-KTAS scenarios × 30 independent repetitions
papers.n: 100 scenarios; trained and untrained LLM vs 10 active-duty 119 paramedics
papers.finding: Accuracy: trained LLM 0.81 vs paramedics 0.80 vs untrained LLM 0.69 (trained LLM and paramedics > untrained, p<.001); trained LLM lowest under-triage (6.1%) and highest sensitivity (0.95); paramedics highest specificity (0.96) and PPV (0.93)
papers.caveat: Simulated text scenarios, Korean triage scale, repetition inflates apparent precision, no field validation
papers.shortTitle: Trained ChatGPT matched paramedics on triage scenarios
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of artificial intelligence tools in supporting prehospital triage accuracy and under-triage risk.

papers.title: Virtual Physician Interpretation of Paramedic-Acquired Point-of-Care Ultrasound Across Device Modalities: A Mixed Methods Usability Pilot (Preprint)
papers.summary: A usability pilot had four physicians interpret paramedic-acquired lung and IVC ultrasound remotely via a cloud platform across laptop, tablet and smartphone, with substantial diagnostic agreement (0.68–0.80) and the laptop version rated most usable.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Tiny — four clinicians, four vignettes — and a preprint, but remote interpretation of crew-acquired ultrasound is exactly the model rural and remote services would need.
papers.design: Mixed-methods usability pilot, 4 physicians × 3 sessions × 3 device modalities
papers.n: 4 physicians, 4 clinical vignettes with lung and IVC clips
papers.finding: Chance-adjusted agreement: laptop 0.80, smartphone 0.72, tablet 0.68; observed agreement lung 80-83%, IVC 73-75%; SUS scores 76.5 laptop, 59.5 smartphone, 55.0 tablet
papers.caveat: Very small pilot, preprint, physician raters not paramedics, no patient outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Remote reads of paramedic ultrasound held up in pilot
papers.learningGoal: Understand how device choice affects remote physician interpretation of paramedic-acquired point-of-care ultrasound in Australian prehospital care.

papers.title: Development of a quality metric to measure bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out of hospital cardiac arrest: A modified Delphi study
papers.journal: International Journal of Nursing Studies Advances
papers.summary: A UK-led modified Delphi study with an international panel of doctors, paramedics, nurses and laypersons reached consensus on 11 dichotomous indicators — compression rate, depth and recoil plus dispatcher instruction, time from recognition to emergency call and AED use — to measure bystander CPR quality in OHCA.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Bystander CPR measurement matters to every Australian system, but this is a provisional consensus metric from one UK-led process that still needs validation before it informs anything on the ground.
papers.design: Modified Delphi consensus study (two survey rounds plus a virtual consensus meeting)
papers.n: 104 panellists registered; 62, 48 and 18 completed rounds 1–3
papers.finding: Consensus (≥75% agreement) on 11 indicators covering chest compression rate, depth and recoil and contextual factors including dispatcher instruction, time from recognition to emergency call and AED use; two composite indicators were created and all criteria scored dichotomously.
papers.caveat: The metric is provisional and unvalidated, and panel attrition left only 18 participants in the final consensus round.
papers.shortTitle: Defining quality in bystander CPR
papers.learningGoal: Understand how bystander CPR quality indicators can inform community responder and dispatcher practice in cardiac arrest care.

papers.title: Initial shockable rhythm detection among patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest by arrest location: A population-based cohort study in Japan
papers.summary: A Japanese population-based registry of 2,478 medical-origin OHCA cases found an initial shockable rhythm in 36.3% of nursing-home arrests versus 7.1% at home (adjusted OR 12.35), with 97% of shockable nursing-home patients receiving an AED shock but only 0.8% surviving with good neurological outcome.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander AED use and early rhythm detection are the same in Australia, and residential aged care is a common arrest location here; the finding speaks to where AED access changes what rhythms crews first see.
papers.design: Population-based registry cohort, descriptive plus multivariable logistic regression
papers.n: 2,478 medical-origin OHCAs, Japan, 2016–2024
papers.finding: Initial shockable rhythm: 36.3% in nursing homes vs 7.1% at home (aOR 12.35, 95% CI 8.93–17.24) and 33.4% in other locations; 97.0% of shockable nursing-home cases got an AED shock; one-month favourable neurological survival lowest in nursing homes at 0.8%
papers.caveat: Descriptive by design — the authors themselves attribute the rhythm gap to earlier AED access rather than proven causation, and survival was worst in nursing homes despite the shockable rhythms
papers.shortTitle: Nursing-home arrests more often shockable, linked to early AED
papers.learningGoal: Weigh whether early AED access in residential aged care settings changes shockable rhythm detection and outcomes in cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Experiences and coping strategies of bystanders involved in out-of-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation: A qualitative study
papers.summary: A Scottish qualitative study of 11 bystanders who performed CPR in an OHCA found a substantial emotional impact — worst when the patient died or was known to them — with themes of being compelled to help but unprepared, and identified better emotional preparation in CPR training and access to a knowledgeable independent person as ways to reduce it.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander experience after CPR is the same in any system, and CPR training and post-event support are things Australian ambulance services directly shape.
papers.design: Qualitative — semi-structured interviews, reflexive thematic analysis
papers.n: 11 bystanders (9 knew the patient), recruited via social media, Scotland
papers.finding: Four themes: emotional impact; managing multiple roles; compelled to help but unprepared; talking to the right person
papers.caveat: Small, self-selected sample recruited through social media advertisements
papers.shortTitle: Bystanders describe heavy emotional toll of doing CPR
papers.learningGoal: Understand the emotional impact on bystanders performing CPR and how dispatcher support can better prepare them.

papers.title: Patient Rights Breaches by Aotearoa New Zealand Paramedics and Nurses: An Exploratory Study
papers.journal: Whitireia Journal of Nursing, Health and Social Services
papers.summary: A New Zealand descriptive analysis of Health and Disability Commissioner decisions from 2014–2024 found nine paramedic and 100 nurse Code of Rights breaches, but per 1,000 practitioners paramedics were three times more likely to breach than nurses and at higher severity, with Right 4 (appropriate standard of care) most common in both professions.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — An Aotearoa NZ paramedic workforce studied under a statutory complaints framework closely mirrors Australian regulation, and error-reporting culture is a live issue across Australian services too.
papers.design: Descriptive statistical analysis of published regulatory breach decisions
papers.n: 109 breach decisions (9 paramedics, 100 nurses), NZ, 2014–2024
papers.finding: Per 1,000 practitioners, paramedics were three times more likely than nurses to breach the Code and breached at a higher severity rate; Right 4 was the most prevalent breach in both professions
papers.caveat: Small paramedic numbers make the per-1,000 comparison fragile, and published decisions capture only reported and upheld breaches in one country
papers.shortTitle: NZ paramedics breached patient rights more often than nurses
papers.learningGoal: Understand the professional conduct risks that lead paramedics to breach patients' rights to appropriate standards of care.

papers.title: Remote triage with unmanned aerial vehicles in mass-casualty and prehospital emergency care: a scoping review
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A scoping review of 20 studies on UAV-assisted remote triage in mass-casualty and prehospital care found technical feasibility of remote vital-sign acquisition is demonstrated, but only one randomised comparison reached effectiveness — UAV-assisted triage took about 3.5 minutes longer with identical accuracy — and no study validated remote triage in real-world responses.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — UAV triage is not part of Australian MCI practice today, but drones are actively trialled here, and this review maps what would need to be proven before it changes triage on the road.
papers.design: Scoping review (JBI methodology, PRISMA-ScR), 20 original studies
papers.n: 20 studies — 8 acquisition, 11 decision-support, 1 effectiveness
papers.finding: Remote capture of heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature, SpO2, consciousness and location is feasible; the single randomised comparison showed UAV-assisted triage took ~3.5 min longer with identical accuracy; no validated remote triage standard exists
papers.caveat: Evidence is concentrated in disaster/mass-casualty settings under controlled conditions, with no real-world validation or patient-centred outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Drone triage feasible but unproven in real MCIs
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and delays of unmanned aerial triage against conventional methods in mass-casualty responses.

papers.title: Feasibility of using a mobile cardiotocograph device in an ambulance during maternal transport
papers.summary: A Japanese feasibility study transferred 68 pregnant women from nine primary obstetric clinics to a university hospital with real-time remote CTG monitoring from an ambulance, achieving legible fetal heart-rate traces in all transfers (median 91.1% legible recording time) with no sessions lost to connectivity issues over median transport of 34.5 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Remote fetal monitoring during maternal transport is not standard in Australian ambulances, but the model — transmitting CTG ahead to the receiving obstetric unit — fits how Australian services already pre-notify specialist centres.
papers.design: Prospective feasibility study with staff surveys
papers.n: 68 women with singleton pregnancies beyond 22 weeks, Japan, 2021–2023
papers.finding: All 68 fetal heart-rate records legible, median 91.1% legible recording time; median ambulance time 34.5 min (range 15.0–67.0); no monitoring sessions discontinued for connectivity
papers.caveat: Feasibility only — no clinical outcomes, and the Japanese system of clinic-level birth with frequent transfers differs from Australian maternity networks
papers.shortTitle: Ambulance CTG streamed to hospital during maternal transfer
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of remote fetal heart-rate monitoring during maternal transport in Australian maternity networks.

papers.title: Improving the safety and efficacy of whole blood resuscitation from hemorrhagic shock with a novel scavenger protein cocktail
papers.summary: A US-led laboratory study in hamsters found that haemolysis in stored whole blood correlated with worse microvascular flow and more organ injury after shock resuscitation, and pre-treating the blood with an experimental scavenger protein cocktail binding haemoglobin, heme and iron mitigated capillary collapse and tissue injury in moderate- and high-haemolysis blood.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is carried by a handful of Australian services, most don't, and this is early animal work — it informs the stored-blood safety question those programs face rather than anything usable on the road now.
papers.design: Animal laboratory study — haemorrhagic shock and transfusion in hamster dorsal window chamber model
papers.n: Adult male Golden Syrian hamsters across stored-blood groups with low, moderate or severe haemolysis
papers.finding: Stored whole-blood haemolysis correlated negatively with haematocrit, microvascular flow and functional capillary density, and positively with organ injury markers and lactate; the scavenger protein cocktail mitigated capillary collapse and tissue injury but caused haemodilution without recovery of haematocrit, pH or lactate to baseline
papers.caveat: Animal model with an experimental additive — a long way from clinical transfusion, and the cocktail's own haemodilution is unresolved
papers.shortTitle: Lab work targets haemolysis in stored whole blood
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the risks of haemolysis in stored whole blood when considering prehospital transfusion in major haemorrhage.

papers.title: Ventilation Monitoring in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care
papers.summary: A US prospective before/after study in Milwaukee found real-time BVM feedback (Real BVM Help) was associated with the share of OHCA ventilations meeting both rate and tidal-volume targets rising from 7.5% to 39.0%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bag-valve-mask ventilation and ETCO2 monitoring are core skills on every Australian ambulance, and most crews ventilate arrests with a BVM and little more than ETCO2 to go on.
papers.design: Prospective before/after quality assurance study
papers.n: 278 adults with OHCA (148 before / 130 after)
papers.finding: Ventilations in-target for both rate and tidal volume rose from 7.5% to 39.0% with real-time feedback; with ETCO2 monitoring alone only 6.8% met both, and 58.2% of ventilations delivered a lower-than-target tidal volume
papers.caveat: Before/after design without randomisation, in a single US county system
papers.shortTitle: Real-time BVM feedback linked to better arrest ventilation
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ventilation technique during cardiac arrest resuscitation by using feedback to improve rate and tidal volume.

papers.title: Sex differences in bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation and survival to hospital discharge for public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in North Carolina and Singapore: a retrospective cohort study
papers.summary: A retrospective cohort of 10,445 public out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in North Carolina and Singapore found women were less likely to receive bystander CPR in both regions (aOR 0.87 and 0.78), with survival favouring women in North Carolina but men in Singapore.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander CPR rates are a system-wide measure every Australian community can act on, and the gap replicated across two very different registries a decade apart.
papers.design: Retrospective dual-registry cohort (CARES North Carolina, Pan-Asian RESC Singapore)
papers.n: 6,828 OHCAs in North Carolina and 3,617 in Singapore
papers.finding: Public bystander CPR: 48% of men vs 44% of women in North Carolina (aOR 0.87) and 59% vs 52% in Singapore (aOR 0.78); survival to discharge favoured women in North Carolina (aOR 1.15) but men in Singapore (aOR 0.63)
papers.caveat: Registry data, and the opposite-direction survival findings between the two regions are unexplained
papers.shortTitle: Women still get less bystander CPR in public
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how sex-related barriers to bystander CPR in public settings affect my cardiac arrest care.

papers.title: Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014-2020 Dataset
papers.summary: A Japanese national registry study of 259 witnessed paediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrests given adrenaline, using time-dependent propensity matching to address resuscitation-time bias, found no adrenaline timing window was associated with better one-month survival or neurological outcome.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Adrenaline is carried by every Australian ambulance service and paediatric arrest is among the hardest calls crews run, so timing evidence on a drug all crews deliver is directly relevant.
papers.design: Retrospective national registry cohort with time-dependent propensity matching (JAAM-OHCA, Japan)
papers.n: 259 children with witnessed OHCA who received adrenaline
papers.finding: No timing window (1–10 through 26–30 minutes after EMS contact) showed an association with one-month survival; risk ratios ranged 0.97–2.94 with confidence intervals crossing 1
papers.caveat: Only 259 children split across six timing windows, leaving every interval underpowered
papers.shortTitle: Adrenaline timing not tied to paediatric OHCA survival
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of adrenaline timing in my management of witnessed paediatric cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Early Identification of Recurrent Out-of-hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Clinical ECG Features
papers.summary: A US retrospective cohort of 1,298 post-ROSC OHCA patients found routine ECG features — wider QRS, lower heart rate, higher heart-rate variability — were associated with rearrest, with prediction best one minute before it (AUROC 0.74).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Continuous ECG monitoring after ROSC is standard care on every Australian ambulance; the question it raises — watching for rearrest rather than waiting for it — is one crews can act on.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort, 2018–2024
papers.n: 1,298 adults with OHCA achieving ROSC
papers.finding: 40.7% of post-ROSC patients rearrested; identification was highest one minute before rearrest (AUROC 0.74) and declined beyond three minutes; rearrest carried lower survival (20.4% vs 43.1%) and favourable neuro outcome (7.8% vs 21.2%)
papers.caveat: Retrospective, single US region, and no prospective test of acting on the prediction
papers.shortTitle: ECG signs appear minutes before post-ROSC rearrest
papers.learningGoal: Recognise ECG warning signs that precede rearrest in post-ROSC patients to intervene earlier.

papers.title: Prevalence of Persistent Severe Hypertension and Rates of Treatment Among Pregnant Patients in the Prehospital Setting
papers.summary: A US national EMS dataset study of 39,546 responses for pregnant patients beyond 20 weeks found persistent severe hypertension in 3.1%, of whom only 0.8% received guideline-adherent treatment with both magnesium and an antihypertensive.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Magnesium for pre-eclampsia sits in nearly every Australian formulary, but the paired antihypertensive the new US guideline wants is carried by only a handful of services, so the full pathway doesn't transfer yet.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort (2024 ESO Data Collaborative)
papers.n: 39,546 EMS scene responses for pregnancy beyond 20 weeks
papers.finding: Persistent severe hypertension in 3.1% (1,234/39,546); of those, 6.2% received magnesium only, 1.5% an antihypertensive only, and 0.8% both magnesium and an antihypertensive
papers.caveat: US retrospective dataset, and treatment rates pre-date the 2025 ACOG-NAEMSP prehospital guideline
papers.shortTitle: Severe hypertension in pregnancy rarely treated to guideline
papers.learningGoal: Recognise persistent severe hypertension in pregnancy as a prehospital risk requiring timely treatment decisions.

papers.title: Heat Stroke Cooling Devices for Prehospital Use: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: A US systematic review of 18 commercial heat-stroke cooling devices found only three reached the ideal prehospital cooling rate (at least 0.155°C/min) and just five met single-person portability, with most relying on water, power or disposables.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Heat illness is a summer mainstay for Australian crews and rapid cooling on scene is the established treatment, so which devices actually perform in the field matters directly here.
papers.design: Systematic review of commercially available cooling devices
papers.n: 18 commercial cooling devices
papers.finding: Three of 18 devices met the ideal cooling threshold (≥0.155°C/min), two were acceptable (0.078–0.154°C/min), 61% reported no cooling-rate data, and five met the ≤16 kg single-person portability limit
papers.caveat: Device specification review with no clinical outcome data, and cooling-rate figures were missing for most products
papers.shortTitle: Few heat-stroke cooling devices suit the prehospital setting
papers.learningGoal: Weigh which cooling devices suit prehospital heat stroke care given portability and cooling rate trade-offs.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: A South Korean single-centre study built an AI-assisted ECG decision tree that classified about half of post-OHCA patients as 'ACS not likely' with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified in development or temporal validation.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Cath-lab activation after ROSC is a triage decision Australian crews feed into, and this tool needs multicentre prospective validation before it leaves the research setting.
papers.design: Single-centre retrospective cohort with temporal validation
papers.n: 400 adults with post-ROSC OHCA (329 development / 71 validation)
papers.finding: The tree labelled 52.0% of development and 45.1% of validation patients 'ACS not likely' with zero missed ACS cases; yield concentrated in non-shockable rhythms (64.8% of non-ACS cases excluded, AUROC 0.824)
papers.caveat: Single centre and retrospective, using a deep-learning ECG platform nowhere near ambulance deployment
papers.shortTitle: AI ECG model excludes ACS after cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of AI-assisted ECG interpretation in guiding post-ROSC destination and cath lab decisions.

papers.title: Challenges in Infection Prevention and Control in Paramedicine: A Modified Nominal Group Technique Consensus Study
papers.summary: An Australian modified nominal group technique with ten experts ranked human factors — organisational culture, compliance fatigue, inconsistent education — above equipment provision as the main drivers of infection prevention and control compliance in ambulances.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian-led consensus on how ambulance design, culture and education shape infection control, directly applicable across services nationally.
papers.design: Modified nominal group technique consensus study
papers.n: 10 experts (infection prevention, paramedicine, governance, education, operations)
papers.finding: Human factors ranked first among determinants of compliance, followed by education and training, physical environment, equipment and consumables, and contaminated equipment management
papers.caveat: Expert consensus from ten participants with no outcome data
papers.shortTitle: Ambulance infection control hinges on human factors
papers.learningGoal: Understand how organisational culture and compliance fatigue shape my infection prevention practices in ambulances.

papers.title: Effect of the CP@clinic program (Community Paramedicine at Clinic program) on health care utilization from administrative data during and after the intervention: a cluster-randomized controlled trial
papers.summary: A Canadian cluster-randomised trial across 30 low-income apartment buildings found the CP@clinic community paramedicine program was associated with lower hospital admission rates during (aIRR 0.75) and after (aIRR 0.82) the trial, with no difference in ED visits.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Canadian community paramedicine model in social housing; some Australian services run similar programs, but it is a different service model from emergency response.
papers.design: Cluster-randomised controlled trial with repeated cross-sectional analysis
papers.n: 30 apartment buildings across five Ontario communities
papers.finding: Hospital admission rates were lower in intervention buildings during the 12-month trial (aIRR 0.75) and the following year (aIRR 0.82); primary care visits fell then rose post-trial; ED visits unchanged
papers.caveat: Analysis used linked administrative data in a low-income older-adult housing population, so effects may not generalise
papers.shortTitle: Community paramedicine cut hospital admissions in cluster RCT
papers.learningGoal: Understand how community paramedicine programs in community settings can reduce hospital admissions for vulnerable older adults.

papers.title: Quality of prehospital emergency care at high altitude (3,450 m) by non-acclimatised EMS physicians: a randomised assessor-blinded simulation crossover study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: In a Swiss randomised crossover simulation study, 20 non-acclimatised EMS physicians showed no significant drop in overall performance at 3,450 m altitude (composite 82% at baseline vs 74% acute exposure, p=0.082).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A physician-staffed Swiss model, but hypobaric hypoxia affects any crew working helicopter rescue or alpine retrieval, which parts of Australia do.
papers.design: Assessor-blinded randomised crossover simulation study (physician-staffed crews)
papers.n: 20 non-acclimatised EMS physicians (17 analysed)
papers.finding: Median composite performance 82% at baseline, 74% during acute exposure to 3,450 m, 82% with supplemental oxygen at 4 L/min, and 83% after 20 hours at altitude; overall difference not significant (p=0.082)
papers.caveat: Simulation only, 17 of 20 physicians completed all conditions, and the study crewed doctors rather than paramedics
papers.shortTitle: Simulated EMS care held up at altitude
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how acute altitude exposure affects my own clinical performance and when supplemental oxygen protects decision-making.

papers.title: Assessing Swedish guidelines for prehospital bleeding control: a cross-sectional appraisal using AGREE II
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A Swedish cross-sectional appraisal of regional prehospital bleeding-control guidelines from 15 of 21 regions using AGREE II found low methodological quality overall, with rigour of development and editorial independence scoring poorly.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Swedish guideline appraisal, but it speaks to how any ambulance service builds, links to evidence and maintains its clinical guidance, including here.
papers.design: Cross-sectional AGREE II appraisal of regional clinical practice guidelines
papers.n: Guidelines from 15 Swedish healthcare regions
papers.finding: Clarity of presentation scored highest; rigour of development, stakeholder involvement, applicability and editorial independence scored poorly; most guidelines lacked evidence search strategies, evidence links and update procedures
papers.caveat: Appraised document quality only, with no link to patient outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Swedish bleeding control guidelines scored low on quality
papers.learningGoal: Understand how guideline development rigour affects the trustworthiness of prehospital bleeding control recommendations I follow.

papers.title: Mapping the research landscape of UAV- and eVTOL-enabled emergency medical services: a bibliometric analysis, scoping review, and policy tool assessment
papers.summary: A Chinese-led bibliometric and scoping review of 168 drone and eVTOL emergency medical services studies found drone-delivered AEDs arrived before ambulances in 67% of cases (median lead 3 min 14 s) and drone blood delivery cut transport time by 61%.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Drone-delivered AEDs and blood logistics remain trial-stage technologies; the pooled numbers sketch what a network could do, not current practice.
papers.design: Bibliometric analysis, scoping review and policy document analysis
papers.n: 168 studies reviewed; 62 Chinese policy documents analysed
papers.finding: Drone AEDs arrived before ambulances in 67% of cases (median lead time 3 min 14 s); drone blood delivery reduced transport time 61%; modelled networks were cost-effective with OHCA survival gains of 21–46% under model assumptions
papers.caveat: Synthesis plus Chinese policy analysis, and the survival figures come from models rather than measured outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Drone AEDs arrived first in two-thirds of arrests
papers.learningGoal: Understand how drone-delivered AEDs and blood products could integrate with Australian emergency medical response systems.

papers.title: Prehospital Facial Recognition Technology: Randomized Controlled Simulation Study
papers.summary: In a US double-blind randomised simulation study, 90 firefighter-paramedics using a cloud facial-recognition app identified a noncommunicative standardised patient far more often than controls (83.3% vs 21.4%, OR 13.87).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A simulated US trial of a self-enrolled patient database; no such system runs in Australian ambulances, and the privacy and enrolment scaffolding would need building from scratch.
papers.design: Double-blind randomised controlled simulation study
papers.n: 90 firefighter-paramedics (48 experimental / 42 control)
papers.finding: 83.3% of the app group identified the standardised patient vs 21.4% of controls (OR 13.87); secondary outcomes included retrieving key medical information and treatment appropriateness
papers.caveat: One scripted urosepsis simulation, and the approach assumes patients pre-enrolled their own medical data
papers.shortTitle: Facial recognition helped paramedics ID unknown patients
papers.learningGoal: Understand how facial recognition technology could support identification of noncommunicative patients in Australian prehospital care.

papers.title: Reduced-Frame Lung Ultrasound Transmission Under Medical Transport Bandwidth Constraints: A Deep Learning Evaluation
papers.summary: A US deep-learning evaluation of 1,844 lung ultrasound clips found 5-frame clips kept B-line sensitivity within 0.7 points of 32-frame clips (89.4% vs 90.1%) while cutting package size 84%, easing transmission over weak transport links.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Remote ultrasound review during air and critical care transport is an emerging capability, and this finding is engineering feasibility rather than bedside evidence.
papers.design: Retrospective deep-learning evaluation of expert-labelled clips
papers.n: 1,844 expert-labelled lung ultrasound clips from 214 patient groups
papers.finding: B-line sensitivity 89.4% with 5 frames vs 90.1% with 32 (paired difference −0.7 points); package size fell 84% (526 to 84 KB) and idealised transfer at 0.1 Mbps fell from 43 to 7 seconds
papers.caveat: Model-based labels on retrospective clips, consolidation sensitivity dipped 3.1 points, and no clinical outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Fewer ultrasound frames preserved remote B-line detection
papers.learningGoal: Understand how reduced-frame prehospital lung ultrasound transmission affects remote B-line interpretation over low-bandwidth links.

papers.title: Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre
papers.summary: A prospective 12-month UK national service evaluation across 20 HEMS and 26 major trauma centres studied 116 resuscitative thoracotomies (82 prehospital) and found 43.1% achieved ROSC but only 6.9% survived to discharge, with no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital thoracotomy is a doctor-delivered HEMS skill in the UK model, not an Australian paramedic intervention — but the 10-minute ceiling and the tamponade-versus-exsanguination split inform how trauma arrest patients are triaged to major trauma centres here.
papers.design: Prospective national service evaluation (PHOTON, TERN, NaTRIC networks)
papers.n: 116 patients undergoing resuscitative thoracotomy (82 prehospital)
papers.finding: 43.1% achieved ROSC and 6.9% survived to discharge; outcomes were substantially better with cardiac tamponade than exsanguination, and there were no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest
papers.caveat: Prospective service evaluation without a comparator group — patient selection for thoracotomy drives the outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Resuscitative thoracotomy: no survivors past 10 minutes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh patient selection for prehospital resuscitative thoracotomy, especially in traumatic arrest from exsanguination.

papers.title: Point-of-care ultrasound for confirming endotracheal tube placement in prehospital and critical care transport: a scoping review
papers.summary: A scoping review of 51 studies on point-of-care ultrasound for confirming endotracheal tube placement in prehospital and critical care transport found only one primary study of diagnostic accuracy in actual out-of-hospital patients and none measuring patient-oriented outcomes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Ultrasound isn't carried on every Australian ambulance and intubation is an advanced-practice skill in most services — and the review shows the out-of-hospital evidence base behind in-hospital accuracy figures simply doesn't exist yet.
papers.design: Scoping review (Joanna Briggs Institute framework, PRISMA-ScR)
papers.n: 51 studies from 2,447 records
papers.finding: Only one of 51 included studies evaluated diagnostic performance in adult patients in an out-of-hospital setting; no included study measured patient-oriented outcomes
papers.caveat: Most included work is cadaver, simulation, training and feasibility studies rather than diagnostic accuracy in transported patients
papers.shortTitle: Ultrasound tube confirmation: thin evidence on the road
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the reliability of ultrasound for confirming endotracheal tube placement when verifying intubation in the prehospital setting.

papers.title: Early Prediction of Good Neurological Recovery in Comatose Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivors Using Machine Learning: A Multicenter Prospective Registry Study
papers.summary: A South Korean multicentre prospective registry study developed a machine-learning model for comatose OHCA survivors that predicted good 6-month neurological recovery before targeted temperature management with AUROC 0.929, outperforming conventional scores like CAHP.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prognostication happens in intensive care, but the strongest predictors are the prehospital variables crews generate — initial rhythm, collapse duration — so early, accurate handover documentation is where this touches the road.
papers.design: Multicentre prospective registry (Korean Hypothermia Network, KORHN-PRO)
papers.n: 1,358 comatose adult OHCA survivors treated with targeted temperature management
papers.finding: The voting-classifier model predicted 6-month neurologically intact survival (29.3% of patients) with AUROC 0.929 and AUPRC 0.850; the top five predictors were prehospital initial rhythm, arrival rhythm, age, PaCO2 and total collapse duration
papers.caveat: Single-country registry from 2015–2018 and the model has not been externally validated
papers.shortTitle: Machine learning predicts good recovery after OHCA
papers.learningGoal: Update my judgement on early prognostication for comatose cardiac arrest survivors in the Australian context.

papers.title: Do trends in alcohol harm mirror consumption? An analysis of adolescent ambulance attendances
papers.summary: An Australian study of the National Ambulance Surveillance System tracked 25,928 adolescent alcohol-intoxication ambulance attendances in Victoria from 2012 to 2023 and found rates stayed largely flat despite falling teen drinking, with a small decline only among males in major cities.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian ambulance data on a Friday-night workload that lands on crews everywhere — the gap between survey-reported drinking and actual ambulance harm matters for prevention planning in any state.
papers.design: Retrospective registry analysis with multivariable regression, stratified by gender and remoteness
papers.n: 25,928 ambulance attendances for adolescent alcohol intoxication (ages 10–19), Victoria 2012–2023
papers.finding: A small but significant monthly decline occurred only among males in major cities (B = −0.01, P < .001); no significant trends for males in regional areas or for females in metropolitan or regional areas
papers.caveat: Attendance data capture acute harm presentations rather than drinking behaviour, and the data are Victorian only
papers.shortTitle: Teen drinking falls, alcohol ambulance call-outs don't
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how adolescent alcohol harm persists across gender and remoteness despite falling teen drinking.

papers.title: Locating automated external defibrillators in urban areas: considering different travel modes
papers.summary: A Chinese spatial optimisation study of 17,842 OHCA dispatch records in Wuhan modelled AED coverage under different responder travel modes and found demand-weighted coverage ranged from 85% (driving) to 32% (walking), with universal walking coverage needing 521 extra AEDs versus 68 by car.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Chinese megacity model rather than an Australian deployment, but the core insight — AED planning collapses if volunteer responders walk instead of drive — applies to any community responder program here.
papers.design: Spatial optimisation modelling (multimodal location set covering and maximal covering problems)
papers.n: 17,842 ambulance dispatch records and 3,569 existing AEDs across 1,161 grid cells in Wuhan
papers.finding: Baseline demand-weighted 4-minute coverage was 85.07% for driving, 68.27% for cycling and 31.55% for walking; universal coverage required 68 additional AEDs under a driving assumption versus 521 under walking
papers.caveat: Modelled demand in a single city with no link to actual survival outcomes
papers.shortTitle: AED coverage depends on how responders travel
papers.learningGoal: Understand how responder travel modes shape AED coverage and placement in Australian urban communities.

papers.title: Prehospital Analgesia in Trauma: A Systematic Review of Current Evidence
papers.summary: An Israeli-led systematic review of 17 multinational studies (6 RCTs, 17,115 injured adults) found opioids, ketamine, methoxyflurane and paracetamol all effective for prehospital trauma analgesia, with no drug-attributed serious adverse events reported apart from one opioid study.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — All four agents are standard across Australian ambulance formularies, so the safety findings apply directly to current practice.
papers.design: Systematic review of RCTs and observational studies
papers.n: 17 studies, 17,115 injured adults over 15 years
papers.finding: All four agent classes (opioids, ketamine, methoxyflurane, paracetamol) showed effectiveness; no drug-attributed serious adverse events except one opioid study, with minor effects like nausea and drowsiness common.
papers.caveat: Only 6 of the 17 included studies were RCTs — most of the evidence is retrospective or observational.
papers.shortTitle: Trauma analgesia safety confirmed across four drug classes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the safety profile of opioid, ketamine, methoxyflurane and paracetamol options when selecting prehospital trauma analgesia.

papers.title: Left behind: Association of prehospital field undertriage and outcomes after injury
papers.summary: A US retrospective cohort of 59,095 injured adults in Pennsylvania found a 53% field undertriage rate, with undertriage associated with a 19% higher relative risk of in-hospital mortality (aRR 1.19) and, for patients over 60, a lower chance of discharge home.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Triage and destination decisions are core work for Australian crews; the US trauma-system geography differs, but the undertriage question is the same one Australian triage tools try to answer.
papers.design: Retrospective statewide cohort with doubly robust causal modelling
papers.n: 59,095 injured adults, 2023 Pennsylvania discharge data
papers.finding: Undertriage rate 53%; adjusted risk ratio for in-hospital mortality 1.19 (95% CI 1.07–1.33); shorter length of stay (-0.29 days); over-60s less likely to be discharged home (aRR 0.95).
papers.caveat: Administrative claims data with ICD-coded criteria for undertriage, which can misclassify both criteria and injury severity.
papers.shortTitle: Undertriage in trauma linked with higher in-hospital mortality
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on recognising major trauma in older adults to reduce undertriage to major trauma centres.

papers.title: Prehospital factors associated with calcium derangements upon arrival to the trauma center from scene - A subanalysis of a multicenter prospective study
papers.journal: The American Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A US prospective multicentre subanalysis of 1,047 trauma patients brought by EMS found calcium derangements on arrival associated with lower survival, with 56.6% of the 136 patients given prehospital blood hypocalcaemic on arrival and 5 hypercalcaemic patients having received prehospital calcium.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is limited to a few Australian services, so this informs the debate more than current practice; prehospital calcium itself is not something Australian ambulances carry.
papers.design: Preplanned subanalysis of a prospective multicentre observational study
papers.n: 1,047 EMS-transported trauma patients at 3 US trauma centres
papers.finding: 235 patients hypocalcaemic and 39 hypercalcaemic on arrival, both associated with lower survival; 77 of 136 (56.6%) who received prehospital blood were hypocalcaemic; 5 hypercalcaemic patients had received prehospital calcium, suggesting possible iatrogenic hypercalcaemia.
papers.caveat: Subgroup analysis confounded by indication — the sickest patients were the ones given blood, and calcium was not measured before arrival.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital blood linked to arrival hypocalcaemia in trauma
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when prehospital blood products may drive calcium derangements in major trauma.

papers.title: Effects of prehospital blood pressure on 90-day functional outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion
papers.journal: Journal of Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases
papers.summary: A Japanese cohort of 1,106 EMS-transported acute large-vessel-occlusion stroke patients found prehospital SBP ≥180 mmHg associated with lower odds of good 90-day functional outcome (aOR 0.43) compared with SBP <120, with the association significant only in patients treated with endovascular thrombectomy.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Scene blood pressure measurement is universal Australian practice, but the actionable signal sits with stroke-pathway teams; thrombectomy is hospital care and association is not causation.
papers.design: Retrospective multicentre cohort
papers.n: 1,106 EMS-transported LVO stroke patients, mean age 79, 60% thrombectomised
papers.finding: SBP ≥180 vs <120 mmHg: adjusted OR 0.43 (95% CI 0.22–0.84) for mRS 0–2 at 90 days; significant in EVT-treated patients, not in non-EVT patients (interaction p=0.007); haemorrhagic complications similar across groups.
papers.caveat: Retrospective Japanese cohort; no prehospital antihypertensive treatment was tested, so management implications are unproven.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital SBP ≥180 linked with worse stroke outcomes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the risks and benefits of prehospital blood pressure management during suspected large vessel occlusion stroke transport.

papers.title: Feasibility of Prehospital Central Venous Cannulation During Cardiac Arrest in an Ambulance
papers.summary: A US simulation study in a standard ambulance found central venous cannulation technically feasible during simulated refractory shockable cardiac arrest, completed in all runs with left femoral access identified as the most practical site and ACLS interventions maintained throughout.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Central venous access is beyond current Australian paramedic scope — an intensive-care-tier idea at best, and this was a manikin study with a physician on the team.
papers.design: Simulation-based feasibility study
papers.n: Repeated simulations with a multidisciplinary team (EMS clinicians plus a physician) in a standard ambulance
papers.finding: Cannulation successful in all simulations via standard sterile technique; left femoral vein identified as the most practical site; main challenges were confined workspace and fixed stretcher height.
papers.caveat: Manikin simulation with a small expert team — no patient data, and real-world sterility and time costs are untested.
papers.shortTitle: Central venous access during arrest feasible in simulation
papers.learningGoal: Weigh whether prehospital central venous access offers practical advantages over intraosseous access during refractory cardiac arrest.

papers.title: A Diagnostic-Focused Mobile Stroke Unit Model Integrated with Emergency Medical Services for Scalable Prehospital Stroke Care
papers.summary: Japanese authors describe a conceptual EMS-integrated diagnostic-focused mobile stroke unit model that keeps CT diagnosis at the scene or rendezvous point but hands treatment and transport to existing EMS vehicles, aiming to cut cost, staffing and operational complexity.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — No Australian service runs a CT mobile stroke unit — this is a design concept for systems weighing one, and the model assumes physician staffing on scene.
papers.design: Conceptual model design informed by a global survey of MSU programmes
papers.n: Not reported (conceptual model, no patient data)
papers.finding: The model separates CT-based diagnosis from treatment and transport; patients are moved to a standard EMS vehicle after CT evaluation, which the authors argue may make MSU deployment feasible in resource-constrained regions.
papers.caveat: Purely conceptual — no clinical or operational outcome data.
papers.shortTitle: CT stroke unit model separates diagnosis from transport
papers.learningGoal: Understand how diagnostic-focused mobile stroke unit models could fit within Australian EMS stroke pathways.

papers.title: International Fixed-Wing Air Ambulance Repatriation: A Retrospective Observational Cohort Analysis With Regression Modeling of Fox Flight Air Ambulance Inc. Patient Repatriation Characteristics 2009 to 2024
papers.summary: A Canadian retrospective cohort of 3,905 international fixed-wing air ambulance repatriations (2009–2024) found in-flight events in 26.7% of transports but major events in only 3.9%, with independent predictors including age, trauma and neoplasm diagnoses, oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — International repatriation is a small corner of Australian aeromedical practice, mostly fixed-wing contract work, but the event rates and crew-mix findings speak to the same transport medicine.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort with multivariable regression
papers.n: 3,905 international fixed-wing repatriations, single Canadian provider, 2009–2024
papers.finding: In-flight events in 26.7% of transports, major events 3.9%; independent predictors of events were age, orthopaedic/trauma and neoplasm diagnoses, oxygen therapy, invasive ventilation and transport year; acuity increased over time.
papers.caveat: Single private provider's charts; causality between team composition and events cannot be inferred from retrospective data.
papers.shortTitle: In-flight events uncommon in international air repatriation
papers.learningGoal: Understand which patient factors increase the risk of deterioration during long-haul aeromedical repatriation.

papers.title: Fatigue Characteristics and Perceptions in US Helicopter Air Ambulance Pilots
papers.summary: A US survey of 120 helicopter air ambulance pilots across 21 operators found 53% reporting poor sleep quality, 34% admitting to nodding off during a flight, 87% reporting sleep inertia affecting work performance, and fatigue rated worst on the return-to-base leg.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian aeromedical crews face similar rostering and fatigue pressures even though this surveyed US pilots; fatigue risk management is a shared aviation-medicine problem.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey with standardised sleep questionnaires
papers.n: 120 pilots across 21 US HAA operators
papers.finding: 53% reported poor sleep quality; 71% felt fatigue was most prevalent on the return-to-base leg; 69% named flight request volume as the biggest schedule-related contributor; 34% reported nodding off in flight; 87% said sleep inertia affected performance.
papers.caveat: Self-reported survey of volunteers — response rate not reported and self-report of nodding off may undercount.
papers.shortTitle: Fatigue common among US helicopter air ambulance pilots
papers.learningGoal: Understand how aviation fatigue and sleep inertia affect safe aeromedical retrieval practice in Australia.

papers.title: Enhancing High-Fidelity Simulation Flight-Based Training for Critical Care Paramedics in EMS Aviation: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: A Norwegian-affiliated systematic review of 7 articles found high-fidelity simulation feasible and engaging for critical care paramedic flight training, but insufficient evidence on whether it improves self-awareness or real prehospital performance.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian aeromedical services use simulation-based training for critical care crews, and the review's core message — learner enthusiasm is well shown, performance benefit is not — applies to any service buying sim time.
papers.design: Systematic review (CASP appraisal of 7 articles)
papers.n: 7 studies of high-fidelity simulation for critical care paramedics
papers.finding: Learners reported improved expertise, engagement, motivation, responsiveness and mood; evidence was insufficient on self-awareness and on performance of trained crews in the prehospital setting; authors recommend standardised training and assessment.
papers.caveat: Only 7 heterogeneous studies, none showing a link to real-world prehospital performance.
papers.shortTitle: Flight simulation training: engagement shown, evidence thin
