papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on whether simulation training skills transfer to real prehospital critical care performance.

papers.title: Developing an introductory training programme for newly employed nurses in the ambulance service through participatory action research
papers.summary: A Swedish participatory action research study in one ambulance service identified four challenges in introductory training for newly employed nurses — theory-heavy structure, variable supervision, weak leadership connection and role ambiguity — and translated them into three programme interventions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Sweden crews ambulances with nurses rather than the paramedic model used here, but the induction-design lessons — practice integration, prepared supervisors, peer learning — translate to any new-starter programme.
papers.design: Qualitative participatory action research (2020–2024)
papers.n: One Swedish ambulance service organisation (newly employed nurses, supervisors, management)
papers.finding: Four interrelated challenges consolidated; three interventions implemented (restructured theory and practice, prepared clinical supervisors, integrated peer learning); reflection showed theory-practice integration, supervision, leadership and peer learning were interdependent.
papers.caveat: Single organisation, small qualitative material base, and results are process descriptions rather than outcome evidence.
papers.shortTitle: New ambulance nurse induction: four challenges, three fixes
papers.learningGoal: Understand how structured supervision, peer learning and leadership support shape induction for new ambulance clinicians.

papers.title: Transport mechanical ventilation during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: an exploratory prehospital pilot study
papers.summary: A Thai exploratory pilot compared transport mechanical ventilation (HAMILTON-T1, volume-controlled) with bag-valve ventilation during CPR in adult OHCA and found no significant differences in PCO2, pH, pO2, sustained ROSC or 28-day survival, with mechanical ventilation operationally feasible.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Transport ventilators for ongoing CPR are a critical care capability rather than standard kit on most Australian ambulances, and drug-assisted intubation is an intensive care paramedic skill in most services — but this is exactly the crew the findings speak to.
papers.design: Prospective, time-sequenced exploratory pilot (6 months bag-valve, then mechanical ventilation)
papers.n: 41 adults with OHCA (29 bag-valve, 12 mechanical ventilation)
papers.finding: No significant differences in PCO2, pH or pO2, sustained ROSC or 28-day survival between groups; mechanical ventilation feasible despite implementation challenges
papers.caveat: Exploratory pilot, not powered for clinical outcomes, and the unequal groups (29 vs 12) were sequential rather than randomised
papers.shortTitle: Transport ventilation during CPR feasible in pilot
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and practical challenges of mechanical ventilation during transport CPR in adult cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Association between On-Scene Interval and 24-Hour Mortality among Code Red Emergency Medical Services Patients: A Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: A Thai retrospective cohort of Code Red ALS activations found on-scene intervals of 21-25 minutes were associated with higher odds of 24-hour mortality compared with 5 minutes or less (adjusted OR 5.61), and intervals of 20 minutes or longer came with 321.7 fewer expected survival minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Scene-time benchmarks are an operations question for any ambulance service, but a Thai physician-supported ALS dispatch model and the observational design mean sicker patients likely drive some of the long scene times.
papers.design: Retrospective cohort, ALS dispatch, restricted cubic splines
papers.n: 2,321 Code Red EMS activations, Saraburi Province
papers.finding: On-scene interval of 21-25 minutes was associated with higher odds of 24-hour mortality versus 5 minutes or less (aOR 5.61, 95% CI 1.58-19.97); non-survivors had a longer median on-scene interval (12 vs 9 minutes)
papers.caveat: Prolonged scene time may reflect necessary on-scene care in sicker patients, and spline estimates at longer intervals were imprecise
papers.shortTitle: Longer on-scene intervals linked to 24-hour mortality
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on which on-scene interventions justify extended scene time in critically unwell patients.

papers.title: Telemedicine in Disaster Medicine-Use of Paramedics as Tele-Consultants to Guide Personnel with Limited Medical Training at the Disaster Site
papers.summary: In a German mass-casualty simulation, tele-consult support delivered by experienced paramedics performed similarly to tele-physician support and on-site physician care on indicated treatments addressed (51% vs 56-57%) and analgesia provision (~60%), both far ahead of EMT-only care (8% and 7%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian services don't run tele-consultant models for mass-casualty scenes, but the finding that experienced paramedics can fill the remote expert role speaks directly to any service designing MCI telehealth support.
papers.design: Prospective simulation-based controlled quasi-experimental study within a 7.5-hour MCI exercise
papers.n: 151 simulated patients across 7 treatment tents
papers.finding: Indicated treatments addressed: 51% tele-paramedic vs 57% tele-physician vs 56% on-site physician vs 8% EMT-only (p < 0.001); analgesia addressed in 60%, 59%, 68% and 7% respectively; time to first treatment order did not differ
papers.caveat: Single simulation exercise with simulated patients — real-disaster performance untested, and patient contact definitions differed between telemedicine and non-telemedicine groups
papers.shortTitle: Tele-paramedics matched physicians in MCI drill
papers.learningGoal: Build my understanding of how paramedic tele-consultation can support less-trained clinicians at mass-casualty incidents.

papers.title: “You could be in the target group yourself”: Lived experiences of community first responders without a professional healthcare background in Denmark - an interpretive phenomenological study
papers.summary: An interpretive phenomenological study of ten Danish lay community first responders — part of a 60,000-volunteer national system, about 70% without healthcare backgrounds — identified four themes: a sense of duty, acting under uncertainty as a civilian-turned-responder, navigating relational roles with crews, and carrying personal identity into crisis.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Community first responder schemes exist in parts of Australia and New Zealand but are nothing like Denmark's national 60,000-strong system, so this informs how volunteer integration with crews could work rather than describing current practice.
papers.design: Qualitative interpretative phenomenological analysis, semi-structured interviews
papers.n: 10 community first responders without a professional healthcare background
papers.finding: Four themes: a sense of duty, acting under uncertainty as a civilian-turned-responder, navigating relational roles with professionals and peers, and carrying the self into crisis; volunteers driven by moral duty, meaningfulness and community
papers.caveat: Ten volunteers recruited via social media in a single national system; IPA is about lived experience, not generalisable effect estimates
papers.shortTitle: What drives lay community first responders in Denmark
papers.learningGoal: Understand the lived experience of volunteer community first responders so I can better support them on scene.

papers.title: Improving emergency medical services in the context of paramedic training: a phenomenological study
papers.summary: A Turkish phenomenological study of fifteen paramedic participants found problems in paramedic training and service delivery varied by setting — station issues were linked to the system itself while emergency department problems were tied to patients and staff attitudes — with large student numbers negatively affecting both education and service delivery.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Turkey's paramedic model and student volumes differ from Australian pathways, but the placement-setting split — system problems at stations versus interpersonal problems in EDs — is a familiar tension in Australian clinical placement discussions.
papers.design: Qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis
papers.n: 15 paramedic and student participants, Turkey
papers.finding: 10 sub-themes across 36 codes: station problems were linked to the system itself, emergency department problems to patients and staff attitudes, and high student numbers were seen as harming both education and service delivery
papers.caveat: Single-country qualitative study of 15 participants in a different training structure; no outcome measures
papers.shortTitle: Paramedic training problems vary by placement setting
papers.learningGoal: Understand how placement setting and student supervision capacity shape the quality of paramedic clinical education.

papers.title: Self-Rated Health and Burnout Dimensions Among Prehospital Emergency Medical Services Physicians: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.summary: A Serbian cross-sectional study of 151 prehospital emergency physicians using the Maslach Burnout Inventory found higher emotional exhaustion was associated with less favourable self-rated health (OR per 10-point increase 1.31, 95% CI 1.04-1.64), with depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment showing no clear adjusted associations.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Serbia crews its ambulances with physicians, but the emotional exhaustion and perceived health link is workforce-wellbeing territory that translates to paramedic crews, whose burnout research shows the same pattern.
papers.design: Cross-sectional study, ordinal regression models, convenience sample
papers.n: 151 prehospital emergency physicians, one Belgrade EMS
papers.finding: Higher emotional exhaustion was associated with less favourable self-rated health (OR per 10-point increase 1.31, 95% CI 1.04-1.64); the association weakened after mutual adjustment (OR 1.30, 95% CI 0.96-1.75); depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment showed no clear associations
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional convenience sample from a single physician-staffed service — no conclusions about direction or causality
papers.shortTitle: Physician burnout dimension linked to self-rated health
papers.learningGoal: Understand how emotional exhaustion relates to how paramedics perceive their own health and wellbeing.

papers.title: The experiences of patients, their families, and carers during care from alternative ambulance response units: A scoping review
papers.summary: A scoping review of patient, family and carer experiences of alternative ambulance response units found that people value receiving competent care at home, avoiding hospital transport, and referral pathways with continuity of care beyond the initial episode.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Non-transport and alternative response models run across Australian services in various forms, so the experience themes are relevant — but only three small studies with mixed methods underpin them.
papers.design: Scoping review
papers.n: 3 studies across diverse settings
papers.finding: Key experience constructs: convenience of home-based care, avoiding unnecessary ED attendance, perceived competence plus interpersonal communication, reassurance and psychological safety, and perceived longer-term benefit from referral and continuity of care
papers.caveat: Only three studies with heterogeneous methods were found — the evidence base for experience measures in this model is thin
papers.shortTitle: What patients think of alternative response units
papers.learningGoal: Understand the factors that shape patient, family and carer experiences of alternative ambulance response units in my practice.

papers.title: ‘Taking the fear factor out of it’: Family member and first responder experiences of the HUGS@Home psychological first aid programme
papers.summary: A qualitative study of a family-focused psychological first aid programme for first responders found participants felt more confident starting difficult conversations at home, with less stigma around operational stress, though gaps remained in organisational integration and programme sustainability.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Occupational mental health support is a live issue for every Australian ambulance service, and most still leave families outside their wellbeing programmes — this shows what a family-inclusive approach could look like.
papers.design: Qualitative interviews and focus group, reflexive thematic analysis
papers.n: 11 interviews plus one focus group of 5, 6–9 months after training
papers.finding: Four themes: communicating with care and confidence, navigating the 'not normal', creating an open culture, and sustaining support beyond the programme; participants reported better work-to-home transitions and stronger family and peer relationships
papers.caveat: Small purposive sample from a single programme interviewed 6–9 months after training — no outcome measurement
papers.shortTitle: Psychological first aid for paramedic families
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to hold open, confident conversations about operational stress with family and peers.

papers.title: Bystanders and Close Ones in Unsuccessful Resuscitation: An Overlooked Population in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.summary: An Italian perspective paper argues bystanders and relatives involved in unsuccessful out-of-hospital resuscitation are an overlooked group at risk of lasting psychological distress, and sketches supportive follow-up and referral roles for emergency clinicians.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — As community responder schemes grow, more Australians will perform CPR that fails — but this is a perspective piece with preliminary evidence, framed around nursing roles.
papers.design: Perspective/review
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: Unsuccessful resuscitation involvement can cause emotional distress, intrusive memories, guilt and PTSD symptoms; supportive follow-up contact and referral pathways are proposed over formal debriefing
papers.caveat: A perspective paper — the evidence on supportive follow-up effectiveness remains preliminary
papers.shortTitle: Supporting bystanders after failed resuscitation
papers.learningGoal: Understand my role in recognising and supporting bystander psychological distress after unsuccessful resuscitation.

papers.title: Transcutaneous overdrive pacing for refractory polymorphic ventricular tachycardia in the prehospital setting: A case report and practical considerations
papers.summary: A prehospital case report describes transcutaneous overdrive pacing used as rescue therapy for refractory polymorphic ventricular tachycardia after cardiac arrest, highlighting the gap between guideline options and what ambulances actually carry.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Transcutaneous pacing is an intensive care paramedic skill on Australian trucks, and this is a practical rescue option when drugs and shocks fail — but it rests on a single case.
papers.design: Case report
papers.n: 1 patient
papers.finding: Transcutaneous overdrive pacing was implemented prehospital as rescue for recurrent polymorphic VT after OHCA when transvenous pacing was unavailable
papers.caveat: Single case with no comparison or outcome detail beyond the index event
papers.shortTitle: Overdrive pacing for refractory pVT prehospital
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when transcutaneous overdrive pacing is appropriate rescue therapy for refractory polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

papers.title: Evaluation of Surface Contamination in Prehospital Emergency Units: Identifying Hotspots and Hygiene Priorities
papers.summary: An Iranian cross-sectional study sampling 23 high-touch sites in ambulances (1,932 ATP tests) found the worst contamination on patient-contact kit — pulse oximeter and blood pressure cuff — and showed handwashing cut paramedic hand contamination nearly tenfold.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Vehicle cleaning between patients and hand hygiene are universal practice, and the hotspot equipment sits in every Australian ambulance — though this is one low-resource Iranian fleet.
papers.design: Cross-sectional ATP bioluminescence sampling
papers.n: 23 high-touch sites per vehicle, 1,932 total tests
papers.finding: Pulse oximeter (>1,100 RLU) and blood pressure cuff exceeded the very-high contamination threshold; paramedic hand RLU fell from 349.79 to 34.79 after handwashing
papers.caveat: Single Iranian university-affiliated fleet; ATP RLU thresholds are proxies, not infection outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Ambulance contamination hotspots: cuffs and sats probes
papers.learningGoal: Recognise which shared patient-contact equipment poses the highest infection risk and strengthen my hygiene practices between cases.

papers.title: Enhancing Educational Programs and Communication Strategies to Address Alcohol Use Among EMS Providers
papers.summary: A US qualitative study of 31 EMS clinicians found alcohol-related education for staff is limited and patient-focused rather than wellbeing-focused, with participants wanting EMS-specific content, personal narratives and stronger peer and family support.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Occupational drinking as a coping mechanism and how education addresses it translate across ambulance services, though the US certification mix and sample differ from Australian crews.
papers.design: Qualitative semi-structured interviews
papers.n: 31 EMS clinicians across multiple US certification levels and regions
papers.finding: Existing alcohol-related education described as limited, passive and patient-care focused; participants wanted EMS-specific data, physiological content, personal narratives and interactive delivery plus peer and family support
papers.caveat: Self-selected qualitative sample of non-fire-based US providers
papers.shortTitle: EMS alcohol education: limited and patient-focused
papers.learningGoal: Understand how alcohol-related education and peer support shape clinician wellbeing within the Australian paramedic workforce.

papers.title: Pre-hospital pulse pressure as an early predictor of active hemorrhage in trauma patients
papers.summary: A retrospective study of 2,177 adult trauma patients across three Canadian level 1 trauma centres found prehospital pulse pressure predicted active haemorrhage (AUC 0.73), with each 10 mmHg narrowing raising the odds by 51% and a cut-off of ≤45 mmHg most useful for ruling bleeding out.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Pulse pressure is just two numbers off the cuff you already take — no new equipment or drugs, so it applies to Australian practice as it stands. The outcome (transfusion or haemorrhage control) is hospital-side, but the flag is raised on scene.
papers.design: Retrospective multicentre cohort
papers.n: 2,177 adult trauma patients (68 with active haemorrhage)
papers.finding: Prehospital pulse pressure predicted active haemorrhage (AUC 0.73, similar to SBP 0.74); each 10 mmHg narrowing raised the odds by 51% (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.28–1.79), and PP ≤45 mmHg was best for rule-out given high negative predictive value
papers.caveat: Retrospective design with only 68 bleeding patients, so the cut-off needs prospective validation
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital pulse pressure flags trauma bleeding
papers.learningGoal: Recognise narrowing pulse pressure as an early sign of haemorrhage in trauma patients before blood pressure falls.

papers.title: Earlier Versus Later Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Sequential Landmark Target Trial Emulation
papers.journal: European Heart Journal. Acute Cardiovascular Care
papers.summary: A target trial emulation in 58,668 patients with refractory OHCA from the Korean nationwide registry found ECPR was associated with higher 30-day survival at 15, 30 and 60 minutes after ED arrival (+15.0, +14.4 and +7.7 percentage points); an exploratory analysis found the benefit narrowed but remained significant to 120 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ECPR is an in-hospital tool — Australian crews don't deliver it — but the refractory-arrest transport and destination decisions that get a patient to an ECMO centre are ours, and the finding questions the 60-minute cut-off many systems apply.
papers.design: Nationwide registry target trial emulation (sequential landmark)
papers.n: 58,668 patients with refractory OHCA (909 received ECPR)
papers.finding: Weighted 30-day survival with ECPR vs conventional CPR was 31.0% vs 16.0%, 21.6% vs 7.2% and 10.9% vs 3.2% at 15, 30 and 60 minutes after ED arrival; an exploratory analysis found benefit narrowed but stayed significant to 120 minutes
papers.caveat: Propensity-adjusted observational design, not randomised — residual selection bias about who gets ECMO is likely
papers.shortTitle: ECPR timing in refractory OHCA: survival gap persists
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and uncertainties of ECPR for refractory cardiac arrest beyond the conventional sixty-minute window.

papers.title: Six-degree-of-freedom manikin neck for immobilisation training, incorporating linear potentiometers for real-time motion feedback
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers. Part H, Journal of Engineering in Medicine
papers.summary: Australian engineers built and tested a proof-of-concept instrumented manikin neck with six-degree-of-freedom motion and real-time head-position feedback for immobilisation training, achieving angle measurement error under 0.89° versus motion capture.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — A device prototype, not evidence about patient care — interesting for training programs, but nothing here changes what crews do yet, and the authors note it needs work before paramedic training settings.
papers.design: Device design, manufacture and bench validation
papers.n: One manikin neck prototype (bench-tested against motion capture)
papers.finding: The prototype delivered six-degree-of-freedom neck motion with realistic low stiffness and head-angle accuracy within 0.89° RMSE versus optoelectronic motion capture
papers.caveat: Proof-of-concept only: range of motion and stiffness were limited by the build, and it hasn't been evaluated in actual paramedic training
papers.shortTitle: Instrumented manikin neck for immobilisation training
papers.learningGoal: Improve my spinal immobilisation technique by understanding how real-time feedback on neck movement reveals excess motion during handling.

papers.title: Association between nighttime heat exposure and emergency hospitalization for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: A time-stratified case-crossover study in Japan
papers.summary: A nationwide time-stratified case-crossover study of 135,898 emergency hospitalisations for OHCA in Japan found hot nights (minimum temperature above the regional 92.5th percentile) were associated with a 9% higher OHCA hospitalisation risk, with the highest risks in people aged 75+ and women in northern regions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Australian summers are trending the same way and our population is ageing identically — this is a hazard pattern crews will meet on night shift, though it is a climate exposure signal, not an intervention trial.
papers.design: Time-stratified case-crossover, nationwide administrative database (2011–2021)
papers.n: 135,898 emergency hospitalisations for OHCA in Japan
papers.finding: Hot nights were associated with more OHCA hospitalisations (RR 1.090, 95% CI 1.047–1.135); RRs were higher in people ≥75 (1.295) and women in northern regions (1.352), and higher again for both groups where air conditioners were less common
papers.caveat: Hospitalisation-based — arrests not transported or dead at scene are invisible, and daily minimum temperature is a crude exposure measure
papers.shortTitle: Hot nights linked to more OHCA
papers.learningGoal: Recognise hotter nighttime temperatures as a driver of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest risk in older and female patients.

papers.title: Rapid Transport to Extracorporeal CPR: Urging Caution Prior to Implementation
papers.summary: A Prehospital Emergency Care commentary reviewing the ARREST, INCEPTION and Prague OHCA trials argues the ECPR evidence is not strong enough for widespread prehospital adoption, because any benefit cannot be separated from the effect of the intra-arrest transport ECPR programs require.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — ECPR for OHCA depends on coordinated intra-arrest transport, so the implementation decision sits with ambulance systems here too; no Australian service runs routine ECPR for arrest, and this is a useful framing piece before anyone is asked to build one.
papers.design: Narrative review/commentary of three randomised ECPR trials
papers.n: Three RCTs (ARREST n=30, INCEPTION, Prague OHCA)
papers.finding: Only ARREST (30 patients) strongly favoured ECPR; INCEPTION and Prague OHCA were not statistically significant, and the authors argue intra-arrest transport effects cannot be excluded as a driver of reported benefit
papers.caveat: A commentary, not new data — interpretation of already-published trials
papers.shortTitle: ECPR for OHCA: pump the brakes
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and harms of intra-arrest transport for extracorporeal CPR candidacy in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Investigating the impact of ambulance service models on paramedic delivery of end-of-life care in England: an exploratory study using case study design
papers.summary: Case studies of three English ambulance services found paramedics deliver end-of-life care with learning on the job and patchy access to patient records, anticipatory medicines and palliative advice, with more innovative models (advanced-paramedic anticipatory medicines, an in-service palliative team and palliative care ambulances) improving resources.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — End-of-life calls are a growing share of ambulance work everywhere, and the gaps it names — no records access, no anticipatory medicines, no one to ring for advice — are the same ones Australian crews describe; the innovative service models are ones our services could copy.
papers.design: Embedded qualitative case study of three English ambulance service models, framework analysis
papers.n: 101 participants (75 healthcare professionals, 26 patients and carers) across 3 services
papers.finding: Learning on the job and limited access to records, anticipatory medicines and palliative advice dominated practice across all three models; paramedic workload was driven partly by primary and community service shortages
papers.caveat: Exploratory, mainly qualitative case studies; three English services selected for their end-of-life service models, so findings may not transfer to other services
papers.shortTitle: How ambulance models shape end-of-life care
papers.learningGoal: Understand how system design shapes paramedic decision-making in end-of-life care in the Australian context.

papers.title: Impact of prehospital scene-to-door time on functional outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy: insights from a regional stroke network
papers.summary: A single-centre Japanese cohort of 121 stroke thrombectomy patients transported directly from scene found scene-to-door time was only associated with outcome in patients with pre-stroke disability, where longer intervals were linked to lower odds of a favourable 90-day outcome (aOR 0.91; ROC cut-off 14 minutes in that subgroup).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Scene-to-door intervals are exactly what Australian crews influence on stroke jobs, but this comes from one Japanese comprehensive stroke centre with its own bypass and activation pathways.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort, comprehensive stroke centre (2018–2023)
papers.n: 121 patients transported directly from scene to EVT
papers.finding: In patients with pre-stroke disability (mRS ≥1), longer scene-to-door time was associated with lower odds of favourable 90-day outcome (adjusted OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.81–0.98; ROC cut-off 14 min); no significant association in the overall cohort (AUC 0.57)
papers.caveat: Single centre, only 121 patients, retrospective design
papers.shortTitle: Scene-to-door time and stroke thrombectomy
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how on-scene time affects functional outcomes in stroke patients with pre-existing disability needing thrombectomy.

papers.title: Community Paramedics Addressing the Evolving Opioid Crisis: A Case Series Addressing the Kratom Derivatives 7-Hydroxymitragynine and MGM-15
papers.summary: A US case series describes community paramedics treating severe withdrawal from concentrated kratom derivatives (7-hydroxymitragynine and MGM-15) with full-dose buprenorphine and rapid linkage to outpatient medication for opioid use disorder, with both patients retained in treatment at 30 days.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Buprenorphine is not something Australian ambulances carry — adoption would need a guideline change — but concentrated 7-OH products are sold over the counter and online, and crews will meet the dependence and withdrawal they cause.
papers.design: Case series, US community paramedic buprenorphine program
papers.n: 2 patients
papers.finding: Buprenorphine 24 mg and 32 mg/8 mg with naloxone treated severe 7-OH/MGM-15 withdrawal; both patients were linked to outpatient treatment within 48 hours and retained in treatment at 30 days
papers.caveat: Two cases, no comparison or systematic outcome measurement
papers.shortTitle: Kratom derivative withdrawal treated prehospital
papers.learningGoal: Recognise emerging synthetic kratom derivative toxicity and withdrawal presentations that may require buprenorphine-based management.

papers.title: Psychological Well-Being of Helicopter Emergency Medical Service Personnel: A Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.summary: A nationwide survey of Danish HEMS personnel (73 of 82 responding) found no participant met criteria for PTSD, anxiety, depression or secondary traumatic stress despite high trauma exposure — but 48.6% exceeded the personal burnout cutoff and 23.2% the work-related burnout cutoff.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Physician-staffed HEMS is not our crewing model, but the pattern it shows — trauma scores low, burnout high — is one Australian critical-care and road crews will recognise from their own wellbeing surveys.
papers.design: Nationwide cross-sectional survey, Danish HEMS (April–May 2024)
papers.n: 73 physicians, HEMS crew paramedics and pilots (89% response rate)
papers.finding: 48.6% exceeded the personal burnout cutoff, 23.2% work-related and 17.4% patient-related; no one met PTSD criteria; trauma exposure correlated with PTSD symptoms (r=0.30) and work-related burnout (r=0.33)
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional self-report in a single country's physician-staffed HEMS, with wide confidence intervals on the between-group exposure comparisons
papers.shortTitle: HEMS burnout high even without PTSD
papers.learningGoal: Recognise early signs of personal burnout in my critical care practice before they affect patient safety.

papers.title: Infrequent exposure to prehospital neonatal interventions and resource utilisation by a public EMS in the Western Cape, South Africa
papers.summary: A two-year review of 9,825 neonatal activations in the Western Cape public EMS found neonates were just 0.7% of workload with rare high-risk interventions (prehospital intubation 0.4%), and non-specialist crews attended two-thirds of high-acuity cases despite limited neonatal scope of practice.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A low-resource South African public EMS with different scopes of practice, but the core problem is identical in Australia — most paramedics almost never touch a neonate, so skills decay is a shared training challenge.
papers.design: Retrospective review of electronic patient care records, 2022–2023
papers.n: 9,825 neonatal activations
papers.finding: Neonatal activations were 0.7% of EMS workload; prehospital intubation 0.4%; recorded mechanical ventilation 4.6% versus sedation/analgesia 1.1%; specialist retrieval teams were strongly associated with advanced interventions
papers.caveat: Descriptive record review in a low-resource public system — staffing, scope of practice and case mix differ from Australian services
papers.shortTitle: Neonatal calls rare on South African ambulances
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my preparedness for rare high-acuity neonatal cases given limited routine exposure in Australian prehospital practice.

papers.title: Self-Reported Completeness of Neurological Documentation in Prehospital Emergency Care: Associations With Neurological Training and Professional Experience
papers.summary: A survey of 348 Polish paramedics found moderate self-reported neurological documentation completeness (mean 24.57 of a possible 35), worst for documenting temporal neurological change (only 9.2% consistent), with higher scores in those with neurological training or more experience.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Self-reported rather than audited, and from a Polish service, but under-documenting how neuro findings change over time is a known weak spot in prehospital records here too, and it directly affects stroke and TBI handover.
papers.design: Cross-sectional structured questionnaire, southeastern Poland (June 2025–March 2026)
papers.n: 348 paramedics
papers.finding: Mean self-reported documentation completeness 24.57/35; level of consciousness was documented often (81.0%) but only 9.2% consistently documented temporal neurological changes; training was associated with higher scores (26.20 vs 23.24, P<0.001)
papers.caveat: Self-reported documentation with no chart audit to verify, single region
papers.shortTitle: Paramedics under-document neuro change over time
papers.learningGoal: Refine my documentation of temporal neurological change to better capture patient deterioration over time.

papers.title: Visual behavior of flight nurses during initial prehospital care inside an ambulance: A cross-sectional observational study using wearable eye-tracking technology
papers.summary: Wearable eye-tracking on nine Japanese flight nurses across 60 real ambulance cases found gaze behaviour during initial prehospital care differed significantly by experience level, with distinct fixation patterns between novice, intermediate and expert groups.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Flight nurses in a physician-staffed helicopter service are not our crew model, but how novices versus experts visually scan a moving ambulance is a real question for anyone supervising clinicians learning the back of a truck.
papers.design: Cross-sectional observational study, wearable eye-tracking in real ambulance transfers
papers.n: 9 flight nurses across 60 cases
papers.finding: Four principal components of gaze behaviour (fixation count, visit count, fixation duration) were significantly associated with experience group after adjustment for multiple comparisons; novices showed distinctly different fixation patterns from experts
papers.caveat: Nine nurses from one Japanese HEMS base, small groups (2–4 per experience level), limited to initial care after rendezvous with the ground crew
papers.shortTitle: Eye-tracking shows how experience guides ambulance care
papers.learningGoal: Build my ability to interpret how visual attention patterns during patient assessment differ between novice and expert clinicians.

papers.title: Emergency-system drivers of intersectional inequities in prehospital stroke care in coastal eastern England
papers.summary: A qualitative study of 11 stakeholders in coastal eastern England found rural and coastal distance becomes inequity-producing when combined with limited mobility, complex extrication and Category 2 demand, shaping delays in stroke recognition, pre-alerting and transfer to stroke-capable care.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Rural and regional Australia has the same geography — long distances, thin on-scene capability and crowded receiving hospitals — so the system mechanisms it describes transfer directly to our stroke pathways.
papers.design: Qualitative service evaluation, semi-structured interviews with system stakeholders, thematic analysis
papers.n: 11 stakeholders (paramedics, stroke nurses, GPs, managers, a neurologist, a researcher)
papers.finding: Inequity emerged where stroke recognition had to convert rapidly into dispatch priority, on-scene capability, pre-alerting and transfer; rural and coastal distance compounded delay when combined with limited patient mobility, complex extrication and Category 2 demand
papers.caveat: Provider and system-stakeholder accounts only — no patients or carers were interviewed, and it is a single English region
papers.shortTitle: Why rural stroke care lags: system drivers
papers.learningGoal: Understand how geography and system demand shape timely access to stroke-capable prehospital care in Australia.

papers.title: Competence in the use of a semi-automated external defibrillator among undergraduate dental students: evaluation and proposal for improvement
papers.summary: A simulated cardiac arrest assessment of 81 final-year Spanish dental students found fewer than 10% correctly performed 8 of 10 AED steps with standard voice prompts (median time to shock 143 s), and a modified set of instructions significantly improved key actions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The respondents are dental students, not paramedics, but lay-responder AED performance is the same weak link in Australian public-access defibrillation — the finding that clearer voice prompts fix real errors is a device-design lesson for the AEDs we depend on before we arrive.
papers.design: Simulation-based before/after assessment with a manikin
papers.n: 81 final-year dental students
papers.finding: With standard AED instructions, fewer than 10% of students correctly completed 8 of 10 assessed items (median time to shock 143 s); modified instructions significantly improved device activation and later steps (P<0.001)
papers.caveat: Single university, simulated scenario, students are not representative of trained responders
papers.shortTitle: Clearer AED voice prompts fix lay-user errors
papers.learningGoal: Improve my ability to guide bystanders through AED use during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Equity-Related Factors in Emergency Medical Service Use for Acute Coronary Syndromes: A Systematic Review
papers.summary: Systematic review of 14 Australian studies testing whether equity-related factors affect EMS use for acute coronary syndrome — EMS use ranged 36–79%, with under-49s up to 68% lower odds of calling than over-65s, men 11% lower than women, overseas-born 15% lower, non-English speakers 6–20% lower and remote residents 25% lower than city dwellers.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian data on who does and doesn't ring for chest pain — core ambulance business everywhere in the country, no translation needed.
papers.design: Systematic review (PROSPERO-registered) of Australian studies
papers.n: 14 Australian studies
papers.finding: EMS use for ACS ranged 36–79%; under-49s up to 68% lower odds of EMS use than over-65s, men up to 11% lower than women, overseas-born up to 15% lower, non-English speakers 6–20% lower, remote residents up to 25% lower than major-city residents
papers.caveat: Vote-counting synthesis of heterogeneous observational studies rather than pooled effect estimates
papers.shortTitle: Who doesn't call an ambulance for chest pain
papers.learningGoal: Understand the equity-related barriers that lead some Australian patients to delay or avoid calling an ambulance for chest pain.

papers.title: Prehospital point-of-care ultrasound as a decision-support tool: A structured narrative review
papers.summary: Structured narrative review of 38 articles on prehospital POCUS across cardiac arrest, shock, dyspnoea, trauma, paediatric and obstetric uses — it can identify reversible causes in arrest, characterise shock and support trauma triage and destination decisions, but limited sensitivity means it can't rule anything out.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A handful of Australian services carry prehospital ultrasound and most don't, so this shapes the debate about adoption more than current practice.
papers.design: Structured narrative review (38 articles, 9 systematic reviews)
papers.n: 38 articles reviewed
papers.finding: POCUS may identify cardiac activity and reversible causes in arrest, characterise shock mechanisms and improve diagnostic confidence in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; E-FAST has high specificity but limited sensitivity so it cannot be used as a rule-out test
papers.caveat: Single reviewer, no formal risk-of-bias assessment, certainty grading or meta-analysis
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital ultrasound as a decision tool
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how prehospital point-of-care ultrasound findings should influence my treatment and transport decisions.

papers.title: A Community Partnership Initiative in Utah to Enhance Prehospital Perinatal Care in the Prevention of Postpartum Hemorrhage
papers.summary: Quality improvement initiative describing how a rural US state changed its EMS protocols in April 2024 to let paramedics give oxytocin to prevent postpartum haemorrhage and AEMTs give it intramuscularly for prevention and treatment.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Oxytocin for postpartum haemorrhage is standard on Australian trucks, but this paper is about how a scope-of-practice change was won, not whether the drug works.
papers.design: Community-based interprofessional quality improvement initiative (implementation science framework)
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: State EMS protocols changed in April 2024 to allow paramedic oxytocin for PPH prevention and AEMT intramuscular oxytocin for PPH prevention and treatment
papers.caveat: Single-state process description with no clinical outcome data
papers.shortTitle: How Utah widened paramedic oxytocin scope
papers.learningGoal: Understand how expanded paramedic scope for oxytocin can strengthen prehospital postpartum haemorrhage care.

papers.title: Guideline adherence in helicopter versus ground emergency medical services: an indication-based analysis of 129,783 patients from the TraumaRegister DGU®
papers.journal: European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery
papers.summary: Retrospective analysis of 129,783 severely injured patients in the German TraumaRegister DGU (physician-staffed helicopter and ground services) found HEMS patients, who were younger and more severely injured, had higher rates of guideline-recommended prehospital interventions, such as advanced airway in impaired consciousness (96.5% vs 82.9%) and prehospital chest drains (14.0% vs 5.5%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A physician-staffed model, and chest drains sit beyond Australian paramedic scope while advanced airway is an intensive care paramedic skill in most services — but the helicopter-utilisation question is live here too.
papers.design: Retrospective multicentre registry cohort (TraumaRegister DGU, 2016–2024); both arms physician-staffed
papers.n: 129,783 adults with severe trauma (25% HEMS)
papers.finding: HEMS patients had higher guideline-recommended intervention rates in every indication subgroup (advanced airway in impaired consciousness 96.5% vs 82.9%; prehospital chest tube 14.0% vs 5.5%); HEMS patients were also younger and more severely injured
papers.caveat: Both arms physician-staffed; descriptive analysis with no adjustment for injury severity or scene factors, so sicker HEMS patients may explain part of the gap
papers.shortTitle: HEMS vs road: guideline adherence in trauma
papers.learningGoal: Understand how transport mode and scene factors influence adherence to trauma care guidelines in Australia.

papers.title: Challenges and opportunities in using digital health technologies for decision-making in prehospital non-emergency situations in Norway: a qualitative study
papers.summary: Qualitative interview study of 12 Norwegian paramedics on digital health tools for prehospital non-emergency decision-making — four themes emerged around call assessment and resource allocation, shared situational awareness, interprofessional communication, and the challenges of patchy implementation.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Nordic paramedic service rated on its merits, and the low-acuity decision-making burden it describes is the same one Australian crews carry.
papers.design: Exploratory qualitative interview study (reflexive thematic analysis)
papers.n: 12 paramedics interviewed
papers.finding: Four themes: digital support for call assessment and ambulance resource allocation, digital patient information for shared situational awareness, digital communication for interprofessional consultation, and implementation challenges despite established prehospital infrastructure
papers.caveat: Single-country qualitative study with purposive and snowball sampling of 12 paramedics
papers.shortTitle: Paramedics on digital decision support
papers.learningGoal: Understand how digital decision support tools shape non-emergency call assessment and interprofessional communication in paramedic practice.

papers.title: Cluster Versus Individual Randomization in Prehospital, Emergency and Critical Care Trials: A Meta-Epidemiological Study
papers.summary: Meta-epidemiological study of 65 meta-analyses (212 trials, 315,276 patients) comparing cluster-randomised with individually randomised trials in prehospital, emergency and critical care — no difference in mortality effect estimates, but cluster trials reported significantly smaller effect sizes for length-of-stay-type outcomes.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Methods evidence about how prehospital and emergency trials behave, which applies to any ambulance service reading the literature.
papers.design: Meta-epidemiological study of meta-analyses
papers.n: 65 meta-analyses, 212 RCTs (39 cluster), 315,276 patients
papers.finding: No statistically significant difference in mortality effect estimates between cluster and individually randomised trials (MD lnOR −0.110, 95% CI −0.093 to 0.313); cluster trials showed significantly smaller effect magnitudes for length-of-stay/days-alive outcomes (Hedges' g MD −0.202, 95% CI −0.392 to −0.012)
papers.caveat: Observational comparison across heterogeneous meta-analyses with only 44.7% of eligible meta-analyses reporting randomisation type
papers.shortTitle: Cluster trials read differently to individual ones
papers.learningGoal: Understand how cluster randomised trials differ in design and how that shapes interpreting prehospital evidence.

papers.title: Association between meteorological conditions and dizziness-related ambulance transports: a population-based study in Kochi Prefecture, Japan
papers.summary: Population-based study of 270,120 emergency transports in Kochi, Japan linking weather to dizziness-related ambulance call-outs — hotter days and short-term temperature spikes raised the odds of high-volume dizziness days, peaking in summer.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Japanese physician-diagnosed dataset, but heat-driven demand spikes are a planning problem Australian ambulance services face every summer.
papers.design: Retrospective population-based cohort (2017–2023)
papers.n: 270,120 emergency transports, 8,981 dizziness-related
papers.finding: Higher mean air temperature consistently associated with increased odds of high-frequency dizziness-transport days (≥5/day), as were short-term maximum-temperature increases and smaller diurnal temperature ranges; most frequent in summer
papers.caveat: Modest absolute differences in meteorological variables and dizziness defined by receiving-facility physician diagnosis
papers.shortTitle: Hot days drive dizziness call-outs
papers.learningGoal: Understand how heat and temperature swings influence demand patterns and my management of dizziness presentations in Australian summer conditions.

papers.title: Infant carry sling-associated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and other circumstances surrounding such events in children under two years: A five-year regional registry analysis
papers.summary: A five-year English regional registry review of 162 cardiac arrests in children under two found only two linked to infant carry slings, while co-sleeping featured in a third of cases.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Sleep-related infant arrests — co-sleeping, found unresponsive in a cot, bed, sofa or pushchair — are the same scenes Australian crews attend, and nothing about a single-region English ambulance registry makes the numbers system-specific.
papers.design: Retrospective registry service evaluation
papers.n: 162 children under two who received a resuscitation attempt
papers.finding: Only 2 of 162 OHCA were carry sling-associated (1.8% of the 114 infant cases); co-sleeping accounted for 33.3% and children found unresponsive 26.3%
papers.caveat: Small single-region sample relying on free-text narrative review — two events over five years can't exclude a rare risk
papers.shortTitle: Infant carry slings rarely linked to OHCA
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how carry slings and co-sleeping environments contribute to sudden deterioration in infants under two.

papers.title: Reproducible intubation contrast without evidence of a unique threshold at Glasgow Coma Scale 8: a two-era nationwide retrospective cohort study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A two-era Japan Trauma Data Bank analysis of roughly 138,000 adults found recorded intubation more likely at GCS 8 than 9, but no evidence of a unique risk threshold at that boundary.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It's in-hospital registry data from a physician-assisted Japanese system, and drug-assisted intubation is an intensive care paramedic skill in most Australian services — but the GCS 8 cutoff it interrogates drives prehospital airway and trauma triage thinking everywhere.
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide registry cohort (two eras)
papers.n: 138,405 adults transported directly from scene (71,988 + 66,417)
papers.finding: Recorded intubation was 9.1–10.6 percentage points more frequent at GCS 8 (pooled aOR 1.61, 95% CI 1.36–1.91), but model fit favoured a graded GCS–outcome relationship over a discrete jump at the 8/9 boundary in every outcome and both eras
papers.caveat: Outcomes are post-arrival hospital records in patients with no prehospital advanced airway, so the prehospital intubation decision itself isn't tested
papers.shortTitle: No unique GCS 8 threshold for intubation
papers.learningGoal: Weigh trauma airway decisions against graded consciousness rather than relying on a fixed GCS threshold.

papers.title: Paediatric out-of-hospital clinical deterioration: A scoping review
papers.summary: A scoping review of 28 studies found no standardised definition of paediatric out-of-hospital clinical deterioration and almost no research on how crews actually recognise it.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Recognising the deteriorating child is the same clinical problem for Australian crews as anywhere, and most included research comes from health systems structured like ours.
papers.design: Scoping review (JBI methodology)
papers.n: 28 studies published 1990–2026, mostly retrospective and from high-income countries
papers.finding: No study offered an operational definition of paediatric out-of-hospital deterioration; research leans on single-timepoint vital signs, trauma-specific indices and hospital-derived early warning scores, and no study examined physiological trajectories
papers.caveat: A scoping review maps the field without pooling effects, and most included studies were retrospective
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric deterioration in the field poorly defined
papers.learningGoal: Recognise early physiological deterioration in paediatric patients beyond single vital sign readings.

papers.title: Pediatric Clinical Interventions and Adverse Safety Events Among Emergency Medical Services Encounters in Agencies With and Without a Pediatric Emergency Care Coordinator: An Observational Study
papers.summary: A US cross-sectional study of 2,219 paediatric EMS encounters found agencies with a paediatric emergency care coordinator delivered more procedures and medications, with fewer and less severe adverse safety events.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — No Australian service runs a dedicated paediatric EMS coordinator role, but the safety gap it targets — missed procedures and medication errors in children — is the same everywhere.
papers.design: Cross-sectional chart review
papers.n: 2,219 paediatric encounters across 15 EMS agencies, 2019–2023
papers.finding: Coordinator agencies performed more procedures (55.4% vs 26.8%) and gave more medications (23.4% vs 7.7%); procedure adverse safety event rates were 13.7% vs 20.0%, with lower assigned harm severity
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional design — agencies that adopt a coordinator may differ systematically from those that don't, and adverse events came from chart review
papers.shortTitle: Paediatric care coordinators linked to fewer EMS errors
papers.learningGoal: Understand how paediatric care coordination roles within agencies influence the safety of prehospital interventions.

papers.title: Establishing the Priorities for Emergency Care Research in Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand
papers.summary: ACEM's Clinical Trials Network, with the James Lind Alliance, has launched a priority setting partnership to set the emergency care research agenda for Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand for the next 5–10 years.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — It's an ED-led process rather than an ambulance one, but the resulting agenda shapes the emergency care evidence Australian paramedics work from, and the partnership is explicitly seeking clinician and consumer participation.
papers.design: Guideline / statement
papers.n: Not reported
papers.finding: No results yet — the partnership is underway, aiming to prioritise unanswered questions across the ~11 million annual ED presentations in both countries
papers.caveat: This is an announcement of a process, not findings, and prehospital questions may or may not feature in the final priorities
papers.shortTitle: AU/NZ emergency care research priorities being set
papers.learningGoal: Understand how national emergency care research priorities are set and where paramedic perspectives can shape the agenda.

papers.title: A multifaceted intervention to increase bystander CPR rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in France: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised, controlled trial
papers.summary: A stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial in French EMS agencies found dispatcher training in arrest recognition, telephone CPR and a geolocated volunteer responder app was associated with more bystander CPR (61.4% to 70.9%, adjusted OR 1.54), an effect that lost significance after adjusting for secular trends; clinical outcomes did not improve.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Dispatch-assisted CPR and community responder schemes are core business for every Australian ambulance service, and this is a large prospectively registered randomised trial.
papers.design: Stepped-wedge cluster-randomised controlled trial
papers.n: 1,684 adults with non-traumatic OHCA from the 12 originally randomised French EMS agencies (intention-to-treat)
papers.finding: Bystander CPR before EMS arrival rose from 61.4% to 70.9% (adjusted OR 1.54, 95% CI 1.09–2.19), but not significantly after adjusting for secular trends; clinical outcomes did not improve
papers.caveat: The effect was no longer significant after adjustment for cluster-specific secular trends or baseline characteristics, and it did not translate into better clinical outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Dispatcher training + volunteer app: more CPR, no outcome gain
papers.learningGoal: Understand how dispatcher training and volunteer responder systems influence bystander CPR and survival outcomes in cardiac arrest care.

papers.title: Real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a before-and-after study (VEntilation during Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Study, VECARS-2)
papers.summary: A Paris before-and-after study of 163 arrests found real-time feedback during bag-valve-mask ventilation improved insufflated-volume adherence (68% vs 42% of breaths in the 400–600 mL range) and cut leak volume by 12%, although expired tidal volumes were unchanged.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bag-valve-mask ventilation during 30:2 CPR is standard practice on every Australian ambulance, so ventilation-quality feedback speaks directly to how crews are taught and audited.
papers.design: Before-and-after observational study
papers.n: 4,300 ventilations in 163 adults with OHCA
papers.finding: With feedback, insufflated volume fell within guideline range in 68% of ventilations vs 42%, dispersion dropped 35%, and leak volume was 12% lower (mean ratio 0.88); expired tidal volume was unchanged
papers.caveat: Before-and-after design without randomisation, single basic-life-support system, and no patient outcomes reported
papers.shortTitle: Real-time feedback tidies BVM ventilation in arrest
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to deliver consistent tidal volumes during bag-valve-mask ventilation in cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population Based Cohort Study
papers.summary: A Victorian population-based cohort of 728 out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors found fatigue in 35.8%, anxiety in 22.6% and depression in 18.0% at 12 months, with heavier symptom burden linked to worse quality of life, function and return to work.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian registry data on what happens to the patients we resuscitate, and survivorship aftercare is a live question for every service running cardiac arrest follow-up pathways.
papers.design: Prospective population-based cohort
papers.n: 728 OHCA survivors (68.2% of those eligible) interviewed at 12 months in Victoria
papers.finding: Fatigue 35.8%, anxiety 22.6%, depression 18.0%; fatigue exceeded population norms (SMD 0.64) and higher symptom burden tracked with worse EQ-5D, GOSE and return-to-work rates
papers.caveat: Self-reported symptoms with about a third of eligible survivors lost to follow-up
papers.shortTitle: Fatigue common a year after cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Recognise fatigue, anxiety and depression as common post-cardiac arrest survivors' needs when supporting recovery and follow-up.

papers.title: Association Between Capnographic Changes During Pulse Checks of Varying Durations and Clinical Outcomes During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Multicenter Study From Türkiye (CaPTuRe)
papers.summary: A 252-patient quasi-randomised multicentre study in Türkiye found pulse checks completed within 5 seconds were associated with roughly double the ROSC rate of checks lasting 6–10 seconds (36.3% vs 19.5%, OR 2.39), alongside better capnographic dynamics.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Pulse-check duration is something every rescuer on every arrest controls, wherever they work, and capnography-guided CPR quality is standard monitoring practice.
papers.design: Multicentre prospective quasi-randomised controlled study
papers.n: 252 cardiac arrest patients (124 with ≤5-second checks, 128 with 6–10-second checks)
papers.finding: Shorter pulse checks were linked to higher ROSC (36.3% vs 19.5%; OR 2.39, 95% CI 1.35–4.24) and more favourable ETCO2 loss and recovery patterns
papers.caveat: Quasi-randomised, not truly randomised, so healthier arrests may have had quicker checks; the abstract doesn't say whether arrests were in or out of hospital
papers.shortTitle: Shorter pulse checks linked to more ROSC
papers.learningGoal: Improve my technique for keeping pulse checks brief during cardiac arrest resuscitation while interpreting capnography trends.

papers.title: Identifying the Operational Bottleneck to Shock Delivery After Automated External Defibrillator Activation
papers.summary: Timestamps from 8,115 remotely monitored Japanese AEDs showed pad application consumed a median 81% of the power-on-to-first-analysis interval, with completion inside about 50 seconds marking shocks delivered within 60 seconds of power-on.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Public access defibrillation performance is the same problem everywhere — the device workflow, not the health system, is the bottleneck.
papers.design: Retrospective analysis of remotely monitored AED timestamps
papers.n: 8,115 AED activation events (900 initially shock-advised with recorded shock)
papers.finding: Median power-on-to-pad-application was 42 seconds, accounting for 81% of the power-on-to-first-analysis interval; a threshold of ≥51 seconds identified shock delivery beyond 60 seconds
papers.caveat: Device log data only, with no linkage to patient outcomes or rescuer type
papers.shortTitle: Pad application is the AED time bottleneck
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to minimise delays between AED power-on and pad application during cardiac arrest resuscitation.

papers.title: Low-Titer O + Whole Blood Implementation in the EMS System for Metropolitan Oklahoma City and Tulsa: Significance, Success, & Sharing Lessons Learned
papers.summary: The first two years of a prehospital low-titre O-positive whole blood program in Oklahoma (71.6% penetrating trauma) showed significantly improved prehospital vital signs after paramedic transfusion, with improved systolic blood pressure tied to higher survival to hospital arrival.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is limited to a handful of Australian services, so this program report informs the should-we-carry-blood debate more than current practice.
papers.design: Retrospective descriptive observational study
papers.n: Patients transfused low-titre O-positive whole blood by paramedics across two US cities, Dec 2022–Feb 2025
papers.finding: Systolic blood pressure, heart rate and shock index improved significantly after transfusion, and improved systolic blood pressure carried 9.7-fold greater odds of survival to hospital arrival
papers.caveat: Descriptive before-after design with no control group, and a predominantly penetrating trauma mix that differs from Australian patterns
papers.shortTitle: Whole blood on ambulances: first two years
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on when prehospital whole blood transfusion benefits trauma patients with haemorrhagic shock.

papers.title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
papers.summary: A 129,207-case Korean difference-in-differences study found regions adopting video physician-directed prehospital ALS for cardiac arrest had modestly higher prehospital ROSC (+1.35 percentage points) but no gain in survival or neurological outcome, with prehospital times stretching about 4 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Real-time physician direction of paramedic ALS is not the Australian crew model, but the finding feeds the broader question of how much on-scene advanced care buys in cardiac arrest.
papers.design: Retrospective difference-in-differences cohort
papers.n: 129,207 adults with OHCA across South Korea
papers.finding: SALS regions gained prehospital ROSC (+1.35 pp, 95% CI 0.56–2.15) but not survival to discharge (−0.35 pp) or favourable neurological outcome, while prehospital time rose 4.12 minutes
papers.caveat: Event-study analysis suggested differential pre-intervention trends, weakening the time-interval finding
papers.shortTitle: Physician-directed ALS: no survival gain
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and system costs of physician-directed prehospital advanced life support in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Prehospital management and hospital outcomes of severely injured patients during routine civilian mass casualty incidents: a 1:4 matched cohort analysis of the TraumaRegister DGU®
papers.summary: A matched German trauma-registry cohort (423 severely injured MCI patients vs 1,692 routine controls) found mass-casualty patients waited longer on scene (85 vs 67 minutes) and received more intubation and tranexamic acid, yet in-hospital mortality was similar (13.5% vs 11.7%).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Mass-casualty triage, on-scene time and transport decisions are core ambulance planning everywhere, though the German physician-staffed and helicopter-heavy response model differs from Australian MCI plans.
papers.design: 1:4 matched registry cohort
papers.n: 423 severely injured MCI patients matched to 1,692 controls
papers.finding: Median prehospital time was 85 vs 67 minutes; prehospital intubation (33.6% vs 20.9%) and TXA (32.1% vs 15.0%) were more frequent, but in-hospital mortality did not differ significantly
papers.caveat: Observational matching could not fully balance injury severity, which was higher in the MCI group
papers.shortTitle: Mass casualty care: slower but no deadlier
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the impact of prolonged on-scene times on outcomes for severely injured patients in mass casualty incidents.

papers.title: Prehospital Flumazenil: Five-Year Review of Use, Indications, Outcomes, and Adverse Events in Suspected Benzodiazepine Overdose
papers.journal: The Western Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A five-year Kansas review of 69 prehospital flumazenil administrations for suspected benzodiazepine overdose found clinical improvement with no seizures or adverse events recorded, even where possible contraindications existed.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — No Australian ambulance service carries flumazenil, so adoption would need a guideline change — the value here is challenging the reflex that the antidote is too risky for the road.
papers.design: Retrospective observational cohort
papers.n: 69 prehospital flumazenil administrations over five years
papers.finding: No seizures or adverse events were associated with flumazenil use (0/69; 95% CI 0–4.3%), with GCS improvement in the treated cases
papers.caveat: A tiny retrospective sample with a confidence interval wide enough to hide a real 4% adverse-event rate
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital flumazenil: 69 doses, no seizures
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the risks and benefits of benzodiazepine reversal in overdose, given flumazenil is not carried by Australian services.

papers.title: Quantifying discrepancies between EMS time intervals in the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and emergency medical dispatch data: A 10-year analysis
papers.summary: Linking 56,969 Swedish OHCA registry records to dispatch-centre data showed unit response times matched almost exactly, but registry-recorded total response times ran a median 81 seconds shorter than the dispatch clock.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Every Australian OHCA registry and service benchmark is built on the same kind of time intervals, so systematic drift between data sources matters to how performance is read.
papers.design: Retrospective registry linkage analysis
papers.n: 56,969 OHCA registry records linked to dispatch data, 2015–2024
papers.finding: Unit response time differed by a median 0.3 seconds between sources, but total response time was systematically 80.9 seconds shorter in the registry, with large regional variation
papers.caveat: Single-country registry comparison where the two sources use different time definitions, so the gap reflects both recall bias and definitional drift
papers.shortTitle: OHCA registry clock times run short
papers.learningGoal: Understand how inconsistent time definitions in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest data can distort quality improvement decisions.

papers.title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services
papers.summary: Semi-structured interviews with 20 Queensland paramedics and dispatchers framed frontline resilience as a trainable expert skill — a deliberately entered 'work mode' with preparation, containment and recovery phases — rather than a fixed trait.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Australian ambulance workforce research with direct implications for how wellbeing programs are designed and evaluated across services.
papers.design: Qualitative reflexive thematic analysis
papers.n: 20 Queensland paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2–38 years)
papers.finding: Three intensifiers (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) and three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) emerged, with work mode showing features of skilled performance
papers.caveat: Small single-service sample analysed by the interviewers themselves
papers.shortTitle: Resilience as a skill, not a trait
papers.learningGoal: Build my capacity to treat resilience as a trainable skill through deliberate preparation, containment and recovery.

papers.title: Incident location at home and emergency medical services on-scene time for older adults in Japan: a population-based cross-sectional study
papers.summary: Among 26,058 older Japanese patients transported from home, EMS on-scene time ran up to 9% longer when the patient was found in the toilet, bathroom or kitchen and on higher floors, and shorter in corridors and gardens.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Cramped bathrooms, toilets and stairs slow extrication for older patients in any system, even though Japanese housing and ambulance operations differ from Australia's.
papers.design: Population-based cross-sectional study
papers.n: 26,058 people aged ≥65 transported from home over nine years
papers.finding: On-scene time was longer for toilets (aMR 1.08), bathrooms (1.09) and kitchens (1.06) versus living rooms, shorter in corridors and gardens (both 0.95), and rose with floor level
papers.caveat: Single Japanese fire department, cross-sectional design with no patient outcome data
papers.shortTitle: Bathroom jobs eat scene time
papers.learningGoal: Understand how the location of an older patient within the home affects my scene time and extrication planning.

papers.title: Cost-effectiveness of prehospital high-sensitivity troponin i testing versus standard emergency department care in patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome in France
papers.summary: A French economic model built on 737 patients found prehospital point-of-care high-sensitivity troponin reduced ED attendance (90.9% vs 96.7%) and ED length of stay (1.63 vs 2.76 hours) versus standard care for suspected acute coronary syndrome.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital troponin testing is not part of Australian ambulance practice, and this models a physician-dispatched French system, but it sketches what a POC-troponin pathway could buy if trialled here.
papers.design: Decision-analytic semi-Markov model
papers.n: 737 patients with suspected ACS from the French VALIDATE cohort
papers.finding: ED attendance fell 5.8 percentage points (90.9% vs 96.7%, p<0.001) and mean ED stay dropped from 2.76 to 1.63 hours with prehospital hs-cTnI
papers.caveat: A 24-hour horizon that excluded inpatient, ICU and procedural costs, so only short-term economics were captured
papers.shortTitle: POC troponin on ambulances: fewer ED visits
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and limitations of prehospital point-of-care troponin testing in my assessment of suspected chest pain.

papers.title: Impact of a Decision-Support Interface on Mental Workload and Stress in Prehospital Stroke Triage: A Randomized Crossover Trial
papers.journal: The Western Journal of Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: In a randomised crossover simulation trial, 35 Taiwanese emergency medical technicians using a stroke triage decision-support interface showed reduced mental workload (RMSSD up 4.3 ms, heart rate down, NASA-TLX lower) versus dispatch orders alone.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Stroke destination decisions under time pressure are universal, and clinician cognitive load is a growing design question for Australian ePCR and triage tools, though this was a simulation in a different system.
papers.design: Randomised crossover simulation trial
papers.n: 35 EMT-intermediate participants, two 12-minute simulated trials each
papers.finding: RMSSD rose from 28.1 to 32.4 ms (mean difference 4.3 ms, 95% CI 1.57–6.99) and mean heart rate fell with decision support, indicating lower mental workload
papers.caveat: Short simulations with 35 junior clinicians and no patient or triage-accuracy outcomes
papers.shortTitle: Decision support eases stroke triage load
papers.learningGoal: Weigh how decision-support tools affect my cognitive load during stroke triage in the field.

papers.title: Translation and Validation of the TEAM-NL Instrument for Assessing Interprofessional Team Performance in Simulation-Based Resuscitation Training
papers.summary: A Dutch translation of the TEAM team-performance instrument showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's α 0.93) and good three-rater reliability (ICC 0.78) across 104 simulated resuscitation team performances in ALS courses.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — TEAM is already used in resuscitation training internationally, so confirming its psychometrics in another language strengthens the assessment tools Australian instructors rely on.
papers.design: Cross-cultural translation and validation study
papers.n: 52 participant groups, 104 observed team performances, 299 instructor ratings
papers.finding: Internal consistency was high (α 0.93), three-rater reliability good (ICC 0.78) and the total score correlated strongly with global ratings (r 0.86), though ceiling effects affected all items
papers.caveat: Ceiling effects on every item and only moderate reliability with two raters
papers.shortTitle: Dutch TEAM tool validated for resus training
papers.learningGoal: Understand how structured team performance tools can strengthen debriefing quality in simulation-based resuscitation training.

papers.title: Prehospital Pediatric Ventilation Quality Following Use of a Feedback Device: A Randomized Study
papers.summary: Randomised crossover simulation study with 123 EMS clinicians testing a ventilation feedback device on a paediatric manikin — guideline-adherent tidal volumes jumped from 16.2% to 87% of breaths with feedback, and rate adherence from 65% to 88.6%.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bag-mask ventilation of children is core practice on every Australian ambulance and the age-based guideline targets are the same ones used here — the only real catch is that it was done on a manikin rather than patients.
papers.design: Randomised crossover simulation study
papers.n: 123 EMS clinicians across 5 agencies
papers.finding: Guideline-recommended tidal volume in 87% of breaths with feedback vs 16.2% without; rate adherence 88.6% vs 65%; mask leak <30% in 88.4% vs 80%
papers.caveat: Manikin simulation of a 3-year-old at 5 US agencies — no patient outcomes, and real paediatric airways are less forgiving
papers.shortTitle: Feedback device lifts paediatric ventilation quality
papers.learningGoal: Refine my paediatric bag-mask ventilation technique to deliver guideline-consistent tidal volumes and rates in prehospital care.

papers.title: Traumatic Brain Injury in First Responders: From Hidden Burden to Occupational Health Action
papers.journal: The Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation
papers.summary: Introduction to a themed issue on TBI in first responders, finding a substantial but underrecognised burden with no consistent pathways for recognition, rehabilitation or return to duty, and presenting a 28-recommendation multidisciplinary consensus statement.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Return-to-duty and occupational health structures differ across Australian services, but the underrecognition of frontline TBI and its overlap with mental health is just as live a gap here.
papers.design: Consensus statement / thematic review
papers.n: 28 consensus recommendations across a multidisciplinary group
papers.finding: Substantial TBI burden in law enforcement, fire and EMS with persistent gaps in diagnosis, rehabilitation and duty-readiness; 28 recommendations spanning recognition, early assessment, return to duty and organisational policy
papers.caveat: Narrative synthesis of a themed issue — the authors concede first responder-specific evidence remains limited
papers.shortTitle: TBI in first responders needs occupational pathways
papers.learningGoal: Understand how occupational traumatic brain injury in paramedics affects recognition, return to duty and organisational support.

papers.title: Interprofessional continuing education for prehospital behavioral emergency response: a city-wide pre-post study in Taiwan
papers.summary: City-wide single-group pre-post evaluation of a 4-hour interprofessional behavioural-emergency course in Taiwan: self-efficacy rose from 3.16 to 3.54 (dz 0.76) and cognition rose in the 395 paired attendees, but stigma scores did not improve; the authors note these are pre-post associations, not causal evidence.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Training paramedics alongside police, fire and mental health clinicians speaks directly to Australian co-response and joint-training debates, though this ran in a different EMS system with no control group.
papers.design: Single-group pre-post study
papers.n: 750 attendees, 395 in the paired analysis
papers.finding: Self-efficacy rose from 3.16 to 3.54 (mean difference 0.39, 95% CI 0.34–0.44, dz 0.76) and cognition from 3.81 to 3.95; behavioural-emergency stigma rose slightly and substance-use stigma was unchanged
papers.caveat: Uncontrolled single-group design with anonymous demographic linkage and immediate self-reported outcomes only
papers.shortTitle: Joint training linked to higher behavioural emergency confidence
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my interprofessional collaboration when managing behavioural emergencies alongside mental health clinicians.

papers.title: Nursing Competencies in Helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) in Spain: A Qualitative Study of Professional Profiles and Advanced Training
papers.summary: A qualitative Spanish study of 17 HEMS professionals found flight nursing was seen as a highly specialised profile requiring critical-care experience, advanced technical skills, aviation safety training and structured in-person education — with no formalised national training pathway.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Spain runs a physician-and-nurse HEMS model unlike Australian flight services, but the emphasis on critical-care depth, CRM and aviation safety echoes what Australian aeromedical retrieval training already requires.
papers.design: Qualitative study (phenomenologically informed thematic analysis)
papers.n: 17 HEMS professionals interviewed
papers.finding: Four themes: access to the HEMS environment, technical competencies, professional role development and structured professionalisation; online-only training widely seen as insufficient
papers.caveat: Small purposive sample in a single country's physician-staffed system; perception-based, no outcome data
papers.shortTitle: What makes a HEMS nurse: Spanish views
papers.learningGoal: Understand what critical care and aviation competencies underpin safe aeromedical retrieval practice in Australia.
