papers.title: Prehospital predictors of clinical outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity: a JCS-ReSS report
papers.summary: A nationwide Japanese registry study of 442,630 adults with PEA out-of-hospital cardiac arrest found witnessed arrest and shorter response times predicted good neurological outcome at the scene, prehospital ROSC was the strongest predictor at hospital arrival (RR 23.31), and conversion to a shockable rhythm helped only in cardiac PEA while apparently harming non-cardiac PEA.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — PEA arrests are a daily reality for Australian crews, and adrenaline and advanced airways are standard tools across Australian ambulance services, so the prognostic signals map directly onto practice here.
papers.design: Nationwide registry cohort with time-dependent propensity score sequential matching
papers.n: 442,630 adults with OHCA and initial rhythm PEA
papers.finding: Witnessed arrest (RR 1.65) and prehospital ROSC (RR 23.31) predicted favourable neurological outcome at 1 month; rhythm conversion predicted good outcome in cardiac PEA but poor outcome in non-cardiac PEA (RR 0.73); apparent harm from adrenaline and advanced airway management attenuated after time-dependent adjustment
papers.caveat: Prognostic associations from a registry — aetiology was presumed, not confirmed, and no causality can be inferred for the rhythm-conversion findings
papers.shortTitle: Predicting outcomes in PEA cardiac arrest
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on prognosticating outcomes when managing pulseless electrical activity in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: A Drone-Integrated Artificial Intelligence-Based System for Mass-Casualty Triage and Remote Monitoring
papers.summary: A research team built and pilot-tested a drone-integrated AI system that measures heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature from drone-captured video and thermal imaging, assigns triage categories, and streams casualty data to dispatch — feasible under controlled indoor conditions.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Drone and remote-triage programs are emerging in Australia but nothing like this is in operational use — it signals where MCI triage tech is heading rather than changing anything crews do today.
papers.design: System development with pilot accuracy testing
papers.n: Not reported (pilot under controlled indoor conditions)
papers.finding: The system measured four vital signs from drone imagery via video PPG, thermal imaging and neural networks, generated triage decision support, and transmitted casualty location, vitals and triage category to response teams and dispatch
papers.caveat: Controlled indoor pilot only — accuracy on real MCI scenes with smoke, crowds and weather is untested
papers.shortTitle: Drone AI for mass-casualty triage
papers.learningGoal: Understand how drone and AI triage technologies could support mass-casualty response across Australian contexts.

papers.title: Trends in Australian Alcohol Consumption and Related Harms, 2010-2023
papers.summary: An Australian synthesis of national data from 2010 to 2023 found survey and wastewater measures of alcohol consumption generally declined while most alcohol-related harms — including ambulance attendances — increased substantially, questioning the validity of population surveys.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — This is Australian national data with ambulance attendances as a core harm measure — rising alcohol harm is frontline demand every crew sees on a Saturday night.
papers.design: Joinpoint regression analysis of multiple national indicator datasets
papers.n: 13 years of national Australian data across consumption, wastewater and harm measures
papers.finding: Survey and wastewater consumption measures declined from 2010 while rates of most alcohol-related harms, including ambulance attendances, increased substantially
papers.caveat: Aggregated population-level indicators — no link to individual presentations, and differing measures make trends hard to align
papers.shortTitle: Australian alcohol harms keep rising
papers.learningGoal: Understand how rising alcohol-related harms despite declining consumption shape my paramedic practice and system demand.

papers.title: ‘Interprofessional simulation in paramedicine education: Student perceptions of role identity, communication and collaboration’
papers.summary: An Australian exploratory qualitative study of undergraduate paramedic, nursing and medical students found an interprofessional simulation event challenged assumptions about professional hierarchy and role identity, prompting students to reconsider advocacy, handover and assertive communication.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Interprofessional simulation is well established in Australian paramedic programs, so this adds texture to what students take from it rather than pointing to anything new for services.
papers.design: Exploratory descriptive qualitative study (single focus group, reflexive thematic analysis)
papers.n: One focus group of undergraduate paramedic students
papers.finding: Two themes emerged — Negotiating Professional Authority and Preparing for Collaborative Practice — with students reporting the simulation reshaped how they enacted the paramedic role, particularly around advocacy, handover and assertive communication
papers.caveat: Single focus group; the abstract doesn't report the sample size or sites, so perspectives may not generalise
papers.shortTitle: Interprofessional simulation shapes student identity
papers.learningGoal: Understand how interprofessional learning shapes my role identity, advocacy and assertiveness during handover and collaborative practice.

papers.title: Race, Gender, and Survival: a Scoping Review of Disparities in ICU Post-Resuscitation Care and Neurological Outcomes Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
papers.journal: Journal of Racial and Ethnic Health Disparities
papers.summary: Scoping review of 15 studies found Black women in the US received less bystander CPR, slower emergency response, less ICU intervention and more early DNR/withdrawal decisions after OHCA, with the disparities compounding across the chain of survival.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The equity mechanics — bystander CPR gaps and treatment-withdrawal patterns — are a useful mirror for any service auditing its own outcomes data, though the US race-specific findings don't transfer directly to Australian population groups.
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how patient demographics may shape resuscitation care and withdrawal decisions in my own practice.

papers.title: Establishing a regional prehospital whole blood program in a border community: the Trauma Regional Advisory Council-V initiative in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas
papers.summary: Implementation report describing how four Texas border counties built a regional prehospital whole blood program across eight domains — governance, MOUs, rotation systems, provider credentialing and grant-funded equipment for rural agencies.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Prehospital blood is carried by three of seven Australian services and not ACTAS, so this is a playbook for services considering it rather than practice guidance for crews who don't carry blood.
papers.learningGoal: Understand the governance and system factors needed to build regional prehospital blood programs across jurisdictions.

papers.title: EMS response time and patient outcomes in high-acuity emergency responses: a Danish matched cohort study
papers.summary: Danish matched cohort of 171,708 highest-priority (A-level) responses in Region Zealand tested whether EMS response times affect outcomes — mortality did not rise with longer response times, and the longest-quartile group had lower 30-day (OR 0.87) and 2-day (OR 0.82) mortality than the shortest quartiles.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Response-time policy is core business for every Australian service, but this is a Danish single-region registry with matching that can't remove case-mix confounding — and the counterintuitive direction screams residual confounding, so treat it as debate fuel, not a target change.
papers.learningGoal: Understand how response time intervals relate to patient outcomes in high-acuity cases to inform my triage and dispatch judgement.

papers.title: Challenges of turning prehospital prediction of trauma-induced coagulopathy into early administration of tranexamic acid
papers.summary: Editorial using a prehospital machine-learning risk model for trauma-induced coagulopathy found medium- and higher-risk patients still frequently miss tranexamic acid within the 1-hour window, arguing better risk stratification should close the evidence-to-practice gap.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The TXA-in-trauma message travels, but with a twist for Australia: six of seven harvested services carry TXA and ACTAS doesn't, so for local crews this is recognition-and-destination thinking rather than a drug decision — and it's an editorial, not new data.
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my judgement on identifying trauma patients who benefit from early tranexamic acid before arrival at hospital.

papers.title: Emergency Department Operational Measures Associated with EMS Redirection Activation and Duration
papers.summary: Single-centre New York study over 392 days found EMS ambulance redirection activated on 63.8% of days, with ED visit volume associated with activation and door-to-room time associated with both activation and cumulative duration — but boarding and admissions were not.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Hospital redirect is a live access issue for Australian crews, though US central redirection mechanics differ from local hospital-bypass arrangements.
papers.learningGoal: Understand how emergency department crowding measures relate to ambulance redirection decisions and my handover practice.

papers.title: Prehospital Risk Stratification for Early Transfusion in Pediatric Trauma: A National Trauma Data Bank Analysis
papers.summary: Retrospective national trauma registry analysis testing five EMS-observable findings for spotting injured children who need early blood — altered GCS (aOR 8.38), penetrating mechanism (aOR 5.87) and age-adjusted hypotension (aOR 5.39) led, and a three-tier decision tree put 36.8% of early transfusions into just 3.3% of kids.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — The five predictors are basic observations any crew already takes, but prehospital blood is limited to a handful of Australian services, so for most crews this is a destination-and-warning tool rather than a transfusion trigger.
papers.design: Retrospective registry cohort with decision-tree (CART) analysis
papers.n: 79,764 EMS-transported children aged 1–15
papers.finding: All five predictors independently predicted blood within 4 h of ED arrival; low/intermediate/high CART tiers had 1.2%/6.1%/36.7% transfusion rates, and the high-risk tier captured 36.8% of all early transfusions
papers.caveat: The outcome is in-hospital transfusion rather than prehospital shock, and children missing prehospital vitals were excluded.
papers.shortTitle: Five scene findings flag kids needing blood
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my ability to recognise scene findings in injured children that signal a need for early blood product transfusion.

papers.title: Decreasing response phase lights and siren use through modification of dispatch priority response for 9-1-1 responses to personal emergency response system activations: an interventional study
papers.summary: Before-after study switching medical-alert (PERS) activations to non-lights-and-siren dispatch — L&S response fell from 98% to 12% of calls and response-phase L&S hours dropped 86%, with only 0.2% of calls later needing an upgrade to L&S transport.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Response-mode assignment and lights-and-siren policy are universal operational levers, and community alarm activations are a low-acuity call type every Australian service handles.
papers.design: Retrospective pre-post interventional analysis with interrupted time series
papers.n: 3,262 PERS activations (1,634 pre, 1,628 post)
papers.finding: L&S response fell from 98% to 12% of calls and total response-phase L&S hours from 172 to 24 per month (−86%); 4 post-change calls (0.2%) needed L&S transport, only 1 requiring advanced interventions
papers.caveat: Single-agency before-after design with no concurrent control, and the very low acuity of these calls makes harm hard to detect.
papers.shortTitle: Ditch lights and sirens for fall-alarm calls
papers.learningGoal: Understand how dispatch triage for personal emergency response activations can reduce lights and siren risk without compromising patient safety.

papers.title: Prehospital extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a protocol for the Rapid prehospital ACcess to ECPR in Prague (RACE Prague) single-arm pilot feasibility study
papers.summary: Protocol for a single-arm pilot dispatching a mobile ECPR team to cannulate refractory OHCA patients at the scene, aiming to cut collapse-to-flow from the ~60 minutes typical of in-hospital ECPR by at least 15 minutes.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — A physician-staffed mobile cannulation team is a highly specialised model that doesn't map onto Australian ambulance systems; worth watching as the prehospital ECPR evidence builds.
papers.design: Single-arm pilot feasibility trial protocol
papers.n: 20 adults with witnessed refractory OHCA
papers.finding: Primary endpoint is collapse-to-ECMO flow time (target ≥15 min shorter than in-hospital ECPR), tested against historical and contemporaneous in-hospital cohorts; results not yet available
papers.caveat: Single-centre, single-arm feasibility design with no randomised comparison.
papers.shortTitle: Mobile ECPR team cannulates on scene
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the practicality and potential benefit of prehospital ECPR cannulation for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Australia.

papers.title: Health system readiness for out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest management in resource limited settings: A mixed-method study from rural and suburban Sindh, Pakistan
papers.summary: Mixed-methods assessment of the OHCA chain of survival in rural and suburban Sindh found no functional defibrillator across seven hospitals, gaps in basic resuscitation equipment and ambulance availability, and poor community recognition of cardiac arrest.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — A low-resource health system with major infrastructure and access barriers — it describes a chain-of-survival gap, not anything comparable to Australian ambulance practice.
papers.design: Mixed-methods (exit interviews, facility readiness checklist, focus groups and interviews)
papers.n: 163 patient exit interviews and 7 hospitals
papers.finding: Defibrillators present in 2 of 7 hospitals but neither functional, laryngeal mask airways unavailable in all facilities, and satisfaction lowest for communication (26.4%) and financial aspects (31.3%)
papers.caveat: Small facility sample in a very different low-resource setting.
papers.shortTitle: Cardiac arrest systems not ready in rural Pakistan
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how equipment and system gaps across the chain of survival shape out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes.

papers.title: "It's Scary, but I Handle It": A Qualitative Study on Severe Hypoglycemia Experiences and Reasons for Declining to Participate in a Community Paramedicine Trial to Prevent Hypoglycemia Among People With Diabetes
papers.summary: Qualitative interviews with adults who declined a community paramedicine hypoglycaemia-prevention program found they normalised severe episodes within their own management routines — time constraints (56%), perceived lack of benefit (25%) and privacy concerns about home visits (25%) kept them out.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Community paramedicine programs vary widely across Australia, but the recruitment and privacy barriers are the kind any extended-care or call-back model here would hit.
papers.design: Qualitative interview study (thematic analysis)
papers.n: 16 adults with diabetes after EMS-attended severe hypoglycaemia
papers.finding: Non-participation reasons: time constraints 56%, perceived lack of benefit 25%, privacy concerns or discomfort with home visits 25%
papers.caveat: Small US sample of program decliners only — no perspective from those who enrolled.
papers.shortTitle: Why patients decline hypoglycaemia call-back programs
papers.learningGoal: Understand why patients decline community paramedicine hypoglycaemia follow-up and how privacy and trust shape engagement.

papers.title: Factors associated with death before EMS arrival among emergency medical services-attended self-directed violence cases in southern Iran: a cross-sectional study
papers.summary: An Iranian cross-sectional study of 2,280 EMS-attended self-directed violence cases found 5.4% died before EMS arrival, with higher odds in rural locations (aOR 2.08), older patients (aOR 1.03/year) and morning calls (aOR 2.14 vs evening).
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — From a different system with variable ambulance access, but the pattern — rural cases and time-of-day delays in reaching live patients — speaks to response-interval equity issues Australian services also face.
papers.design: Cross-sectional analysis of EMS registry records with multivariable logistic regression
papers.n: 2,280 EMS-attended self-directed violence cases (124 dead on arrival)
papers.finding: Death before EMS arrival associated with rural location (aOR 2.075, 95% CI 1.208–3.564), increasing age (aOR 1.028) and morning (aOR 2.140) and afternoon (aOR 1.882) calls versus evening
papers.caveat: Registry-only data from one Iranian province with no clinical detail on mechanism, lethality or bystander response
papers.shortTitle: Rural self-harm deaths before ambulance arrival
papers.learningGoal: Recognise which patients experiencing self-directed violence face higher risk of death before ambulance arrival.

papers.title: Advanced airway management practice patterns and short-term survival in Poland’s national physician-staffed helicopter emergency medical service, 2020–2024: a retrospective observational study
papers.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
papers.summary: A retrospective analysis of Poland's national physician-staffed HEMS registry tested airway strategies in 8,980 intubated adults against survival to hospital handover — HEMS-performed intubation was most common (49.8%), and in non-traumatic cardiac arrest a sequential supraglottic-airway-then-intubation strategy showed no significant difference from HEMS-performed intubation, while some other strategies carried higher unadjusted odds of not being alive at handover.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Delivered by a physician-staffed HEMS crew, a model Australian services don't run — but the questions it speaks to (intubation vs supraglottic first, and who performs the intubation) sit squarely in the intensive care paramedic skill set across Australia.
papers.design: Retrospective national HEMS registry cohort
papers.n: 8,980 adults requiring advanced airway management
papers.finding: HEMS-performed intubation was the most common strategy (49.8%); sequential supraglottic-to-intubation did not differ significantly from HEMS-performed intubation in non-traumatic cardiac arrest; 32.9% were not alive at hospital handover
papers.caveat: Univariate analyses only, so strategy effects are confounded by patient severity, and the physician-staffed setting limits direct comparison with paramedic-only systems
papers.shortTitle: Airway strategy and survival in Polish HEMS
papers.learningGoal: Weigh a sequential supraglottic airway approach against primary intubation when managing advanced airways in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Prehospital Point-of-Care GFAP for Detection of Intracranial Hemorrhage in Acute Nontraumatic Coma
papers.summary: A UK physician-paramedic HEMS team tested whether prehospital point-of-care GFAP and UCH-L1 blood tests could detect intracranial haemorrhage in comatose patients — GFAP performed strongly (97% sensitivity, AUC 0.94), UCH-L1 less so.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Point-of-care brain biomarker testing isn't something Australian ambulances carry, and the cohort came from a physician-staffed helicopter service already inducing patients — adoption here would need a guideline change and a very different crew model.
papers.design: Diagnostic accuracy study (prehospital point-of-care biomarkers vs CT)
papers.n: 65 adults with acute nontraumatic coma (GCS ≤12)
papers.finding: POC GFAP detected ICH with 97.0% sensitivity (95% CI 84.2–99.9%) and AUC 0.94; ICH was present in 51% of patients and 30-day survival was 46%.
papers.caveat: Small, highly selected cohort — physician-staffed HEMS patients with suspected ICH already undergoing prehospital RSI.
papers.shortTitle: POC GFAP for brain haemorrhage in coma
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of point-of-care biomarkers like GFAP when assessing comatose patients with suspected intracranial haemorrhage.

papers.title: Decreased Early Bystander CPR Initiation Despite Stable Overall Rates: A Nationwide Time-to-Event Analysis During the COVID-19 Pandemic
papers.summary: A time-to-event analysis of the All-Japan Utstein registry found overall bystander CPR rates stayed stable through the pandemic, but initiation within 10 minutes slipped — and earlier starts sharply improved neurological outcomes (aOR 3.27 for 0–3 min vs >10 min).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Bystander CPR timing sits at the front of every Australian chain of survival, and this is one of the largest OHCA registries anywhere, so the timing–outcome gradient travels directly.
papers.design: Retrospective nationwide registry cohort with time-to-event analysis
papers.n: 56,082 layperson-witnessed non-traumatic OHCAs
papers.finding: Overall bystander CPR was stable (58.7% vs 58.6%), but early initiation fell during the pandemic (aHR 0.96); CPR started at 0–3 min carried aOR 3.27 for favourable neurological outcome at 1 month versus >10 min.
papers.caveat: Pandemic-era comparison; the timing–outcome link is associative and residual confounding (dispatch, case mix) can't be excluded.
papers.shortTitle: Every minute counts: early bystander CPR
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my dispatch coaching techniques so bystanders start CPR earlier in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

papers.title: Sports-Related Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest due to External Causes, Including Commotio Cordis, at Schools in Japan
papers.summary: A nationwide Japanese school-sports database reconstructed 30 sports-related OHCAs from external causes and found commotio cordis cases did dramatically better when AEDs were applied fast — 80% favourable neurological outcome — while other external causes fared poorly.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — School and sporting-ground AED response is the same public-access defibrillation landscape Australian crews work within, so the mechanism-to-response lessons apply directly.
papers.design: Nationwide registry case series (SPIRITS database, 2008–2022)
papers.n: 30 cases of sports-related OHCA from external causes
papers.finding: Among 15 commotio cordis cases, AED pads were applied in 93%, shocks in 87%, and 80% achieved favourable neurological outcome; among the other 15 external-cause cases, shocks were rare (7%) and just 7% had favourable outcomes.
papers.caveat: Only 30 cases across 15 years — descriptive data that can't establish causality for the AED programmes.
papers.shortTitle: Commotio cordis outcomes hinge on fast AED
papers.learningGoal: Recognise commotio cordis after chest impact in young athletes and act quickly to apply defibrillation.

papers.title: Prehospital qSOFA Is Associated with 30-Day Mortality Within Emergency Department Triage Strata in Ambulance-Transported Adults with Suspected Infection: An Exploratory Three-Year Retrospective Cohort Study
papers.summary: A Turkish retrospective cohort tested whether the prehospital qSOFA already recorded on the chart adds prognostic information for ambulance-transported suspected infection — it predicted 30-day mortality within every ED triage stratum but added almost nothing to a full arrival model (ΔAUC 0.007).
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — qSOFA needs nothing but the vitals any Australian crew already records, so the question of what that field score tells the receiving hospital applies everywhere.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre cohort
papers.n: 1,077 adults with suspected infection transported by ambulance
papers.finding: Within ED triage strata, a prehospital qSOFA ≥2 roughly doubled the odds of 30-day death (aOR 2.06 triage-negative, 1.84 triage-positive), but added only 0.007 AUC beyond arrival vitals and labs.
papers.caveat: Single Turkish centre with 58% of eligible patients excluded, so selection bias is a serious risk.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital qSOFA adds a little prognostic signal
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the value of prehospital qSOFA alongside triage vitals when judging mortality risk in suspected sepsis.

papers.title: Contemporary Approaches to Prehospital Acute Coronary Syndrome Risk Stratification: A Narrative Review
papers.summary: A narrative review of prehospital ACS risk stratification found HEART-derived pathways combined with point-of-care troponin carry the strongest evidence for safe field risk assessment, while AI-assisted ECG interpretation remains promising but prospectively unvalidated.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Prehospital ECG acquisition and chest-pain triage pathways are standard across Australian services, so the review's map of what works — and what's still unproven — reads directly onto local practice.
papers.design: Narrative review
papers.n: Literature 2020–2025 plus grey literature and citation review
papers.finding: Biomarker-integrated pathways (HEART-derived approaches with point-of-care troponin) showed the strongest evidence for safe prehospital risk assessment; ECG transmission remains foundational for STEMI activation and AI decision-support lacks prospective outcome-based validation.
papers.caveat: Narrative rather than systematic — no protocol, formal search strategy or quality appraisal.
papers.shortTitle: Prehospital ACS risk stratification: the evidence
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the role of biomarker-integrated pathways and point-of-care troponin against ECG-based assessment in prehospital ACS risk stratification.

papers.title: Emergency medical services (EMS) professionals: Unpacking anxiety, burnout, depression, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and social support perceptions
papers.summary: A cross-sectional survey of 315 EMS professionals found burnout, anxiety and depression each tracked with higher suicidal risk, with elevated scores among respondents outside the male/female binary.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Ambulance workforce mental health is a cross-service issue, and the burnout–suicidal-risk link speaks to any service's wellbeing programme.
papers.design: Cross-sectional online survey
papers.n: 315 EMS professionals
papers.finding: Higher scores on anxiety, depression and all burnout domains corresponded with higher suicidal risk on the SBQ-R, with elevated risk among gender-diverse respondents.
papers.caveat: Cross-sectional self-selected survey — associations only, no causation.
papers.shortTitle: Burnout linked to suicidal risk in EMS
papers.learningGoal: Understand how burnout, anxiety and depression contribute to suicidal risk in the paramedic workforce, including gender-diverse colleagues.

papers.title: Ambulance professionals’ perceptions of teamwork and patient safety culture: a TeamSTEPPS intervention study
papers.summary: A Norwegian TeamSTEPPS programme for ambulance staff measured teamwork and safety-culture perceptions at baseline, 4 and 12 months — and found no statistically significant change in any dimension despite the structured training.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Structured team-training programmes are common across Australian ambulance services, so a well-conducted null result is directly relevant to anyone selling the next training package.
papers.design: Repeated cross-sectional questionnaire study within a team-training intervention
papers.n: 90 ambulance professionals at baseline (104 eligible)
papers.finding: No statistically significant changes in any teamwork or patient-safety dimension at 4 or 12 months; error reporting scored lowest (mean 2.56) at baseline.
papers.caveat: No control group and response rates fell from 87% to 53% across the time points.
papers.shortTitle: TeamSTEPPS training shows no measurable gain
papers.learningGoal: Understand why structured teamwork training may fail to shift patient safety culture in paramedic practice.

papers.title: Paramedics' Perceptions and Experiences Providing End-of-Life Care: A Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.summary: A UK survey of 182 paramedics found end-of-life care in the community is undermined by practical gaps — 54% often had no access to the medicines they needed, 88% couldn't reach advance care planning documentation, and only 28% felt competent in the role.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — Community palliative response is a growing part of Australian ambulance work, and the barriers — missing ACP documents, no symptom-control medicines, out-of-hours isolation — map closely onto local experience.
papers.design: Cross-sectional online survey
papers.n: 182 paramedics (34% response rate)
papers.finding: 54% 'always/often' lacked symptom-control medicines, 88% lacked access to advance care planning documentation, 67% reported inadequate pre-registration end-of-life education and only 28% felt very or extremely competent.
papers.caveat: One UK region with a 34% response rate — respondents plausibly more engaged with the topic than average.
papers.shortTitle: Paramedics strained by end-of-life care gaps
papers.learningGoal: Understand the workforce and education factors that shape paramedic confidence in providing end-of-life care.

papers.title: Overtriage of a physician-staffed prehospital emergency resource in Austria : An exploratory retrospective analysis
papers.summary: A retrospective Austrian analysis of 3,454 dispatches of a physician-staffed response vehicle found 76% met retrospective overtriage criteria, and dispatch priority didn't predict appropriateness at all.
papers.relevance: 🔴 Low — Physician-staffed response vehicles aren't part of the Australian ambulance model — this informs dispatch-accuracy debates generally, not current practice.
papers.design: Retrospective single-centre analysis
papers.n: 3,454 primary dispatches over one year
papers.finding: 76.1% of dispatches were retrospectively classified as overtriage (38% with no patient contact); priority level showed no association with appropriateness.
papers.caveat: Retrospective design with appropriateness criteria defined after the fact, at a single service.
papers.shortTitle: Most physician-unit dispatches are overtriage
papers.learningGoal: Understand how dispatch triage criteria affect appropriate use of advanced prehospital resources in Australian settings.

papers.title: Effect of Orientation and Contact Area on Leg-Foot Chest Compression Quality: A Simulation Study
papers.summary: A manikin study of leg-delivered chest compressions found the heel-of-foot technique achieved deeper and more often guideline-adequate compressions than the ball of the foot, with foot orientation making no difference.
papers.relevance: 🟢 High — CPR quality standards are identical across Australian services, so any alternative technique for exhausted or position-limited rescuers is worth knowing about.
papers.design: 2×2 mixed-design simulation study
papers.n: 80 healthcare professionals
papers.finding: Heel technique gave greater mean depth (54.2 vs 51.6 mm) and more adequate-depth compressions (81.8% vs 72.7%); rate, recoil and exertion were comparable and orientation didn't matter.
papers.caveat: Manikin study with healthcare professionals — no clinical outcomes and untested on real arrests.
papers.shortTitle: Heel-of-foot compressions beat ball-of-foot
papers.learningGoal: Weigh the heel-of-foot technique for delivering chest compressions when limited rescuer access restricts standard compressions.

papers.title: Unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries: Insights from 3473 births of a 13-year prospective cohort study in France
papers.summary: A companion French registry analysis of 3,473 unplanned out-of-hospital births found maternal complications in 8.4% and perinatal complications in 4.4%, with preterm birth and neonatal hypothermia — which affected 63% of newborns — the main risk factors.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Neonatal warming is squarely within paramedic control wherever births happen before arrival, making the hypothermia finding actionable here even though the delivering system is physician-staffed.
papers.design: Prospective registry cohort
papers.n: 3,473 unplanned out-of-hospital deliveries (2011–2024)
papers.finding: Neonatal hypothermia affected 63% of newborns and was independently associated with complications (aOR 1.74); birth before 32 weeks carried aOR 25.21 for complications, and birth before the medical team arrived doubled on-site hypothermia risk (aOR 2.02)
papers.caveat: Only 79 of 402 French units contributed, and travel times in France may not reflect Australian geography
papers.shortTitle: Hypothermia common after unplanned out-of-hospital birth
papers.learningGoal: Strengthen my thermothermal care of newborns after unplanned out-of-hospital birth, especially preterm deliveries.

papers.title: Insomnia Severity and Its Demographic and Health-Related Correlates Among Paramedic Students in Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.summary: A cross-sectional study of 238 Saudi paramedic students found subthreshold insomnia on average (mean ISI 11.8), worse in single students and those at private universities or with chronic or mental illness.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — Saudi paramedic education differs from Australia's, but sleep disturbance in ambulance students mirrors concerns in Australian paramedic cohorts and is a fair reminder that sleep health belongs in training.
papers.design: Cross-sectional survey
papers.n: 238 EMS students
papers.finding: Mean Insomnia Severity Index 11.8 ± 5.3; higher in single vs married students (12.1 vs 7.4, p = 0.005) and private vs public university students (19.3 vs 11.6, p = 0.001)
papers.caveat: Self-report, single country, and no measure of clinical placement or shift exposure
papers.shortTitle: Insomnia common in paramedic students
papers.learningGoal: Recognise how student and early-career stressors contribute to insomnia across the paramedic workforce.

papers.title: Circadian and Seasonal Patterns of Recorded Emergency Medical Service Workload by Diagnostic Category: A Two-Year Retrospective Analysis with Forecasting from Türkiye
papers.summary: A two-year Turkish analysis of 60,811 EMS case records found demand peaked at 21:00 at 3.53 times the 06:00 trough, with circadian rhythmicity in all seven clinical groups and workable short-term demand forecasts.
papers.relevance: 🟡 Medium — A Turkish provincial system, but diurnal and seasonal demand rhythms are operationally relevant to Australian ambulance rostering and demand planning.
papers.design: Retrospective analysis with cosinor and ARIMA forecasting
papers.n: 60,811 EMS case records over 731 days
papers.finding: Volume peaked at 21:00 (adjusted 3.53× the 06:00 low, 95% CI 3.28–3.81); circadian rhythms detected in all seven clinical groups; frozen 2024 forecasts transferred to 2025
papers.caveat: Case-record volume as a proxy for demand, single province, and low explained variance for hour-date variation
papers.shortTitle: Ambulance demand peaks at 9pm
papers.learningGoal: Understand how circadian and seasonal demand patterns shape ambulance resource planning across Australian systems.

topPicks.title: Prehospital Extracorporeal Life Support in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
topPicks.authors: Reis Miranda D, Moors X, Ali S, et al.
topPicks.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
topPicks.summary: A nationwide Dutch cohort of 231 adults 50 or younger with refractory OHCA found survival to discharge of 40% with prehospital ECPR-capable HEMS versus 20% with conventional HEMS, and six-month favourable neurological outcome of 36% versus 13%.
topPicks.relevance: 🟡 Medium transferability — prehospital ECPR sits on physician-staffed helicopter services well beyond Australian road practice, so this shapes where the evidence is heading, not what crews do today.
topPicks.featuredReason: The strongest evidence yet that taking the ECMO team to the patient changes the ceiling for refractory arrest — survival doubled and good neurology tripled, though not randomised and with nearly three times the adverse events.
topPicks.n: 231 adults ≤ 50 with refractory OHCA (144 ECPR-capable HEMS vs 87 conventional)
topPicks.finding: Survival to discharge 40% with ECPR vs 20% without (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.59–4.66); favourable neurological outcome at 6 months 36% vs 13% (OR 4.22, 95% CI 2.82–6.32); 32 adverse events with ECPR vs 11
topPicks.caveat: Not randomised — patients attended by ECPR-capable HEMS may differ systematically, and the ECPR group had nearly three times the adverse events
topPicks.shortTitle: Prehospital ECPR linked to doubled arrest survival
topPicks.learningGoal: Weigh the benefits and harms of prehospital ECPR for young adults in refractory cardiac arrest.

topPicks.title: Community and EMS Interventions to Improve Survival in Cardiac Arrest
topPicks.authors: Malta Hansen C, Krychtiuk KA, Starks MA, et al.
topPicks.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
topPicks.summary: A cluster-randomised trial across 55 North Carolina county clusters (22,459 OHCA patients) found a multifaceted community and EMS programme did not improve survival with good neurological outcome (9.0% vs 9.4%, adjusted OR 0.97).
topPicks.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — dispatch recognition, telephone CPR, community training and first-responder AEDs are core parts of Australian systems, making this large null trial directly relevant.
topPicks.featuredReason: A sobering, rigorous check on the system-level bundle everyone invests in: nothing moved. It can't say which component underperformed, but it questions whether adding more of the same changes outcomes.
topPicks.design: Registry-based cluster-randomised trial (CARES registry, North Carolina)
topPicks.n: 22,459 adults with OHCA across 55 county clusters
topPicks.finding: Survival to discharge with good neurological outcome 9.0% (intervention) vs 9.4% (usual care), adjusted OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.75–1.26, P = 0.80
topPicks.caveat: The intervention bundled four components, so it can't show whether one element — such as telecommunicator CPR instructions — underperformed
topPicks.shortTitle: Big community arrest programme didn't change survival
topPicks.learningGoal: Weigh how bundled community and EMS resuscitation interventions influence survival outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.

topPicks.title: Is prehospital opioid administration safe in children? A register-based study
topPicks.authors: Skøtt VN, Oldin NN, Colding-Jørgensen JT, et al.
topPicks.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine
topPicks.summary: A Danish register study of 1,531 children given prehospital opioids (99.7% fentanyl) found 15.1% with at least one sign compatible with opioid adverse effects, serious signs rare (bradycardia and respiratory depression 0.7% each), and 63.6% still in pain at hospital arrival.
topPicks.relevance: 🟢 High transferability — fentanyl is standard prehospital analgesia across Australian services, and a whole-of-country registry speaks directly to how crews dose paediatric pain relief.
topPicks.featuredReason: Reassuring on safety — serious adverse effects under 1% and no antidote given — but two-thirds of kids arriving still in pain means the real story may be under-treatment, not over-treatment.
topPicks.design: Retrospective register-based cohort with medical record review
topPicks.n: 1,531 children aged 0–14 given prehospital opioids, Denmark 2017–2022
topPicks.finding: 15.1% had at least one clinical sign compatible with opioid-related adverse effects; bradycardia 0.7%, respiratory depression 0.7%; no opioid antidote given; 63.6% in pain at arrival and 51% received further in-hospital analgesia.
topPicks.caveat: Retrospective register review — nonspecific signs such as nausea and drowsiness can't be firmly attributed to opioids (no other explanation identified in 9.2%).
topPicks.shortTitle: Paediatric prehospital fentanyl: serious adverse effects rare
topPicks.learningGoal: Refine my assessment and monitoring of prehospital opioid analgesia in paediatric patients to reduce under-treatment of pain.
